AN ANECDOTE OF PETER COOPER.—One day he stape watching the portrait class, who, to the number of thirty pupils or more, were drawing likenesses of the same model from different positions. One scholar made the face in pro- file, another had it turned a little into the shadow, a third saw more of the full face, while others worked still farther into or away from the light. He had stool observing the scene for a few minutes, when he said, "Such a sight as this should be a lesson in charity, when we peiceive how the same person may be so different, according to the way he is looked at by various people." A Dom CALLED "Jo."—Now all this time Joe himself lay perfectly tranqail. Joe had enjoyed his morning's walk; he enjoyed now his stretch by the river. But this peaceful demeanour was in no,manner caused by any ignorance or ' stupidity on his part. Joe was not impervious to the signs of violent grief shown by Susie last night; he had heard Toby's little confident speech; he now watched that hand- kerchief made so heavy with stones. It is my own private opinion that Joe knew the English language perfectly. It is certain that he guessed that his master was going to drown him. The fact did not trouble him much, for the simple reason that he had not the faintest intention of al- lowing himself to be drowned He glanced at the water, he glanced at the stones; the water was to Joe as his native element. He was not at all disturbed. At last Marshall, angry with himself for feeling any softness, rose to his feet, fastened the fatal handkerchief firmly round Joe's neck, and sent him over the bank into the stream. The river here was both rapid and deep, and in the ordinary course of things Joe ought to sink at once. But he did not. He was a powerfully strong creature. Piteous and struggling, for in- deed his danger was great, he managed to reach a part of the river where he could regain his footing. Here he suc- ceeded, not in getting rid of th- handkerchief, but in biting a hole in it with his sharp teeth. The stones began to topple out; the weight was not so great. But now a fur- ther weapon was brought to fight agairst the true fellow's life. Marshall, rendered furious by yielding to his cruelty, ana seeing Joe might escape, flew at the dog, and tried to hurl heavy stones at him from the shore. One of these did hit the poor creature, who gave a piteous cry, but still swam away bravely. Suddenly there was another cry, one long and terified —a hum en cry-. Joe turned at the sound. Marshall, in flinging that lost stone which had hit Joe hard, had overbalanced himself, and in half an instant was strug- gling in the water. Now Marshall, a born Londoner, knew nothing about swimming. He had a horrible moment of fear; all his life seemed to rise before him. He saw the deed he had just committed something as God sees it; he felt the water close over his head, he give a most bitter and terrified cry, then he. remembered no more. . . . A few moments later, a little crowd of eager and admiring specta- tors were clustered round a man who lay dripping, and ass parently drowned, on the grass, while a greet Newfoundlasd dog, with a red handkerchief fastened to his neck, and a great gash in his shouPer, stood over him. The dog had saved the man. That man was John Marshall; the dog was Joe.—From the Christmas Number of" The Quiver." CARLYLE UPON PORTRAITS.—It is commonly supposed that Carlyle was indifferent to art:e's .sts. re would be little difficulty in showing from his works that this is far from being the case and that he could see the beauty of plastic art as vividly as any of his contem- porarite Where be differed from most of them was in thinking it of relatively less importance than they were in- clined to do. Only the most complete ignorance of his work, however, could lead any one to think that he wanted either taste or insight in the matter of portrait-painting. On the contrary, he loved good portraits, and sought for them eagerly. We have all heard of the "Frederick" screen prepared by his wife so that he might have the bodily presentment of the men about whom he was writing continually before his eyes. In judging works of this class he showed a remarkable sense of the value of technical skill. An excellent instance of his sagacity in estimating the value of a portrait is to be found In what be wrote to Emerson about the drawing which was to be chosen for the American edition. Thus does he recommend one done by Mr. Samuel Lawrence :--" It stands thus: there is no Pieta' ter of the numbers who have wasted my time and their own with trying that has indicated any capability of catch- ing a true likeness but one Samuel Lawrence; a young painter of real talent, not quite so young now, but still Only struggling for complete mastership in the management of colours. He does crayon sketches in a way to please almost himself; but hia oil paintings, at least till within a year or two, have indicatsa only a great faculty still crude in that particular. His oil Portrait of me, which you speak of, is almost terrible to behold! It has the look of a jiitun, e of a Scandinavian demon, grim, Bad ass the angel of death —and the colouring is so brickish, the anbthing so coarse, it reminds you withal of a flayed horse's head. DEnna speak ete, Of a pirated copy of this same picture he says further on that it is a " Lais teitimut the beauty" (as Charles Lamb used to say); "a flayed horse's head without the spiritualism good or bad—and simply figures on my mind as a detesta- bility which I had much rather never have seen." In the matter of portraits, therefore, as in other things, Carlyle loved truth and hated iniquity. Those which have been published with his approval may be accepted as giving a more or less accurate representation of the original; and a study of them will kelp is to eetimate the man and his work. —"The Magazine of Art" for December. SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Sating% for conl are being made at Dardsegny, in the ens-1 ton nf Geneva. A. chain now being made at the Chain Works, Troy, New York, is to be six miles long. It is being made ef tem- inch iron rod, and is intended for some Go7ernment project not stated. Steel nails are now made in America. They can be driven into•hard as easily as into soft wood. They have even been driven into a white oak knot without bending. For hard wood flooring, for boxes, house-building, and every kind of carpentry, they are being largely used in the United States. Some carious experiments have been made on the rails laid between Marseilles and Rognac' of the Chemin de Fer Paris-Lyon-Mediterranee. It has been ascertained that all the rails that have been laid some time have been trans- formed, as to their two extremities, into powerful magnets, capable of attracting and holding iron keys and even heavier articles. The wheels of railway and other cars are now made of leather in France by a process of M. de la Roche. Un- tanned buffalo skins are cat into strips, and these are built into solid discs and strongly compressed by hydraulic presses, then bound with two iron rings. A wheel of this kind is noiseless, resists shocks, and is not liable to fracture on a journey. The French physiologists, DlM.Chambrelent andMacssous, have announced in a report to the Paris Academy of Sciences that they have at length succeeded in discovering in the milk of cows affected with inflammation of the spleen the bacillusi of that disease. They have further succeeded in their ex- periments in the reproduction of this micro-organism and in inoculating animals with it. Althongh natural history has always been the favourite science in Switzerland, the Swiss have hitherto had no 1 journal of zoology of their own. The deficency has now been supplied, the first number of the Reeueil Zoologique Suisse having made its appearance. It is edited by Pro- fessor H. Fol, the director of the laboratory of embryology at the Geneva University (Geneva and Basle, Georg.). A curious instance of the association of different orders of animals is reported from Geneva. Last year a medusa was received from Mauritius at the Geneva Museum. Beneath the umbrella-like portion of the medusa a ish of the genus Caranx was discovered by M. Lund. Inquiries since made in Mauritius have disclosed the fact that the \ Caranx appears to have a special partiality for the medusa in question, the two being almost invariably found together. The medusa in question is a venomous species, and it is in- ferred that its stinging powers afford protection to the Cara= against its special enemies. The compensation afforded by the Caranx for the hospitality thus afforded has yet to be discovered. The first two volumes of Lord Lytton's life will be in the hands of the public next week. They are divided late eight books, and embrace the period from 1803 to 1832. A correspondent sends from recollection the following stanza from a ballad by Thackeray (?), which may be found use- ful in connection with this biography, as a sort of memoria teehnica of his many names. It was evidently written at I the time of the removal of the body of Napolean from St. Helena to Paris:— Were I but Sir Edward Wiggate Balwer Lytton Balwer, Bart., I should sing the Belle Poule frigate In the highest style of art. From this it roight be gathered that the founder of the family was named Wiggate ; that he married a Bulwer, and adding Bulwer to his name, obtained the estate in Nor- folk; that subsequently a Balwer married a Lytton, and adding Lytton to his name, obtained the estate in Hertford- shire. But no doubt we shall hear all about these various names in the forthcoming volumes. THE NEW COMET.—A Naples correspondent writes : "Professor Pigorini, of the Observatory at Parma, says the comet discovered on the let September is now visible at night in the north-west near Gamma in the constellation of the Dragon. It loots like a faint nebula nearly round, having a neucleus, and also the rudiments of a tail. From calculations which have been made, it is recognised as the comet discovered by Pons in 1812, which isnow returning, after having been 600,000,000 miles distant from the sun, in May, 1848. Its shortest distance from the sun will be reached on the 25th January, and from the earth (63,000,000 miles) on the Bth January, 1884. It will be most luminous on the 11th of that month. It will then be 145 times more brilli- ant than on the day of its discovery. Its light is still very faint, and only perceptible by the telescope, but in December it will be visible to the naked eve." A STORM TRACED.—At the Meteorological Society re- cently an interesting paper was read by Mr. Chas. Harding, in which he had worked out by a number of details, obtained from the logs of over 300 ships, the entire coarse of the storm predicted by the United States Meteorological Depart- ment on Aug. 27th. Its origin was traceable to two centres of disturbance—one about 450 miles south of Bermuda, on Aug. 26th; the other to the east of the Rock Mountains on the 27th ; the two merging on the 29th at about 300 miles to the north of Bermuda, and going up the American coast to Newfoundland, whence this destructive storm crossed the Atlantic at a speed of forty miles an hour, being double the ordinary rate, and consequently arriving in England some time sooner than was foretold. This is one of the very few instances in which any tracks of storms have been veriiei as to their progress over the sea; and none of the previous attempts have been elaborated in anything like so scientific and masterly a manner.

THE ALPHABET IN A SENTENCE.—For some years the following sentence has stood as the shortest into which all the letters of the alphabet could be compressed :—" J. Grey: Pack with my box five dozen quills." The airove sentence contains thirty-three letters. A Utica gentleman recently improved on it as follows, using only thirty-twit letters :—" Quick, glad zephyrs, waft my javelin box." Geo. W. Pierce, a Boston lawyer, has now forced twenty- six letters of the alphabet into a sentence of only thirty-one letters, as below :—" Z. Badger: Thy vixen jumps quick at fowl."—American Paper. EARLY im,PrtEssroNs.—Before the child can speak it can intuitively discern truth in the actions of those about it, and later on with a deeper impression, such as if a thing promised is withheld, or an act forbidden is yet permitted to be done. So, little by little, here and there, a Child's character is built for evil or good. Domestic training can- not begin too early. The wee things can be taught to play in setting a store cupboard in order, to unpack stores, to take care of twine, of paper and nails, to have a place for everything, and to understand (in play) that if there is net a place just made for everything, things cannot be put away properly. If this instruction grows with their growth —and it is sure to do so by habit—hoot much comfort in a home there will be when the little one is a woman.—Cassell's Family Magazine. LUTHER'S HYMN.—Of what may be called the "War Songs" of Luther, his rendering of the 46th Psalm is, per- haps, the grandest and the best. This was Luther's own in- spiriting hymn when passing through his seasons of gloom and depression. Thus, at times, he would rally his friend Melancthon—"Come, Philip, let us sing the 46th Psalm 1" This has been made familiar to English ears by Miss Wink- worth's characteristic versinn-r- A sure strongholll_ our God is He,

A trusty Shield and weapon; Our help He'll be, and set us free From every ill can happen. We could almost imagine a subsequent verse of this hyms to have been written by suggestion of Luther's Own fearless words on entering the city of Worms to confront his enemies there—" If there were as many devils in Worms as there are tiles on the house-tops, still I would enter it ! " It was said of this remarkable hymn, by Thomas Carlyle. after his owls characteristic trenchant manner, "It ,has something in it like the sound of Alpine avalanches, the first murmur of earthquakes." Heine calls it "The Marseillaise of the Re- formation." To this day this noble hymn continues to be both watchword and war-cry in the Lutheran communities of the German nation. Many and many a time were its solemn and y.et jubilant cadences heard re-echoing in the bivouac and the battle-field during the Franco-German war —deep calling unto deep, on the march, and on the watch, and in the strife, during the prolonged period of siege aid sortie of those now historic days.—" The Quiver." A ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE.—A Chicago correspondent of the San Francimo Bulletin writes :—The papers have bnilded a very handsome romance out of a variety of actual facts. One year ago Alfred, Count Salm-Salm, lived in the city of Bonn, and was a student of its famous University. He was a handsome young man, 19 years of age, with un- limited resources. His father, Prince Frederick Salm-Salm, is one of the highest and wealthiest nobles of the German Empire, and titular chief of the aristocracy of Rhenish Prussia. Prince Salm-Salm, who was Colonel on the staff of General McClellan daring the late war, and at its close entered the service of Maximilian in Mexico as Adjutant- General, and subsequently fell in the service of Emperor William at the battle of Gravelotte in France during the German war, was a relative of Count Alfred. Alfred fell in love with a beautiful lady of the city of Bonn. She was also loved by another student, and the rivalry became so warm and personal that a duel was the consequence. The Prince forbade all further intercourse between his son and the lady, and publicly announced that he would no longer be responsible for the Count's debts growing out of this state of affairs. The Count quitted school and came to America. After the departure of his son, the father became penitent, and a long time having elapsed without any tidings of his son, the Prince through detectives and the press offered a large sum of money for news concerning him, but none came, and so he was given up for dead. Last week Carl Schneider, who had been a private in the King's Hus- sars, garrisoned at Bonn, met Count Alfred, both being com- mon labourers on the Illinois Central Railroad. He advised the Prince by letter, and a trusted messenger, Mr. Von Maltzahn, was despatched from Germany. Be arrived here fevf 4a3's ago. The young Count was found, the father's zorgiveness tendered, his anxiety expressed, and the con- sent of the Count obtained to return home immediately. With his old clothes of a railroad labourer he threw off the name of Frederick Reinhart, by which he was known, and with a new suit he again assumed his hereditary title— Alfred, Count Salm-Salm. He left for New York yesterday, and will sail for home at once. To make the story perfect, he has remained true to the maiden and is to marry her, though he relinquishes a portion of his future in so doing. The current *umber of the "Mineteeath Ceatury " cols- tains a suggestive little article with the somewhat peculiar title of "Our Orchards and Paraffin Oil." The text of the article is, in fact—plant fruit trees and wash them every autumn with paraffin oil. The facts quoted by the writer are striking, aid the experiment seems well worth trying. \A meeting of tenant tarmers, convened by Mr. Gillert Murray, was held last week, for the purpose of taking the prelimiaary steps towards the formation of a show and sale of Shire-bred horses at Derby. It was agreed that a show and sale be established at Derby, and that a committee be elected for the purpose of raaking the necessary arrange-

ments. In reference to the oorrespondence which has been going on with regard to the necessity of a supply of pure water to cattle, the British Medical Journal remarks that "when cattle are provided with water in tanks, agriculturists too often forget to supply them with, at the same time, a liberal supply of rock salt. It is injudicious and cruel to keep cattle without free access to salt. In their desire for saline food animals will roam far, will drink the most impure fluids, and will eat earth. That is a hint which very practical men, such as Mr. Hermann Riddell, who finds the scientific view of the deleterious effects of sewer-water on cattle highly amusing, would do well to consider in their treat- ment of cattle. THE DUKE OF WELLINGTON AND THE GROUND GAMS Am.—According to the Echo, the steward of the Duke of Wellington, at the recent rent dinner at Strathfieldsa.ye, said he wished all the tenants to abandon shooting. He did not want to prevent them having the ground game; but he wished them from henceforward to abandon the use of the gun, because it was impossible, when the keepers heard a shot, for them to know whether the shot was legal or , illegal. The Echo points out that as it is not customary for poachers to shoot in the daytime, the excuse for forbid- ding the use of the gun is a very shallow one. Of course the tenants can do as they please in the matter, so far as shooting ground game is concerned, though yearly tenants who do not wish to get notice to cult will probably con- clude that discretion is the bette: fartof valour. However this may be, the Duke's attempt to deprive his tenants of the benefit of the Ground Game Act is a very shabby one. NEW METHOD OF WASHING BUTTER.—It is stated by Dr. G. C. Caldwell that a new method of washing batter has been patented in Germany. As soon as gathered in the churn in particles about a tenth of an inch in size, it is transferred to a cetnrifugal machine, whose drum is pierced with holes and lined with a linen sack that is finally taken out with the butter. As soon as the machine is set in rapid motion the buttermilk begins to escape; a spray of water thrown into the revolving drum washes out all foreign mat- ters adhering to the batter; this washing is kept up till the wash-water comes away clean, and the revolution is then continued till the last drop of water is removed, as clothes are dried in the centrifugal wringer; the dry butter is then taken out, moulded and packed. It is claimed that the pro- duct thus so fully and quickly freed from all impurities, without any working or kneading, has a finer flavour, aroma and grain, and better keeping qualities than when prepared for market in the ordinary way. WINTER MOTHS.—Miss Ormerod, consulting entomologist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, sends to the press the following timely memorandum :—ln the early part of the summer I so often receive enquiries how to check the ravages of a green " looper" caterpillar, which is exceed- ugly destructive to leafage of many kinds of trees, aid especially hurtful:in fruit-growing districts, that it may be of service to mention that the present time, and for a few weeks onward, is the season to prevent coming attacks. The moths are now hatching, and as the females have wings which are so abortive that they are of no service, and must walk up the trunks of trees to lay, it is a sure preservation to smear the base of the trunk with a ring of anything in which these wingless moths will stick fast. I have recently had an application on the subject, and the plan of sticking the females fast on their passage is answering so well that it is possible some of your readers who have applied to me on the subject may be disposed to try this very simple method of prevention. FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE PRESCRIPTIONS.—On four successive days, give each cow the following mixture: Each dose loz. of chlorate of potash, dissolved in one quart of water; a little boiling. water is requisite to dissolve the ' potash at first. When about to administer the above, add 3drs. of camphorated spirits of wine. If the animal is very prostrate, you may, according to circumstances, increase the quantity of camphorated spirits of wine up to Bdrs. Give plenty of linseed tea, oatmeal gruel, and such like, whilst the animals are unable to eat, or they will sink for want. Half the above quantity is sufficient for calves or sheep.—Salicylic Acid.—Mr. C. Lake, of Oakley, Highans, writes :—" On the 10th inst., foot and mouth disease broke out amongst 41 yearling heifers on my farm. I thought best to let all catch it as quickly as possible, in order the sooner to get rid of it; so had them brought from the marsh into the yard, only separating those diseased hy a row of hurdles. Each beast had 11b. cattle salts when first brought up, and as much linseed cake as ic could eat daily, those infected having their share made into gruel. The mouths and feet, as they broke out, were carefully dressed, morning and evening, with a strong solutioa of salicylic acid (four and a half tablespoons to one gallon of boiliag water). The animals were also made to drink half a pint of the mixture daily, the result being that, by the 22nd inst., only twelve days after the disease first showed itself, not only had every heifer taken the complaint, but they were all perfectly. cured, the amount of conditiop lost being scarcely perceptible. The way in which the acid heals the sores, and the rapidity with which it causes a new and hare skin to form over them, is really wonderful." NORTH LANCASHIRR—It is pleasing to find that we have now a clean bill of health from foot-and-mouth ia Lonsdale North of the Sands, and that the complaint is so far dying out in the county that the Committee of Justices, at a meeting held on Monday, decided not to contilue the restrictions after the end of this month. Considering the lateness of the season, grass lands still look remarkably fresh, but, owing to the storms, cattle have to be kept indoors, and cabbages are found very useful in keeping up the flow of milk. The land is in such a sodden state that very little ley ploughing has yet been done, and not many turnips have been got off—only sufficient for wants of stock. Potatoes have yielded a sound and good crop, the favourite being the Magnum Bonum, as many of the Chant- pions are hollow in the centre, and do not keep well. They are now selling retail at sd. per stone of 141 b.; butter, is. W. to is. ; and eggs, 2d. each. At our auction mart, last week, the following prices were made :—Beef, 81al. to nd., mutton, 9d. to 101 ; lamb, 9.1 d. to 101 ; veal, Bd. to 9d. A few years ago, about Martinmas time, our sheep , markets were wont to be glutted with both store and fat sheep, and prices were very low ; but sech a state of things has not rasulted of late autumns. At present, although many farmers are so well 'off for roots, cabbage, Jrc., that they could winter many more sheep than they have, nrices are quite prohibitive of profit resulting from buying ia additional stock. Preparations are now being made for the Christmas fat stock shows, and farmers are engaged in building up tons of fat for the candle makers. It does seem strange, when one comes to think seriously about it, that a nation that cannot breed and feed sufficient flesh meat for its own wants, should annually feed so much to waste, and that prizes should be given for such superfluous fat. It shows one thing, if nothing else, that we have still a sur- plus of wealth in the land, for a poor nation could not afford such extravagance.—R., in Agricultural Gazette. UNPROFITABLE COWS IN THE DAIRY.—The following article is from the National Live Stock Journal (Chicago) : —November is a good month to weed out the dairy. The season for grazing is nearly or quite over, and the season for more costly food is at hand, when it will not pay to keep animals from which small returns only can be expected. The poor milkers and the old cows should now go. One good cow is worth two poor ones, and it costs no more to winter one than the other. The difference between superior cows and common ones was well illustrated by the experi- ence of a New York dairyman of oils acquaintance. In the rage for keeping large dairies, he crowded on to his farm sixty cows. It was all the farm could sustain, and a little more, for food had to be purchased from outside of the farm to keep them along. This was a source of improvement for the soil, but the large herd, with scanty feed, made him a deal of hard work and but little money. Though they turned out some 400 lb. of cheese to the cow each year, the owner had to squeeze every dollar that came into his hands during the year, to enable him to keep his expenses within his income. Tiring after a while of this life of toil and slavery, it occurred to him that it was better to keep a good dairy than a large one, and he resolved to make a change. He sold his entire herd of common cows, and bought in only superior ones, which he had previously "spotted" in the dairies of his neighbours, paying from 25 to 100 per cent. for them above current prices. He sold 60, but stocked anew with only 30. To these he gave the food which the larger herd had been accustomed to use, and from them made more cheese than he did from double their number. He surprised everybody with his enormous yields of cheese. His aim was to make 1,000 pounds of cheese per cow fa a year, and one year he actually overran 900 pounds to the cow. For several years he averaged over 800 to the cow. This change turned the tide of his fortune. He bgan to make money, and soon became able to let out his dairy and lire on his income. We visited his farm in the height of its proAperity. The herd was composed chiefly of cows from a cross between Ayrshires and Shorthorns—the Ayrshire blood, he said, was for milk, and the Shorthorn for size and constitution. They were certainly the finest dairy we had ever seen, giving, at the time of our visit, in June, to use his own expression, "a bushel of milk a day to the cow," and this, we are assured, they would do for three months in the best of the season. THE USES or ENSILAGE.—Mr. Easdale, a gentleman who is well known in Lancashire scientific circles, has been mak- ing some experiments with ensilage, and has brought a new phase of the subject before the public. The question of expressing the juice from the fodder is one which has oc- cupied the attention of experts for some time. That it is not the moisture but the air which needs expelling is pretty well known; but Mr. Eaadale has this year drawn off all the juice as it collects in the bottom of the silo, and he finds it oily in consistency, and a bright amber in colour. It is drawn off regularly and given to the pigs, mixed with their usual food. It does them good, and some of them do not care to feed unless they have their "gill of juice." It has been suggested that ensilage might be made by persons having land whether they have crops or not, inasmuch as they will be able to sell it when persons in the milk trade, for instance, have learned its value. To such men it will be of inestimable value, for daring winter their cows are de- prived of all succulent food but roots and grains. Ensilage being packed in such small compass it can be carried from farm to town with much greater facility than hay or green

food, and as to prise it should sell remarkably well. In all large dairies delivery would have to be made daily, just as it is with green food in spring, and this would prevent any improper chemical change in the fodder Another idea which has been thrown out, and by a gentleman of autho- rity, is that green fodder might be packed in bales as hay is packed for export. There are two systems of packing— Pilter's, of Paris, in which the bales are round, and De- decker's, in which the bales are rectangular. Take the latter. Supposing that when the fodder is cut it be put through this machine and pressed into bales of great weight and then stacked, would it keep for any length of time? We think it would not, but that even if it did the spoiled portion, that exposed to the air, would be so large a proportion of any rick that the loss would be too heavy. Mr. Easdale has proved that not only grass, clover, and oats, but ryegrass and comfrey can be properly converted into ensilage, and his igures of cost are worth noting, for the labour, includ- ing weighting, does not exceed 3s. a ton; charge on the cost of adapting and building, ed. a ton; ditto on the cost of iron weights, 9d. per ton; or in all 4s. 3d. per ton. He values good ensilage at Ns., or 108. lees than Lord Tolle- nutche. Thus as each acre gives lye to eleven tons, or six to fifteen tons, including aftermath, surely, says a corres- pondent, there is some reason in considering the system a great SUCCESS.
COTTAGE GA.R DENING.

The continuons rains have made it anything but pleasant to carry on work in tie vegetable garden, more especially on heavy soils, but ridging and trenehigg have been pushed forward when it has been dry overhead. PARSNIPS.—These we leave in the groand; but abint this
Imo we take up sufficient Es last a ni—onth or six weeks in

_ case of frost setting in aid making the ground so hard as to make it a very difficult and laborious proem to get them up. Those taken up, we place in a heap and cover with soil, adding short straw when the frost sommences, but still continue to use them from the bed as long as we can get them. Parsnips are superior in Rayons' when left undis- turbed in the ground till required. BHP CABBAGE.—As these are cut for piebling, the stumps should be removed from the ground. It is our practice to pull these and such things as savoys and brocoli up bodily and take them away to trim them, feeling sure that whee they are left in the ground they only harbour vermin, or they form a source of food for them; whilst if they are removed their sustenance is gone and there is hope of their perishing. BLACK CHRRANTS.—The pruning of these may be per- formed any time. All naked wood, or that which is devoid of young bearing wood, should be removed from the bottom, and all young wood proceeding from the base, usually termed "sinkers," should be dealt with in a similar manner, excepting where one is required to fill a gap. In pruning these, some shorten the young growth ; othersleave them their full length. The plant bears its fruit onthe young wood, but no doubt sufficient is left by those who shortea tn produce a crop. If it is necessary to inereasethe stock, the best of the pruning should be collected and tied in bundles and placed in the ground eight inches deep, till there is time to prepare them to be put ia as cuttings, which can be performed 'Very comfortably nyl the fire-side some evening, in the following manner:---Cut the base of the shoot even and just below an eye, and by shortening the other end, so as to leave twelve inches in length, the cutting ia.made, and they can be tied in bundles again till the red currants and gooseberries are ready to go in as well. We defer the pruning of these on account of the birds being very fond of picking the buds at the tips, and if they do it after we prune so mach of oar shoot is rendered useless. .Tlll4 FRUIT STORE will require attention at times. Fruit in a weak condition is mire apt to decay in mild moist weather than in cold and dry. We have been under the impression that one decaying apple or pear imparts decay to its neighbours. A writer in a periodical devoted to hor- ticulture, a short time ago, stated "that this was an erro- neous supposition, and that in turning heaps of fruit over he had frequently met with individual fruits quite decayed, and their neighbours quite sound." We ask how;would they be if left a little longer? The decayed ones had not been in that condition many days. To believe the writer would be to ignore the fact that "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump." THE FEONT GARDEN.—Creepers: These are fastened to the walls of dwellings either by nails and shreds, or wires stretched and supported by being run through galvanised eyes. We will suggest another method. Procure some cast wall nails, and if they are made hot or better still white hot, and dropped in that condition into boiled oil, they will be preserved from rusting for some time, and if they are driven into the wall 9in. each way, and angled at the same time, it will be found that the shoots are sure to be in proximity to one or the other to which they may be tied, and the nails are t• remain as a permanency. It is not wise to put too many in the walls at once, for they are only a disfigurement till covered with creepers. If borders have been prepared as we have described, Roses should do well. The most rampant growers for the purpose are the Ayrshire Roses, and they are the hardiest. The evergreen Roses (R. Sempervireus) are also well adapted, and produce their flowers in large clusters of 20 to 40 flowers in each. One of either of the above sections may be planted at each corner and taken up, so as to cover the upper part of the dwelling, selecting some of the climbing hybrid perpetuals, which are slower growers, to furnish the 'ewer part. The following have also the merit of producing good flowers:— Victor Verdier, General Jacqueminot, Jules Margottin, , Paul Neron, Annie Wood, and Chas. Lefebore. THB WINDOW.—The long winter evenings afford an ex- cellent opportunity for the cottager to construct boxes to fit on the window-sill for the purpose of containing plants to grow in, or to hold some material to plunge plants in pots to prevent them becoming dried up during very hot weather. It was our practice at one time to drill holes in the boards forming the bottom, to allow the water to pass away. This was waste of title, and now we allow spaces between the pieces from half to three-quarters of an inch, ac- cording to the number of boards and the depth of the boxes. Oyster shells or pieces of broken crocks, or even pieces of turf, in shallow boxes will answer the purpose of covering the openings and allow the water to pass. Half- inch stuff will be found sufficiently strong, but three-quarters may be used for the bottom, and if a few pieces of virgin cork are nailed on the front no planing is required, neither is there much advantage in painting them. Vallota Pur- purea (or the Scarboro' Lilly) being now at rest will not require so much water as when it is growing, just sufficient t• prevent the soil becoming dust dry. It is to be regretted that this plant is not more plentiful, so that it might be within the reach of the majority of cottagers, for it is a plant easily grown whea it is once esseiblished.

THE LAZY WORIL—AI lazy worm' as he turned over for another nap, said, " Aha! the early bird shan't catch me." He rose late. The day was hot, and before he had crawled the length of his own body he perished miserably by sun- stroke.—Moral: How often in avoiding Scylla we are wrecked on Charybdis !—Cassell's Magazine. When Sir Walter Scott was at school, a boy ix the same class was asked by the " dominie " what part of speech "with" was. "A noun, sir," said the boy. "You youig blockhead," said the pedagogne, "what example can yox give of such a thing ?" "I can tell you, sir," interrupted Scott; "you know there is a verse in the Bible which says, They bound Sampson with withs.' " A PRESENT.—Abont this time, when devoted wives and daughters are secretly plotting how to surprise "father" with a particularly fine Christmas present, John Henry's hint to his wife will meet the approbation of most heads of families. "Mrs. Henry," he said, "if you give me a Christ- mas present this year, please arrange it so that the bill won't come in until the next month. It is just as well to keep up the illusion for a short time."

ADOLPHUS GETS INSPIRRIP." Dearest, I will build thee a cot all covered with ivy, in some secluded vale close by a purling brook, meandering over its pebbly bottom, inces- santly babbling, in dulcet, tinkling strains, Love, love, love;' where the atmosphere is redolent of soothing, spicy aromas, that make the eyes languish, and the heart dissolve in the liquid fire of love; where the balmy morning zephyrs sigh in the dense forest's leafy maze, counting love's melody; where the tiny songsters that whirl in ethereal space warble nought but love. I will plant thee a garden of gorgeous loveliness, culled from nature's most ardent de- signs, and sweet smelling incense." To which Matilda re- plied, " Dolphy, dear, don't forget to leave a patch for cowcumbers and inynns —they're so nice pickled !" Loox OVER IT.-It is sail that John Wesley was once walking along a road with a brother, who related to him his troubles, saying he did not know what he should de. They were at that moment passing a stone fence to a mea- dow, over which a cow was looking. "Do you know," said Wesley, "why the cow looks over that wall 'P " Ne," replied the one in trouble." " I will tell you," said Wesley, "because she cannot look through it; and that is what you must do with your troubles; look over and above them." Depend upon it, in the midst of all the science about the world and its ways, and all the ignorance of God and His greatness, the man or woman who can say, "Thy will be done," with the true art of giving up, is nearer the secret of things than the geologist or theologian.—Geo. Mac- donald.

CHARLMAGNE.—The private life of Charlemagne was manly and simple. He despised immoderate luxury, and hated drunkenness; he was passionately fond of the chase. During dinner, he listened to music, or caused some one to read to him. He gathered round hint the best scholars of his time, and was not content with promoting education generally, but also, during the latter years of his life, at- tempted to improve his own knowledge. He learned to speak Latin easily; Greek he could understand; and he tried, though with little success, to attain the then profes- sional art of writing. The King and his friends "employed their mother•wit and their curiosity on such learning as was within their reach, relating to the processes of thought and the powers of speech, the laws of numbers and sound, and the motions of the heavenly bodies; and they called it logic, grammar, rhetoric, arithmetie, music, and astronomy." But his German nature is shown by the fact that he at- tempted to compose a German grinmar, and caused the old heroic lays, of which he was passionately fond, to be col- lected in a book. He died in 814. Unlike his father, who was nicknamed from his short stature, he measured "seven of his own feet," and was also broad and well built, with keen eyes,clear voice, and commanding features.—" Cassell's' Illustrated Universal History."
RuYAL MANCHESIER, LITERPOOL, AND NORTH LANCASHIRE AGM-- CULTURAL SOCIETY.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the above society was held at the Lion Hotel, Warrington on Wednesday. Lord Win- marleigh, president, occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. R. H. Nerrer, L. Rawstorne, G. Ashburner, G. C. Hale, Thomas Fair, Robert Lonsdale, W. Scotson, Thomas Finchett, Thos. Wilkinson, R. Webster, J. Southern, John Roberte, John White, J. T. Smith. The business was to receive balance sheet and report of council, fix upon date and place of next year's show, elect council and officers, revise rules and prizes, and other general business. . THE- SOCIETY'S SHOW FOR 1884. The CHAIRMAN first stated that it had been intimated to I him that the Mayor and a deputation from Stockport were in waiting with a view to arranging for next year's show to be held at Stockport. He therefore suggested that the qaestion of the date of the show and the place for it to be held be taken at once, and that the deputation be invited into the room. The deputation consisted of the Mayor of Stockport (Lieutenant Colonel John .McClure), and Mr. Brady, hon. secretary to the local committee of that town, and Mr. E. J. Thompson, and the CHAIRMAN asked them to state as to the provision which would be made in the event of the society holding the show at Stockport. The MAYOR Of STOCKPORT said that his town would be very glad to receive the society. They would do all they , could for the maintenance of its prosperity, and to secure the success of the forthceming show. The site selected was within four minutes walk of the Stockport station, and was near the siding of the Great-Western Railway, which would be convenient for the removalof cattle, machinery, Jac. The Stockport conatpitteo were prepared to subscribe £ll5O to the society's funds. Mr. Jove WHITE said that with regard to the date of their show it had generally been fixed for the end of September, but there was a growing feeling in the society that it would be better if it was held earlier. In September the evenings began to get short, and they lost a large amount of gate money by having to close at such an early hour in the even- ing. He should like te ask.the deputation whether August would be as equally convenient as the month of September. The MAYOR 01 STOCKPORT thought it would be a better arrangement if anything, and they would get a ranch larger number of people. The CHAIRMAN then moved a vote of thanks to the depu- tation for attending that day, and Mr. G. C. HALE' in seconding, said that in addition to the £250, he hoped the Stockport committee would consider whether they could not grant a further contribution tor special prizes. The MAYOR of STOCKPORT said they would take that into consideration. The deputation having withdrawn, The CEAIRMAN asked the meeting to decide the question as to whether the show should be held earlier in the season or not. He did not know what the feeling might be. There was a good deal to be said in favour of September, and much in favour of an earlier date. It had been discussed several times, but it had always resulted in sticking to Septeraber. Mr. Jolts WHITE moved that the society hold the next show at Stockport in the month of August. He thought it would be a much better arrangement and would be better for exhibitors, and he also reminded them that they had to shut out operatives when they closed the show early in the evening. Mr. W. iiCOTSON seconded the resolution that the show be held at Stockport, and thought August would be a much better month if they did not clash with other shows. Mr. T. Fierciewrr moved an amendment that the show be held the first week in September, because if it Look place in the middle of August as proposed farmers would be then very busy with the harvest and could not attend, whilst Cheshire cheese was not fit for exhibition until the first week in September, Mr. Joule Hegose.tr, seconded. September was the best month for exhibits of corn and roots, and as regarded the weather they had been as successful as any other society. • Mr. G. ASHBUBNER supported the amendment. On the resolution being put, the meeting decided to hold' the show at Stockport, and by a large majority, daring the first week in September, viz :—on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Mr. J. MORELN wished to know the plan pursued with regard to the arrangement of the miscellaneous stands. The SBCRETARY, in reply, said they gave the largest ex- hibitors the beet positions, and people living in or near the town in which the show was held, had even a claim before them of positions. They classified the exhibits as much as possible. Mr. MORGAN suggested that the Council should consider the advisability after appropriating the beat positions in the show, to ballot for the positions to be taken by tradesmen and others. He simply threw out the suggestion. REPORT OF THE COG/MIL. The SECRETARY read the report of the Council for the past year as follows :—" In meeting members again at the an- nual mee.ing of the society, the Council is glad to be able to report that the year's transactions have been attemded with much interest to members, and that, notwithstanding the unsettled state of the weather at the time of the show, the financial results are satisfactory. The proposal to hold the show in Liverpool was received with much favour by the Mayor, Wm. Ratcliffe, Esq., and through his good offices an influential local committee was formed, who co-operated most cordially with your Council to ensure its success. Nearly £1,600 was collected by them, and out of this stun they contributed £914 15s to the payment of prizes and the exhibition of Liverpool cart horses, and £4BO 17s 5d to- wards the expenses of the society, in addition to providing three bands of music during the show, and supplying water to the show yard free of charge. For this the best thanks of the society are due, and are hereby heartily given, to the Executive Committee, to its chairman, Halifax Wyatt, Esq., and to all the subscribers to the local fund. Members are aware that in consequence of the prevalence of foot-and- mouth disease amongst cattle through the country, and of repeated outbreiks of it in the neighbourhood of Newsham t'ark, where the show was held, it was resolved, at the general meeting on the 29th of August, to withdraw the prizes offered for cattle, sheep, anti pigs, and to return the entry fees to the intending exhibitors of these animals. This had the effect of limiting the exhibition of live stock in the show yard, and probably of reducing the amount re- ceived at the entrances for admission ; but it will be ac- knowledged that the exhibition of horses was equal, both In number and in variety and character, to any of the pre- ceding shows, while that of cheese and butter, farm and garden produce, dogs and poultry, was better than for some years past. Tne large display of machinery in motion, and of farm implements of all kinds, carriages, carts and wag- gons, excited much attention, and the collection of models of ships, together with the display of horticultural plants, shrubs, bulbe, ac., arranged for by the Local Committee to fill the sheds rendered vacant by the absence of live stock, were inspectei with great interest. The Earl of Derby presided at the public luncheon, supported by the Mayor of Liverpool and by the society's tried and constant friend, Lord Winmarleigh, Sir Richard Cross, Colonel Blackburne, and a large company of members and visitors. The sum received for admission to the show and to the grand stand am ?unted to £2,794, and the nett increase of funds to the society on the year's transactions is £404. As this raised the society's balance with its bankers to nearly £l,BOO, your council ordered an investment of £l,OOO to be made in the Mersey Docks and Harbeur Board Bonds at 4 per cent., for fifteen years, from the Ist January next; and the total capital of the Society, it will be seen from the balance sheet, stands now at £8,208 ; the invested capital being £2,300; plant, £110; silver cups given by the Lord Lieutenant of Lancashire for cattle and pigs, and not awarded, £4O; and cash in bank, £757 16s 7d. Mr. R. H. Norreys was elected a trustee at the August meeting of members in place of Mr. Law, deceased, and the securities have all been duly transferred, and will be deposited for safe keeping in the offices of the society's bankers. Your council arranged for two public meetings during the spring, when papers read by Mr. Smetham and Mr. Holland, the society's chemist and botanist, were submitted te discussion and afterwards printed in the journal. Your emncil has also arranged for printing the lectures that are now being given by Mr. Smetham to the Liverpool science and art classes and for their free distribution to members, in pamphlet form at their close, he society has lost by death two of its oldest the and most veined member during the year. One, the senior of the society's three life president's, the late Lord Egerton of Tattoo, who during the greater part of his life took a deep and constant interest in its wel- fare; and the other, Mr. I. H. Law, who had nearly corn. pleted a service of fifty years as a member of Council and more than thirty as one of the society's auditors. Both of them were members of Council of the Manchester Agricul- tural Society, instituted in 1767, before its amalgamation with the Liverpool Society in 1847, and no men were ever more earnest or more faithful in their desire to serve the cause of Agrieulture and to promote the usefulness of the society. Your Council hopes the first-named may be suc- ceeded as a life-president by the present Lord Egertev, who has already proved his interest in the society by a longer service on the Council than four-fifths of its present mem- bers. His election, and the election of a successor to Mr. Law and to other members of Council resignieg through ill- health and other causes, comes within the duty of the meet- ing to-day. It will be proposed to you that next year's show be held at Stockport. The Mayor and Corporation have res- ponded very heartily to the suggestion and have already formed an influential local committee, a deputation from which will attend the meeting to-day with an invitation to the society. At this meeting also the division of the society in which the show should be held in 1885 should be selected, according to rule, but with the probability of the Royal Agricultural Society of England holding its show in some part of our society's district in that year, your Council thinks it may be considered better to postpone the question to a subsequent meeting, after the decision of the Council of that society shall have been made known. At the meeting of members, that resulted in the withdrawal of cattle, sheep, and pigs from exhibition, as reported, strong feeling was expressed by some members that the measures taken by the Privy Council to check the spread of foot-and- month disease in cattle were insufficient, while they were a source of constant loss and annoyance to farmers in the movement and sale of their stock, and a proposition was submitted to the effect :—" That all importation of live animals from countries where contadous disease in animels was known to exiet should be entirely stopped." It T ',15 thought that such imnortations were the prolific cens, of most of the recent outbraeks of feet-and-mouth disease, end
that unless imports were prohibited the oppressive restrig- tions imposed in individual counties were worse than nee-

less. The proposition yeas not pleased then, but your Council thiak the meetinz of to-day might be permitted to discuss the ginetion briefly, and has reason to believe that an expression of opinion on these lines would be entirely endorsed by the local authorities for regulating the move- ment of cattle all through the society's diatriot. The balance sheet showed the total receipts during the year to be £8,401 16s 11d, inclusiye of £1,?53 15s 3cl, balance hum last year's accounts. included in this amount were the items of £1,438 19e bd from the Local Committee

of Liverpool, £1,495 8s received as entry fees, £2,438 9s for admission to the show yard, and £355 115 for admission to the grand stand. The total amount of money paid dur- ing the year was £7,644 Os 4d, leaving a balance in hand of £7SP Hs 7d. Of this amount £2,586 5s was paid in prizes, £2,176 7s 5d for preparation of stow yard, and £l,OOO was invested in Mersey Docks and Harbour Board bonds. The society is shown to be worth £3,208 14s 7d. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, congratulated the society very much on its favourable char- acter. It was one of the most favourable reports they had had for many years past with regard to the financial concerns of the society. He hoped they would be able to present as favourable report in future. They had an increased balance, they had invested £l,OOO of their capital. and had upwards of £7OO in their bank. Not many societies in Eng- land connected with agriculture could, he thought, present such a favourable statement. (Hear, hear.) Their success in a financial aspect was materially owing to the very favourable reception with which they met at Liverpool, and he thought the Council had taken a wise course in thanking the Mayor and the people of Liverpool for the support they gave te the show. But he thought that no good news came without some little difficulty. On Monday he received a letter from the Birkenhead Agricultural Society saying that they intended to extend their limits into Lancashire. He had no doubt that that was owing to the success with which the society over which he had the honour of presiding met at Liverpool, He wished he could congratulate the society upon agricultural subjects as he could upon the finances. Last year was one of the most favourable for agriculture, but they were still under considerable depression. There was no doubt that there was a slight improvement in all branches of agri- culture. The number of cattle, which had been decreasing for a great number of years, had begun to increase again, and the number of sheep was also increasing. But there was a good deal of ground to make up before the society could say it was in the same satisfactory state that it was sone seven years ago. The report referred to the prevalence of foot-and-mouth disease, a matter which was discussed at Liverpool. He thought that they came to a good decision in excluding cattle from their showyard at Liverpool. He thought that the local authorities had done well in laying great restrictions upon the removal of cattle in consequence of the infliction upon their herds. - He had no doubt they were aware—he knew it from experience—that the decision of the magistrates, good as it was, and necessary as it was, was attended with very great inconvenience to some of the farmers, especially in his own county. The report suggested, or rather commended, to their notice that the meeting should consider that day I whether they would take any part in proposing to the Go- vernment with regard to the importation of cattle from abroad. It was a subject of enormous difficulty, and the agriculturists were sometimes inclined to look at it from a one-sided view. He hoped, however, they would always look at it from a patriotic view, that whilst on the one hand they watclied the interests of agriculture, they would not let the matter of meat and food for the great bulk of the population of this country be neglected at the same time. (Hear, hear.) It was a question whether they should Aide by the present limits of the introduction of cattle into this country, or press for the total exclusion of cattle from any country afflicted with cattle disease. The Chairman then referred to the regent Act of Parliament which they dis- I cussed at Liverpool, and which although it did away with freedom of contract he thought on the whole it was a good one, and would answer the expectations of those who passed it, especially if a cordial co-operation existed between land- lord and tenant in carrying it out. Mr. NORRETS seconded the adoptin of the report and balance sheet, which is,Tre then carried. TM; IMPORTATION OF DISEASED CATTLE.

Mr. RAVSTORNII moved, "That tlaiA meeting believes the ' Importation of live cattle from countries, known to be in- fected with foot-and-mouth, or other contagious cattle diseases, to be the chief cause of the origin and spread of inch disease in our home herds, and calls upon the Govern- ment to put a stop to such further imports with the least pos- sible delay." The.speaker, in the course of his remarks, refer- red to a statement made at the last meeting of the Central Chamber ef Agriculture in London, that the latest outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease could not be traced to the im- portation of foreign cattle. It was to be distinctly traced to the importation of diseased cattle, and it was to the interests of both purchaser and consumer to demand that a stop should be put to this importation of disease. They might ask whether those imports brought cheap meat to con- sumers; they all knew that they had not, and they never would. (Hear, hear.) Of course some would say "Surely farmers ought to be satisfi,d with dear meat," but the farmer would prefer to be able to take a penny or twopence less for his meat if he was insured against disease. Everyone knew the havoc the disease had created amongst their herds and breeding animals, and it could be traced to nothing but this source. An agricultural writer ha the liforniwg Post estimated the home supply of meat at the annual value of .£95,000,000, and the value of cattle from America was estimated at £3,000,000, so if they classed those figures to- gether they would see what a ridiculousamount was involved on that question of which they were speaking. They had suffered thousands of pounds loss through the restrictions, and the remedy was worse than the disease. Farmers, how- ever, were quite willing to continue the restrictions provid- ine. the sources of the dis.:ase were cut off, but be thought it was utterly unfair to ask them to submit to the restric- tions while the disease was being continually brought into the country. They might send from abroad as much dead meat as they liked; they did not object to that, but they objected to the importation of disease. He was sure the pre- sent meeting would feel it their duty to strengthen the hands of those working in that direction. (Hear, hear.) Mr. NORREYS seconded and endorsed the remarks of the proposer of the resolution. There was no doubt that whilst the importation of foreign cattle from diseased countries was permitted they would never cat off the disease in England. They might korm their rules and prohibitions throughout the kingdom, but if the importation of diseased cattle was allowed to go on as it did and enter their large markets, how was it that they could prevent the consequences. They knew how contagious and infectious the ditease was, and , how easily it was transmitted. Surely it was the duty of the Government to protect the agricultural from such an innovation and dreadful consequence. It was one of the main causes of the depression in agriculture at the present thine. He agreed with the last speaker that they as agricul- turists shou'd speak out plainly to the Government, and de- inand that diseased cattle from foreign countries should no longer be permitted to enter their country. They would soon have no breeding of cattle in the country in con- sequence of the disease, and people would not in the long run invest their cipital in such a risky concern as farming was getting. It was most necessary he thought that they should endeavour to prevent the introduction of diseased cattle into the county, and he had accordingly great pleasure in seconding the proposition. Mr. LANSDAL/1 and M. Tietelile FAIR spoke in similar terms. Mr. FINCTIETT complained of the restrictions being differ- ent in one county than another, and thought they should urge on the Government the fact that if the restrictions were the same it would be a convenience both to farmers and dealers. , The resolution was then agreed to nein cola' and the . Chairman said he would sign and convey it to Her Majesty's Government.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT.

It was agreed that Lord Egerton of Tatton be asked to be President of the Society for the ensuing year, and that in the event of his lordship losing unable to attend the meet- ing at Stockport, that his place be taken by Mr. W. Cunliffe Brooks, M.P.

div.head: TRH COUNCIL OF TIIII SOCIRTY.
div.p: TRH COUNCIL OF TIIII SOCIRTY.

The following were the gentlemen elected to the Council: —North-east division: The Hon. A. Egerton (vice-president), Lieutenant-Colonel Starkie (V.P.), Messrs. Robert Lansdale (retiring), Joseph Culshaw, and W. B. Hulton. South-east division: The Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P. (V.P.), Messrs. R. H. Norreys (V.P.), John White, J. T. Smith. North-west division: Messrs. G. C. Hale (V.P.), L. Raw- atom (V.P ), James Birch, and George Woods. South-west division: Messrs. T. Brocklebank (V.P.), F. A. Dickson (V.P.), William Scotsou, and John Whalley. Northern division: Messrs. C. R. Jacson (V.P.), Thomas Fair (V.P.), James Tunstall, and Thomas Crook. It was decided that the amount of money to be offered in prizes be £1,700.

div.head: RE-ELECTION OW SECRETARY.
div.p: RE-ELECTION OW SECRETARY.

The CHAIRMAN had great pleasure in proposing the re- election of Mr. Thomas Rigby as secretary of the society, and paid a compliment to that gentleman for the ability he displayed in the discharge of his duties. This proposition was carried. A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Mr. G. C. HALE, and seconded by Mr. LANSDALE, concluded the meeting. At the luncheon which followed the meeting, Lord WIN- mARLEIGH, who presided, briefly proposed "The Society," which was responded to by Mr. NORREYS, and who conchfl. ded by asking the company to drink ths health of Lord Winmarleigh. who, they all knew, took such a great interest in agricultural matters, and in anything that affected the welfare of the society.—His Lordship, who was warmly greeted on rising to reply, said he was much obliged for the oft paid compliment to him. He did his utmost for the prosperity of the society, but as they knew, he was getting advanced in years and could not attend to his county duties so regularly as he formerly did, but whilst he had health and strength he promised *he members he would do his best to perform his duties in connection with their interest satis- factorily. (Applause.)

At Birmingham, on Wednesday, Edward Yates, gun- maker, was committed for trial on a obarge of attempting to murder his wife. The man had only recently come out of the lunatic asylum, and in a fit of jealousy stabbed his wife twice with a bayonet, inflicting dangerous wounds.

Dr. Weld, Liberal, has been elected President of the Swist Confederation for the ensuing year. A despatch from Durban says it is now regarded as almost certain that Cetewayo will be reinstated at Ulundi. The damage done by the fire at the Belgian House of Representatives is estimated at 12,000,000 francs. Two per- sons were killed and five injured. On Tuesday a crowd of poor persons gathered before the house of M. Gubkim, a rich merchant of Moscow, lately deceased, to receive the donations in money usually dis- tributed on the death of rich persons. The press became ec great that several persons were crushed to death.

A Belgrade despatch to the Times gives us the number of "rebels" who have been shot by order of courts martial. It amounts to 18, and comprise four Orthodox priests, four merchants, one schoolmaster, and nine peasants. A great number of others have been sentenced to penal servi- tude.

De Lesseps and Con- vreux. A police search of his residence resulted in the .dia- eovery of a quantity of explosive materials. "STATE SOCIALISM" IN SPAIN. "State Socialism" it spreading. The Spanish Government has appointed a Ocm- mission to inquire into the condition of the working *lame and the relations between capital and labour. Bills are to be introduced into the Cortes to carry out such recommenda- tions as the Commissioners may make at the conclusion of their inquiries. This Recherr RBYOLT lii SERVIA.—M. Paschitch, the Radical leader' and twenty other members of the party, hays been summoned to appear before the Commission of Judges at Yaitchar on the leth instant to answer for their alleged crimes against the State and Crown. Most of them hays escaped into Bulgaria, and they are not expected to appear in response to this summons. Twenty of the rebels ck3nta demned to death have been reprieved by the King. ErTRAORDINARY ROBB/MT.—A robbery under extraor- dinary circumstances has been committed in the streets of Paris. M. Soriano, a Spanish Prefect, was being drivel it a cab from the hotel where he had been staying to the raik way station. Amongst his baggage on the cab was a trunk containing important papers, five thousand francs in gold ant jewels, and objects of art te the value of fifty thousand francs. About half way to the station the driver was startled by one of the trunks fallink upon him. He pullet up, and was replacing it, when he saw that the strap had been cut, and that a large trunk was missing. This proved to be the one in which the treasure was packed. So dex- terously bad it been abstracted that neither the driver nor his fare had remarked anything until one of the other trunks had fallen as described. THB BRiTIE3II AND Sraterst PROTOCOL.—The text of the protocol sighed between the British and Spanish Govern- ments at Madrid on December Ist was published on.Tuesdiy night. The two governments engage at once to open nego- ciations for a treaty of commerce, including a consular con- vention and treaty of navigation, and to appoint a mined commission to investigate the modifications in the presebt conventional tariff of Spain and the alcoholic scale oflike British tariff as may be found necessary to meet the legiti- mate requirements of the trade of the two nations respkges tively. Pending the conclusion of the treaty, the.tffre, governments agree on a vadus.vivendi as follows :—The Spanish Government to apply at once to the Cortes'for powers necessary to admit British goods according to ttte rates of the second column of the present .Spanish tariff ; the British Government, as soon as Parliament deals with the Budget, to apply for the necessary sanctions to extend the shilling scale from its present limit, 28 degrees, to -31 degrees; this arrangement to subsist until the definitive treaty of commerce shall take effect, with liberty of tan. mination in 1887. During the sabsistence of the moats vivendi the two governments will accord each other the most-favoured nation treatment in regard to all matters re- lating to trade and navigation. Tux LABOtIn Minkal IN QumNALAND : A VirARVINO TO EMIGRANTS.—A letter, dated Maryborougb, Queewslandr October 4, has been received in Liverpool from a working- man who emigrated to that colony during the summer. After a passage of a hundred and one days, the emigrants arrived on September 21, and were kept for a week at the depot at Bundaberg, but could get no work. They were thee. sent to Maryborough, where says the writer, " things are just as bad. There are hundreds walking about the colony both in Brisbane and the north, and as for niggers, there are thousands doing the work of white men, and we have got to compete against them." After describing the voyage, in which the vessel encountered heavy weather off the Cape, he proceeds :—" I think the emigration ought to be stopped, as bringing people from comfortable homes to ;Ili brink of starvation. There are no workhouses here, but if there were they would very soon be filled up. If a mat re- turns to England with a hundred or two it is because; he has friends to push him on. There are men, who have been in the colony for years, glad to come to our dept and,eat dry bread and to sleep under a tree in the bush. There were seven of the single men went to a sugar plantation for £35 a year and rations, the food consisting. of sour bread and beef, and the place they bad to sleep in was a dirty room with no bed. They could not stand the work; it was too hard, so that I would not advise anybody to come out here. There were 1200, arrived in Brisbane last week, and there are, according to the papers, 7,000 mere on their way to Queensland." The friend to whom the letter is addressed had contemplated emigrating; but in conclusion the writer says —"if: you take advice from me, you will stay at home and I wish I was with you." EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.

SIX. HUNDRED AND EIGHTY MEN KILLED: On the 2nd December another disaster happened to the Egyptian troops, 24 miles from Souakim. The force consisted of 500 blacks, 200 Bashi-B izeuke, and 20 cavalry. Accor- ding to one account it was proceeding to relieve Sineat, which is besieged by Arabs. According to another it was reconnoitring. Fourteen hours after starting, two native officers returned to Souakirn reporting that the force was almost annihilated. Of the blacks only nine had returned by the 4th inst. The total loss is said to be 680. Two European officers were with them, and the whole was under the command of an Egyptian major and some native staff officers. A correspondent at Souekim sends the following account, under date Dec. 4, of his interview with one of the surviving officers in the presence of the Egyptian com- mander at Sonakim. The officers say that, being surrounded by 5,009 men, the troupe formed sqaere. The blacks were on three faces and the Bashi-Bezouks on the fourth. The Bashi-Be:soaks fell black, throwing the blacks into disorder. The latter especially fought with great bravery, back to back, against overwhelming numbers. This account is cor- roborated by a wounded soldier. Noun i Bey found the ground covered with the bodies of Arabs as well as blacks. The exact locality of th 3 fight is Hamel. One gun and arms and ammunition were lost. The wife of a Bashi- Beeouk killed at Toka, on searching the spot, found the bodies of the Greeks and another, which was wounded in the leg, chest, and neck, and which, from the account of black whiskers and grey hair and board, answers to the de- scription of Commander Moncrieff. The apathy of the native authorities at Souakim is untqualled. The advanced forts at Souakim are fired on every midnight. Friendly natives have been attacked. The telegraph wire to Djeddab and Jeddah was lately cut within a mile from Souakim. In eonsequence of the disaster at Souakim the garrison is now seduced to 1,000 men. Dervishes, it is known, are appear. lug in Upper Egypt, and propose to preach a Holy War, as they have already done at Sennaar. The whole country beyond Egypt proper is ablaze. In military opinion it will be impossible for Baker Pestle to march to Berber under present circumstances, as the troops are worthless at Soua- kim. Baker Pasha will for the time only watch events. A telegraph cable between Souakim and Sure is uow con- sidered by the Egyptian Ministry to be urgently necessary A despatch from Suez on Tuesday says the Egyptian transport Tanta has arrived here from Souakim after convey- ing to that place a detachment of Egyptian gendarmerie under Colonel Sartorius. The Tanta's news from Souakim is to the 7th inst. Excitement prevails there owing to ap- prehensions of a night attack. Her Majesty's gunboat Ranger was throwing rockets over the town in order to alarm the insurgents. The Government has received news that the body of General Hicks has been found. One haul grasped a sword, the other a revolver. His force had no cartridges left. It is supposed that the rebels have marched or will march into the mountains from Obeid, possibly with the view of going Feund to Dongola, between Khartoum and Upper Egypt. / SERIOUS LOSSES OF THE REBELS.—lntelligence received on Thursday at Cairo from Souakin announces ttrat the French cruiser Internet has left that place. Colonel War- rington has visited the scene of the late battle between the Egyptian battalion add the hill tribes. He states that he counted on the field 4,000 dead bodies. The native sent by the Egyptian authorities from Khartoum to El Obeid has returned, after an absence of 21 days. He confirms the complete destruction of Hicks Pasha's army. The mes— senger adds, however, that the Mandi is almost without followers at El Obeid. He had lost many killed in the engagements with Hicks Pasha, an 4 several of the insurgent tribes had left him to return home. The False Prophet experienced great difficulty, therefore, in organising the forces which he proposed sending into the province of Dar— four and against the Cabbebish tribe.

LORD SnarrnsannT AT $Ollll.-St. Giles's House is built in a quadrangle, and the central part, once open to the sky, is now covered with a glass roof forming a large and splendid hall or saloon, the walls of which are hung with family portraits, wkilst antiquities and works of art are gracefully arranged on all sides. Amongst other interest- ing things I noticed the astronomical clock presented to Sir James South by the King of Denmark, and left by that as- tronomer to Lord Shaftesbury. An organ and grand pianos also have a place in this saloon, upon which the ladies played when the family met for afternoon tea; and so truly enjoyable was this hour and a half that I looked forward each day to the arrival of five o'clock, when Lady Zdith took her place at the organ, and the Hon. Margaret Ashley at the piano, whilst Miss Esther Browne sang most charm- ingly to their accompaniments. Greatly as I appreciated these family concerts, they were exceeded by the Sunday evening "Service of Song. When all the family and some thirty of the servants and retainers met together to sing some sacred hymns and songs, the gathering seemed indeed like a little heaven below, and when the venerable Earl con- cluded the evening service by offering up a simple prayer for his la, usehold, one could not help thinking of the ancient patriarchs.—From" The Quiver" for December. _
