IRELAND. The Lord Lieutenant has prohibited the boldiny, of the rival meetings of Orangemen and Nationalists', arranged to be held at Londonderry on Tuesday next. Four members of an "assassination society" who w,re concerned in the shooting of Martin Lyden and his eon, at Letterfrack, County Galway, were on Tuesday sentenced at Sligo ASIIiZOS to ten years' penal servitude, having pleaded guilty to charges of conspiracy to murder. UTRANGE DEATH OF MR. PARNELL'S BROTHED.-IN-LAW. —A. Renter's telegram from Brussels, dated December 12, states :—" Captain Robert Dickinson, an Irish political refugee, and brother-in-law of Mr. Parnell, has been found dead in his bed. His remains will b 3 conveyed to Ireland." Ala ILLICIT DISTILLERY IN Dunrata. —On Wednesday the police made a raid on a house in Dublin, and found there an illicit distillery in full working order. They seized all the machinery, and forty gallons cf spirits, forty gallons of wine, and eighty gallons of wash: They arrested two men whom they found on the premises. gEIEURE or ARILS IN DUBLIN.-0a Thursday morning the police proceeded to a house in Dolier-street, Dublin, oc- cupied by a man named Dunne, and seized there four rifles, several revolvers, a quantity of powder, and a number of military belts. Dunne, who is a prominent Nationalist, has been arrested. THE PRIESTS AND THE PARNELL BANQUET. Though several Roman Catholic priests, attended the Parnell ban- quet, none of them spoke, although it had been arranged that they should propose and respond to different toasts. Their silence throughout the evening was owing to a stern injunction from the heads of the Roman Catholic Church to maintain this attitude. MR. RUSSELL'S FEES IN THE O'DONNELL CASE.—The Whitehall Review understands that, as the leading counsel for the defence of O'Donnell, Mr. Charles Russell received a retaining fee of 2,000 guineas, drawn Men entendu from the coffers of the Land League and adds :—Thaiso large a sum for the almost hopeless defence of a murderer whose conviction seemed from the outset so certain is, we can readily believe, without precedent in the history of the bar. THE PARNULL BANOUST.—At the Parnell banquet in Dublin, on Tuesday night, at which the member for Cork was presented with a substantial financial token of the Irish people's gratitude for his past services, the Lord Mayor, in proposing "Ireland a Nation," recalled the fact that in 1782 volunteers met in that hall on the evening of &nation's downfall; now, he hoped, they were on the eve of a nation's resurrection. Mr •Davitt, in responding, eulogised Mr. Parnell, and said Ireland was working out a political servitude from which deliverance would come in the life- time of those present through the employment of open de- termined democratic organisation. Mr. Sexton, who also re- sponded, declared that England was no longer mistress of the sea, or the equal of the military nations of Europe, and Irishmen should hate their oppressors and resolve to set their country free.

POLITICAL. Mr. Arthur Peel has decided to accept tho nomination for the Speakership. Mr. Mundella addressed his constituents on Tuesday night at Sheffield, and claimed for the past session that it had been more fruitful of beneficial legislation than any session during the past ten years. After Easter more good work was done than had been accomplished by the late Govern- ment in three sessions. A vote of confidence in the right hon. gentlenaan was adopted. LIBERAL MEETING AT WAREFIELD.—On Saturday a Liberal meeting was held at Horbury, near Wakefield, at which addresses were delivered by the Hon. H. W. Fitz- william, M.P., and Mr. C. Milnes-Gaskell, who has been invited to become a candidate in the place of Mr W. H. Leatham, who will retire at the next election. The Hon. Mr. Fitzwilliam in referring to a recent address by Lord Hartington, urged that the franchise bill required was a plain, simple, and honest measure, not a measure which could be so manipulated as to give any political party a temporary advantage, but one which would de away with the manifest injustice of the present system. Mr. Milnes- Gaskell expressed himself in favour of an extension of the- franchise, but he could not believe that the Government would extend household suffrage to Ireland. MR. FORSTER'S REPLY TO MR. FARNELL.—Mr. Forster, in addressing his constituents at Bradford on Thursday night, strongly endorsed the programme that the Liberal party is pledged to follow. In speaking of the Franchise Bill, he emphatically said that he would include Ireland in it, and, in stating that he was not surprised at Mr. Parnell's speech, declared that he sometimes thought Mr. Parnell and his friends did not wish Ireland to be included in the bill, believing that if it were excluded it would secure them larger support in Ireland. He admitted that for a time an extension of the franchise in Ireland might strengthen the Parnell party, but the Government would at least have the satisfaction of encountering the evil is the House of Com- mons instead of in Ireland. As to a coalition between either of the two great parties and the Irish party, an appeal to the coantry would speedily dispose of such a combina- tion. Distribution, Mr. Forster maintained, should follow the Franchise Bill, and his own opinion was in favour of equal electoral districts. In conclusion, he expressed ap- proval of the Ilbert Bill and of Australian confederation. TRH IPSWICH ELECrION: GREAT LIBERAL ViCToEY.— Mr. H. W. West scored a decided victory for the Liberal party at Ipswich, on Wednesday, by securing 3,266 votes against 2,816 recorded for Sir W. T. Charley. From 1847 to 1868 this constituency returned a Liberal and a Conser- vative to Parliamont, but at the general election in 18138 two Liberals were returned, of whom Mr. West was one. In 1874, however, two tories headed the poll, and at the death of the senior member in 1875, Mr. T. 0. Cebbold, the late Conservative member, was returned by 2,213 votes, against 1,607 given for Mr. W. Newton, Liberal. At the general election in 1880, Mr. T. C. Cobbold again headed the poll with 3,142 votes, Mr. Jesse Collings coming next with 3,074, after him Mr. West with 3,025, and Mr. Bulwer, Conserva- tive, at the bottom, with 2,979. Until yesterday a Liberal has not headed the poll in Ipswich since 1888; but Mr. West has now added 192 to the vote cast for Mr. Jesse Col- lings at the last general election, while Sir W. T. Charley has fallen 326 below the late member's score. There is every reason to be satisfied with this result, which more than counterbalances the return of Sir F. Milner for York. MR. Bition-r AT EEIGHLEY.—Mr. John Bright arrived at Oakworth House, Keighley, on Wednesday morning, on a four days' visit ,to Mr. Isaac Holden, M.P. During the afternoon 50 of the principal gentlemen in the district were invited to lunch with Mr. Bright. In response to the toast of his health, Mr. Bright delivered a brief address. He spoke on the question of extending the franchise a measure which he had no doubt would be pissed in the douse of Commons next session,and which, in his opinion, the Lords: would not dare to reject. Referring to Ireland, he thought that what had been done for that country would result in a beneficent change, and the promotionlof its future peace and pros- perity. He doubted not that there were those now living who would live to see Ireland as contented and happy as Scotland. About foreign affairs Mr. Bright spoke in an anxious tone. He thought that the itutlook was far from promising. In Egypt he was afraid it would be proved that the first interference with the aountry would be less free from complications than its ulterior results. Mr. Bright re- ceived an address from the Keighley Liberal Association, last night, and briefly replied. MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE AT ERAIILEY.—Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., addressing a large meeting at Bramley, near Leeds, on Saturday evening, said he hoped the people of England and Irelamd would read and mark the corres- pondenoe between Lord Salisbury and Mr. Lockwood, which proved once more that the methods adopted by Lord Salis- bury were repugnant to all who appreciated the courtesies of political life and the welfare ani honour of the country. Referring to colonial questions, he expressed a hope that the colonies would themselves be able to undertake the work of colonisation and defence, and trusted that the Mart Bill, as modified by the Governmant, would soon become law. With reference to the future, he admitted that the Conservatives could force a dissolution by throw- ing oat in the Lords all measures passed by the Com- mons; but the Government would then go to the country, not on any particular measure, but against the Lords. He believed the Lords would throw out that part of the Fran- chips Bill relating to Ireland, which would be equivalent to rejecting the whole Bill; but for his part, he did not think there would even then be reason why the Government should not accept the position and go forward with measures to which they were pledged and then again take up the Fran- chise Bill. If once the Liberal party came into collision with the Lords on a question like that it would be an awk- ward circumstance for the Lords. Toe Government would go forward with the unfinished work whioh was promised at the last general election. EARL GRANVILLE AND TRH LIBERAL UNlON'.—Earl Granville presided, on Tuesday evening, at a banquet held at the Cannon-street Hotel. London, in connection with a conference under the auspices of the London and Countiesl Liberal Union. In responding to the toast of 'Her Majesty's Ministers," which was proposed by Mr. W. Fowler, M.P., Earl Granville declined to further crush the violent attacks made by leading Conservatives upon the Government, which attacks bad absolutely no other result than to produce a feeling of satiety in the public mind. The Foreign Office, he pointed out, did not suffer so ranch as some departments from Parliamentary obstruction, but it had to bear the brunt of a multitude of questions fat in ex- cess of those put byleading Liberals to the late Government on foreign affairs. Whilst the Government desired to give information, it was sometimes undesirable for them to de- clare fully before the whole world what they had done or were going to do in transactions of a difficult and delicate character. After alluding to the prevalence of bribery in some quartersat the last general election, and the demoral bled public sentiment in some constituencies en the subject, his Lordship referred to the careful precautions neessary in future elections under the Act. He urged Liberals to be prepared for a dissolution of Parliament, which he said was always within human possibilities. The Liberal party, he pointed out, suffered under great difficulties. They not only suffered for their faults, but for their merits. Their business was to abolish abuses and remove grievances, and as one result they incurred the hostility of those whose in- terests were supposed to suffer. However, they must not attempt to conciliate an individual class; they must place conidence in the great public feeling ef the country.

SIR R. A. CROSS AT Si. HELENS. The Right Hon. Sir R. A. Cross, speaking at a Conservative demonstration at St. Helens on Tuesday evening, said that it was now quite time that those who were wishful to uphold this constitution should bestir themselves in order that they might see no danger happened to it. He was not going to waste their time at present by entering into any great mis- takes and faults which the present Government had com- mitted during their period of office. That they were told was past history. (Laughter.) And he was not going to do it for two reasons. In the first place, their blunders were so many that he should not have time to explain them all; and in the second place he thought the dangers of the fu- ture were so great that it was absolutely necessary to ad- dress oneself to them. It was curious to see how thin-skinned their opponents were when they were touched, and their Mende in the Press seemed to think that it was waste of time on the plrt of anyone to touch them. (Laughter.) Even Lord Hartington, when he spoke in Lancashire the other day, and defended the course of the Government—he did not say that he did it, but he did his best to defend it— was roundly abused by his own friends in the Press, who said that he was wasting time in so doing. The Govern- ment could not bear to hear themselves criticised, bat his I consolation was that the time would soon come when the general election would be at hand, and then the Conservatives would pay off old scores, and explain all the iniquities which they had committed. (Cheers.) They were called upon by their friends of the present Govern- ment to say that they ought to propound a policy, but that was a doctrine he entirely protested against. It was for them to say how they were going to govern the country, and it was for the Conservatives to tell them whether they thought it right or not. (Applause.) But if he were forced to make any recommendation, although he entirely protes- ted against being called upon to do so, he would say that ,their programme for the next session of Parliament ought to be that they had had from the Prime Minister a state- ment made years ago of the large amount of arrears of legis- I lation which up to the present time stood against them; and he held that the proper course for them to take would be to have taken up one or two of these measures which they thought most conducive to the public interest and the social welfare of all their fellow-countrymen, and the most important measures were to redress grievances where they had existed. (Applause.) Difficulties, however, had arisen on that point—the Liberal party were not at one amongst themselves, and the result was that as they did in former years so they had done again—when they could not see a straightforward policy—they said, "For goodness sake let us have a reform bill." (Cheers.) That was exactly the posi- tion they had at the present moment, and no one had asked for that reform bill except some of the extreme Radicals. The present were no ordinary times, because amongst the Liberal party the extreme Radicals were doing all they could to drive away the Whigs from the position they had held, and they were going to say to the Prime Minister that un- less he followed their dictation, they would not follow him and woutd tarn him out. (Cheers.) Coming to the im- mediate future, they were told by a Cabinet Minister that Inanhood suffrage and equal electoral rights were the ob- jects he had in view. They had at all events the consolation of knowing that the present Government had been in power pretty nearly four years, and at all events should have had time to make up their minds as to what was right to be done on the great principles of reform, if it were to be done at all. There ought to be no difficulty about it, and if they had net made up their minds on the great and essential principles which they felt themselves bound to put forward, they ought to hold their tongues. (Cheers.) He could assure the Government that if they felt certain that as a matter of conviction that the bill which the Government were going to produce had been really one which they had thought out to the end, which they believed to be ne- cessary for the country, and which they handed to Parlia- ment as a united Cabinet—although the Conservatives were told that they were opposed to all reform, he could assure them that any bill brought forward in that sense and spirit. and after that consideration, would receive at their hands the most careful attention and consideration before it was opposed. (Cheers.) But they had not this consolation. They found that there were no principles settled at all, that the Government had not got a mind of their own, that the Governm-nt within two months—and probably less—of the meeting of Parliament not only had not made up their minds, but were still of opposite and totally different minds upon the important principles of that measure. He ventured to say that any measure, on the main principles of which the Government were not agreed within two mouths of the meeting of Parliament, was a mere compromise which was not worth look- ing at, and would not receive that consideration which a carefully prepared measure ought to have had. (Cheers.) They must remember what the stake was; it was a matter of vast importance. They were told by Sir Charlee Dilke that the object was a total redistribution of political power. They were told by Mr. Chamberlain—(hisses)— that it was a vast struggle upon which they were at present entering; and they were told by Mr. Childers, who everyone thought at all events was a moderate member of the Cabinet, that the bill which was coming forward was the first and the chief of a series of measures which were to create a greater revolution in our existing arrangements than any- thing which had taken place since 1689. All he could say was that if it was to be such a revolutionary proposal as Mr. Childers shadowed out, that was not what the people of Vngland would have. (Loud cheers.) He wished to say a word to the Liberals who were present, and to that moderate section of Liberals who would feel themselves represented by Mr. Goschen strong Liberal as he was that it was quite time to make up their minds that they

On Monday flier!, Mr. Rylauds, M.P. for Burnley, ad- dressed a crowded meeting of his constituents in the Mechanics' Hall. He said some might think that the last session was not a fruitful one; still, it was trot a barren one, and amongst other bills was passed one dealing .with cor- rupt practices, rendered necessary to put a stop to corropt practices in peccant boroughs. Bribery was always punish- able, but now not only the giver but the receiver of a bribe was liable to a very severe penalty. Another part ef it was to make it possible that eters than *coy rich men should be able to obtain seats in Parlia- ment. The number of paid agents would have to be gesatly reduced, and they would hare to depend more upon the enlightened judgment of tne people. Then they had passed an• Agrielultural Holdings Act, the object of which was to give tenants greater se- curity for their improvements on the soil. That act did not go far enough, owing to the number of large landowners in the House of Commons. They had also passed the Bank- raptcy and Patents Acts, both of which he hoped would be of great advantage to trade. He was not satisied with the amount of expenditure at present under the control of the Government. (Applause.) It was only fair to admit that they had had to find two millions of money to clear off debts incurred by their predecessors. It was also true that the late Government raised the expenditure to a very high point, and it was always difficult to bring down expenditure after it had got up. But, even making these allowances, the expenditure was entirely unwarranted, and ought to be materially reduced. From 1880-1 to 1882-3 the annual charge for the army was increased £3,800,000, and for the navy £1,830,000; total increase, £5,700,000. He was not one of those who said that the country ought to be without de- fences, but he believed that millions of money are wasted annually on these great eervices, and if the pruning-knife were applied to them we might have an equally efficient army and navy at a much less cost. The cost of the civil service had increased by £8,000,000 daring the last twelve years. He admitted there had been reductions of debt and large grants in aid of local taxation, much of which, he was beund to say, had been of an objectionable nature; also greater expenditure in the postal service and on education. Still there was room for a considerable paring down of the civil service estimates. An alarming part of the civil service expenditure, which was gradually increasing, was the pen- sions paid to servants of the Crown. He had no hesitation in saving that this pension system was one open to very serious abuse. Many were pensioned for no other reason than that others lower down might go a step higher. The pensions amount altogether to £8.838,377, a year. This was a very considerable item. It was a very easy thing to give a pension • and the moment after it had been given it ceased to be under the control of Parliament, and became a permanent charge upon the country. He did not say that pensions ought to be abolished altogether, but they ought to be put under much more stringent conditions. It was difficult to lessen expenditure when the item of £60,000 ap- peared for the repair of the Qtseen's yacht, which had cost the country about 11 000 every time it had been used. The spending servants of the Crown were like the , horse leech, crying "Give give," but were never satisfied. The army and navy cost now nearly £27,000,000 a year,- and yet, whenever there was any discussion In regard to our foreign operations, the military gentlemen were always saying that the services were ineffcient—that they were going to the dogs. With the experience of other nations, and with the aid of the militia and volunteers, he believed we could have an efficient army and navy for twenty millions a year. Tory orators were going abont the country, evidently in the hope of copying Mr. Gladstone when he overthrew Lord Beaconsfield's Government. He need hardly say these orators were much smaller men than Mr. Gladstone, amid they forgot also that he dealt with high principles of conduct, both with regard to home and foreign affairs,. which stirred the conscience of the country. In regard to Ireland, a great deal had been said about the- rights of property, but he believed in the rights of property on both sides. The Irish Land Act was beginning to tell, and he believed had that Act been passed 50 years ago we should not have had our regent dificulties in Ireland. It was the policy which was a danger to property, and the present state of the 'land was also a danger to property. Al to the franchise, he I was in favour of making the franchise absolutely the same in the counties as in the boroughs. (Applause.) If the 405. freeholder were retained at all, he would only let those who were resident vote. He expected that when this bill came up the House of Lords would reject it, and that there would be a dissolution, and this would bring to the front the present position of the House of Lords. (Applause.) That struggle would be a great one, but he had no doubt as to what the result would be. (Loud cheers.) The following resolution was carried unanimously : "This meeting desires to express its continued and unabated confidence in Mr. Ryland& as member for this borough. and to accord its heartiest thanks to him for his valuable ser- vices to the town and in the House of Commons during the year, and especially for his unwearying endeavours to effeet a reduction in the national exnenditure "

Ss. 3d. per ton. property in the boroughs should vote for the boroughs, al- though they did not happen to reside within the limits of the ordinary parliamentary constituency. If they were go- ing to disfranchise the 40s freeholders they would be taking a fatal step for the liberties of this country. Sir Henry James went further still. He said if they did that they could not stand up for the representation of the non-resi- dential members of the universities, and that they too must also go. They would see, therefore, that the proposition was that all the influence which property now had and which learning and education possessed were to go to the wall simply because of this new fangled notion of equality. The whole spirit of Lord Hartington's speeches was that this matter bad not been thought out, whilst Mr. Chamber- lain pressed his views with vigour and only took this as a means to an end—an end which every one in that room was determined should not take place. (Cheers.) There was another question which they would have to consider in the question of the franchise, viz, how were they going to deal with the minority vote in the three-cornered constituencies? This minority vote did not affect St. Helens, but it did his friends in Liverpool. Mr. Fawcett, who was probably the most independent thinking Liberal of the Uovernment, was strongly in favour of it, and although he said at the present moment it was under a cloud owing to the action that had been taken in the Radical towns of Birmingham and Glasgow, he stuck up for it in every way, while Mr. Chamberlain would sweep away all these silly, ridiculous, unconstitutional and new-fangled notions. (Laughter and cheers.) At all events on the three points, on the question of Ireland, on the question of what they meant to do with the county franchise, and on the question of the minority vote, within six or eight weeks of the meeting of Parlia- ment the members of the Government themselves had not made up their minds. And what was worse, they had got one member of the Cabinet going about—a thing unheard of, because a member of a Cabinet ought only to speak when he reflected the opinion of the whole Cabinet—(cheers)—utter Radical as he was, the avowed champion of manhood suf- frage and equal electoral districts, bidding for popular sup- port as against his more prudent and thoughtful colleagues—a thing which England never heard of before, and which he hoped it would never hear of again. (Loud cheers.) There remained one more question of still greater vital importance than any other, and that was the geestion of the redistribution of seats—a matter which affected them very seriously. All he could say up i a that was that they might have the franchise or do anything they liked, but if the Government had got the manipulation of the redistribution of the seats, they might work it to meet their own ends just like a conjuror manipulated a hat. (Cheers.) Supposing they had a Parliament elected after they had passed the extension of the franchise, and had not settled the redistribution of seats, in that Parliament they would have every anomaly that now existed intensified to the greatest possible degree, and they would have eve 7 evil that existed multiplied a hundredfold ; vet to that Par- liament so elected, so full of the anomalies arid evils already existing, they would confine the delicate question as te- how seats were to be redistributed. (Cheers.) At all events they had a right to ask if they had any principles to put before the country. They should ask whether the minds of the members of the Government were made up, or whether they were in a state of chaos and intended to go entirely according to the Leeds Conference for equal electoral distribution, or, on the other hand, they would accept the view of Mr. Fawcett, their intelligent Radical, or of Si! Charles Mike, by which London would have the same number of members of Parlia- ment as the inhabitants of the whole of Scotland. Or, farther, whether they would follow the Prime Minister, who told the Scotch people not long ago that because they were so far from London they ought to have more representation than they had. (Laughter.) Or, again, whether they were going to give to the agricultural labourer the vote to which they said he was entitled, on the one hand, and, on the other, to take away all the privileges they had given, be- muse they were going to attach him to a neigh- bouring borough, which would swamp every vote which he gave and would leave him in a worse state than he was at the present moment. All those and many others were vital questions about which Conservatives were en- titled to be informed. (Cheers.) The Conservatives were not to be called upon to propose a reform bill; they thought that there were a great many other things which might be done first. He admitted that there were great communities amongst them at the present moment which had not mem- bers, and which ought undoubtedly to have them. (Cheers.) He sew a return only that day which had been presented to the House of Commons showing those places which were unrepresented and the populations which they contained. He noticed very high in that list the town of St. Helens, and he thought that under these circumstances they were entitled to a member. (Cheers.) The only regret he felt was that when this member was granted to them—as he had no doubt it would be—he should feel sorry at parting with so many and such intelligent constituents as he saw be- fore him. He also thought that when a large borough en- larged its boun'elaries, and was inhabited beyond its boun- daries by people whose business lay within those limits, it was very fair that those living outside should be attached to the borough in order that they might have votes for the cameniunity in which they were most interested. (Cheers.) It was owing to the differences and troubles amongst the Liberals themselves in other directions that he believed that they had fallen back upon this great principle of re- form, and he was convinced that he believed that the whole matter was supported and had arisen from the great Radical caucuses which existed throughout the country, as he thought unhappily, who were trying through those Radicals they had got in the Cabinet to force the hands of the Prime Minister, and make him undertake this great question, be- cause they thought that if they did not pass it while he was in power they would have a very small chance of attaining their ends at any other time. (Cheers.) He was opposed to any reform that would in any way lead to what would be a disastrous result to this country. or would give manhood suffrage or equal electoral districts. (Cheers.) It he saw any bill of reform working on the old lines of the Constitu- tion which would meet with the modern wants of the per- petually floating population, caused by great industries, arising here and there, the increasing population, increasing wealth, increasing intelligence, increasing education, by all means extend the basis of their Constitution, but do it with this end only in view—not to work it out in the interests of one party only, but do it with the sole purpose of doing good to the nation at large. (Cheers.) There was a ques- tion which was of vital importance to us as a ' nation about which he must enter his solemn protest, and that was the Egyptian question. I (Hear, hear.) He had always said that it was much easier to go into Egypt with honour than to come out of it with honour, and events had proved that he was right. (Cheers.) At the beginn'ng of the last session of Parliament Lord Hartington announced that he thought that in six months' time they might withdraw the British troops from Egypt, but he was bound to say that he thought it was pure mad- ness for anyone to form that opinion. (Cheers.) What little foresight the Government bad! They had been com- pelled not only to withdraw the order for the retirement of the troops from Egypt,but they had had to send more troops to lligypt. (Cheers.) The order for the withdrawar of the ' troops was simply at the dictation of the Radicals. It was done in consequence of the pressure from Sir Wilfrid Law- son; it Was done because if they had not consented to with- draw the troops they would have bad withdrawn from them the support of the extreme Liberals. He never wished to raise the question of British interests, but after the expen- diture of blood and money which had taken piece in Egypt they were bound to insist that the work in Egypt should be done once for all, and if they withdrew, to take care that some other nation did not step in and do for us what we should have done ourselves. (Cheers,) We un- dertook this question because of the anarchy which pre- vailed in Egypt, and let them take care they did not leave the Egyptians in a worse condition than they found them, because if we did the honour and glory of this empire would greatly suffer. He wished he could be convinced that the present Government had that desire which he had—to maintain the integrity of the empire absolute and entire

UNVEILING OF A STATUE OF MR. GLADSTONE. On Thursday afternoon the statue.of Mr. Gladstone at tha City Liberal Club was unveiled by Mr. a W. Currie, presi- dent of the City of London Liberal Association, the pro- ceedings being presided over by Earl Granville, the president of the club. The preliminary proceedings took place in the library, which was crowded with members and friends, and amongst those present were Alderman Sir J. Lawrence, M.P., Alderman W. Lawrence, M.P., Mr. W. Fowler, M.P., Sir W. WArthur, M.P., Mr. R. B. Martin, M.P., Mr. R. K. Causton, M.P.—Lord Granville, who was received with cheers, said: I hays for a long time considered it a great honour to be president of this club, but I have never dis- charged the duties in connection with that office with so much pleasure as I do upon this occasion. (Hear, hear.) I. beg on behalf of the city of London Liberal Club so well represented here to-day to accept with warm thanks the present which has been made to this club of the statue of the remarkable man the leader of the Liberal party whose principles this institution was created to promote. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Currie has rightly interpreted the reason why I thought it better to , decline the honour which was proposed to me of taking the principal part on this occasion. I prefer confining myself Ito the duties of the official situation I bold. I made acqtaintance with Mr. Gladstone some 50 years ago. I be- came first his colleague some 30 years ago. During the latter half of the later period I had the honour of serving under him as my chief. During that time our relations, political and personal, have year by year become stronger and closer. (Cheers.) I feel that if I was merely to state simply and plainly my own opinion of Mr. Gladstone gathered by thcse years of observation my expression might appear to others to have a. colouring of something like ful- some exaggeration. But the language is not necessary. It takes a long time to build up a character like that of Mr. Gladstone. His official, his Parliamentary, his literary career have been as long before the public, so well observed or scanned, se appreciated that it requires no per- sonal friend to come and explain his claims to the gratitude of his countrymen. (Cheers.) There is one point, and one point only, on which I can speak with rather more authority than anyone here present. I have served under several Prime Ministers, men for whom I had high respect and for whom I had the greatest attachment, but I can say this, that I never knew one who showed a finer temper, greater patience, or more consideration for his colleagues than Mr. Gladstone in all deliberations upon any subject. In his official position with his knowledge, with his ability, and the wonderful power of work which characterises him, he. of course, has immense influence upon the deliberations of the Cabinet, but notwithstanding his enacity of purpose, his earnestness, it is quite extraordinary bow he attends to the arguments of all,:and excepting upon any question of real vital principle, he is willing to yield his own opinion to the general sense of the colleagues over whom be presides. (Cheers.) As to those who believed in Mr. Gladstone's being without any restraininginfluences, any influences of a Conservative kind in the best and highest sense, I think it just possible that they may find their mistake, even after their formation of the next Tory Government. (Cheers and laughter.) lam quite sure you agree with me in hoping that that event will be for a long time delayed. But Ido think that in the meanwhile it is well that passing events, such as the election at Ipswich yesterday—(cheers)—and the more general expression of opinion in such a representative assembly as this in this great city, should come to cheer one who, having no personal object of ambition left, is yet applying his unexhausted energies to the best interests and best services of his country. (Cheers.) I beg to accept in your name the statue which has been offered to the club this day. (Loud cheer- ing.)

ASHTON.

MAGIC LANTERN ENTRRTAINMENT.—A magic lantern entertainment was given in the Congregational School, Ashton, on Monday evening, by Mr. Arthur L. Evans of Raydock. The subject was "China and Chinese," after which a miscellaneous assortment of views and portraits were thrown upon the screen. Owing to the inclement weather there was not a very good attendance, but the en- tertainment was greatly enjoyed. PRESENTAT,ON TO A RETIRED YEOMANRY CORPORAL.— Corporal Paul Ogden, of the "A" (Ashton) troop of the Lancashire Hussais Yeomanry Cavalry, having decided to retire after 17 years' zealous and diligent service, his fellow Hussars showed their respect and esteem for him last even- ing (Thursday), when they presented him with a very handsome and valuable weather barometer. The members of the troop and a few friends partook of a sumptious repast at the house of Mr. Charles Paiater, the Robin Hood Hotel, after which the presentation was made. The barometer bore the following- inscription on a silver plate, "Presented to Corporal Paul Ogden by the officers, non-commissioned officers, and .men of the A' troop, Lancashire Hus- sars, as a mark of their esteem on his retirement after 17
- ' , ~ years service.

Bandies and Abbott came through the roof with a crash about half-past one, but luckily the bedrooms were not occu• pied, and the in.nales of the cottages found shelter with their neighbours. The wind was north-west, and the anxious and sleepless night of Liesday last will long be remem- bered.

div.head: CADISHEID.
div.p: CADISHEID.

A fierce storm raged over the whole of this village (luring the night asid the greater part of to-day (Wednesday). It has done cnsiderable damage to the roofs and chimneys of houses. Some of the houses literally trembled beneath the fury of the blast.

CHANGE RINGING.—On Sunday five of the local company assisted by Mr. W. Brown, of Runcorn, rang at the Parish Church for Divine service in the afternoon a 720 of plain bob misor in 2E3 minutes. The ringers stood as follows D. Houghton, sen , treble (conductor); P. Johnson, (2nd), W. Brown, (3rd), T. Ellison, (4th), P. iiimblett, (sth), T. Houghton, tenor.

FRODSFIAM. LUTHER COMILEMORATION.—A meeting was held in the Girls' School, Frodsham, on Monday evening, when Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., presided, and addresses were delivered by the Revs. C. LI. Wainwright, and W. Preston. WESLEYAN Foamlox MISSIONS.—The annual missionary meeting was held in the Five Crosses Chapel on Wednesday evening. The Rev. F. F. Edmonds presided, and the cause was advocated by the chairman, Rev. R. Harper, Widnes, and Rev. G. L. Allen, of Frodsham. CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS.—The annual sermons 'on behalf of the Church Sunday Schools were preached in the Parish Church on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rer..C. H. Wainwright, M.A., vicar of Christ Church, Blackpool. The collections amounted to upwards of £l4. SERVICE OF SONO.—A service of song entitled "Gems from the life of John Ashworth," was given in the school. room, adjoining Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Thursday evening, by a junior choir, which was ably assisted by a few friends. Mr. Kent conducted, and the choir gave evidence of careful training. The connective readings were read by the Rev. G. L. Allen, and Mr. Samuel Sharp presided at the harmonium. A DANGEROUS CORNER.—On Wednesday afternoon about half-past two, a gentleman was crossing, the Station-road, iu Church-street, Frodsham, when, without the slightest warn- ing, the driver of a farmer's spring cart which had been standing opposite Mr. Clarke's shop, made a sudden start for the station, and the shaft of the conveyance caught the un- suspecting pedestrian a smart blow on the shoulder, and but for his activity he would doubtless have sustained more ~serious injury. The inconvenient and dangerous approach to Frodshoin station has already been brought under the no- tice of the Riii way Company, and it is to be hoped that some improvement may be carried out. THE GALE.—The severe storm which prevailed on Tues- day night did considerable damage at Frodsham, the roofs of rl my of the houses on Wednesday morning presenting a wr, •Aed appearance. The Golden Lion :ne, at the corner of Church-street, suffered severely. and • a chimney to a house belorging to Mr. Wilson, in Fllnn-lane was blown down. At lielsby a chimney to cottages occupied by la.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLIORNE CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL. In aid of the funds of this school, the young men connected with the school gave the popular temperance drains, entitled "Trial of John Barleycorn,' on M:mday eveeing. The performers were attired in full and thoroughly representative court cos- tume, and as the piece was most excAlently gone through. the audience were amply repaid. We believe the "Trial" gave every satisfaction to those present. CHARGE OF DRITNIENNMS —At the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday lest, before G. McCorquodale, R. Hough- ton, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington, Esqs., Joseph Wyndhurst, of Golboroe, Iva!" charged with being drunk 3-td disorderly on the 3rd December. The defendant pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Whiting deposed that about 11 o'clock on the morning of the previous Monday he was sent for from Messrs. Brewis's Mid, by Mr. Richard Brewis.-... lie (Mr. Brewir) said the defendaat had come to his work drunk and refussd to leave when Ite was reqnested. He (witness) was oViged to turn him away.—William Bate,. lodgekeeper at the mill, gave eorrobolative evidence. The defendant stated that Mr. Brawls had discharged .him simply through spite, and that he (the defect) had only re-, ceived 235. per week, upon which he liksds to keep eight of a. family. Ile was-nea:dy "clammtd " out of the village. The Benoit c:!smissed the cam on the defeaChnt promising to pay costs.

div.head: ritTTON.
div.p: ritTTON.

WORKIEGMFeE; CLUB.—At the ordinary cemmittee meet- ing of the above held en Wednesday. .L .sesolation was' passed to close • the club,- which will tike elect in about three months' time. The institution has been ii existence seven years and e-belf. Its funds have latterly' fallen into arrear through vaeieus causes; Teti STORM..—The storm of Tuesday night peesing over this district caused consideratle' damage to preperty. A large stone was blown eff Huytou Perish Churchrand one of the few rernainineetketched cottages of the village occu- pied by a news agent,, was partially unroofed. bout 36' feet of the front breendary wail of the volunteers' new quarters was thrown down,• as were also walls he other exposed places. EZYTON FRIENDLY TONTINE rI.INEVIT SOCIETY.—.-Ther • above held their annual ieeting for the purpose of passing' the accounts of the p Ist year and election of officers, on - Monday last, in the read'ag-room of the Huyton Working- men's- Club. From the raport, it appears the past rear has-- been'a heavy one on the vick fund, £3S 'lloe. 40. haying been" paid in,sick relief; the freziety nurneere-63 members; and the income, £lll 18s. 7d. After deducting the amount paid.' to sick, working expenses, end new member proportion for " reserve fund, there remaincd £52 ss. 51. ler division, yield- - ing a dividend of 163. Bd. p.e• member, a result very gratify. Ting and surprising. The f ollowing were elected to serve' during the ensuing year :—President, John Large ; vice- - preaident, incr. Pinnington ; trustees, Philip Guy, Hy. Hewitson, and Win. Forrester ; treasurer, J. M. Walmsley ; secretary, James Whittaker; auditors. Wne. Sephton, James Barker, and James Walmsley. CIERISTMAS TREE AND SALE' Or WORlL.—khr Saturday,. a Christmas tree and sale of week was held- in. the Huyton Park Congregational Schoolrooms, on behalf of. the Zenana Mission. Notwithstanding the -unfavourable weather the attendance was large, and upwards of £7O was realised. Ihe rooms were very prettily decorate The laege Christmas tree, with ita lights and decorations and small articles for sale, was very attractive to the children. A well supplied and elegantly arranged refreshment stall wee presided over by Miss Turner, assisted by the Misses Capper and Moorby. An exceedingly popular feature of the afternoon and even- ing was the exhibition of living waxworks in-tableaux, re- preeenting characters from the woles of • Charlate Dickens. Great credit is due to Miss De Vooeld, who organised this entertainment, and also to her very efficient helpers. Amongst those who presided at tiee stalls, Chistmas tree, &e, were—Mrs. E. S. Eccles, Mrs. T. Evans, Mee. R. A. Gaskell, Madame De Vooghd, Mrs. Ward, Misses Banner, Blackleg-, Dean, Holt, Metcalfe, Walker, and Watkins. ENTERTAINMENT.—Mr. Win. A Stanley (of London) gave one of his dramatic and humorous recieals in the • Elnyton and Roby schools on Monday last,- under the auspices of the Church of England Temperance Society (Huyton Branch.) The vicar, Cancer Penrhyn, presided. Tht audience was good considering the very inclement weather. The programme, which consisted of two Dart's, was well received, Mr. Stanley being recalled at the close. Dur- an interval the Rev. H. A. Maenaughten (vicar of Prescot)e. gave an eddress ; he illustrated with humourous anecdotes the different views people took of the temperance question. Remarking on the difficulties of ths. early temperance workers' he said the Church of England Temperance Society had just come of age, having been in existence 21 years, and had made its power for good felt in all ranks and classes of society. The ladies of the committee were-wearing their blue ribbon at their universities. Five hundred under. graduates had joined their society, and the medical men were turning round to their side. HITYTOM COMPANY 2ND ENGINEER VOLUNTEERS : NEW HEADQUARTERS.--The above premises, known as Whitfield House situate in Roby, were opened on Monday evening. The place has been thoroughly renovated, painted, papered, fitted, and furnished on a liberal scale with every requisite for use as military quarters and a recreative club. The house stands back from the road in its own grounds, surrounded with gardens well planted with trees and shrubs. On the ground floor are—a spacious room, provided with papers, dominoes, draughts, chess, cards, &c; a billiard room for the use of officers and honorary members, and a canteen •, to the rear is a large building which has been partitioned. One portion, measuring 30 by 21 feet, is to be used as an armoury; the other, about 30 feet square, has been fitted for a billiard room for the use of sappers and non-commissioned officers. The painting and decorating was entrusted to Mr. Wainwright, if Huyton; and the fitting and furnishing were carried out by Messrs. Okell, of Liverpool. The rooms are all laid with linoleum with the exception of the officers' quarters, which have a rich carpet of neat design: The furniture is upholstered in maroon leather. A portion of the premises are occupied by Drill-Instructor Goss ; and the newly-appointed manager, D. G. Johnson, also resides on the spot. The rooms are open from a.m. to 11 p.m. A feature of the institution is that honorary members are admitted to its privileges by payment of ea annual subscrip- tion of a guinea, whilst those joining the corps subscribe six shillings per annum. HUYTON• QUARRY.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL—A public tea meeting and lecture took place in the above place of worship, on Monday last, in aid of the Mission Funds. About 250 sat down to tea,. the tables were provisioned at the expense of a number of ladies and gentlemen of the congregatioa. The following ladies presided :—Mrs. Varley, Mrs. Wilkinson' Mrs. and Miss Lydiatt, Miss Fryer, Mis. Barton, Mrs. Hodgeon, the • Misses Wainwright, the Misses Ellisons, Mrs. Perkins, Mrs. Itimraer, and Mrs. Preston. When the tables were removed, Mr. J. Jones took the chair, there were also on the platform the Rev. B Varley, Mr. William Thartne (of Liverpool),. and Mr. Barton. The proceedings opened with singing and prayer, after which the choir,. under the leadership of Mr. Edward Jones, sang the anthem, "Put on thy strength, CP, Zion," Miss Wainwright presiding at the harmonium. The Chairman, in a few brief remarks on the object of the meet- ing, commended the liberality displayed And the energy put forth to accomplish it. He then introducad Mr. Theme, who gave a lecture on " Hogarth and his pictures." At the. close of the lecture the choir again sang an anthem "In Jewry is Gnd known." The proceedings closed with hearty votes of thanks.
IRLAM.

A temperance sermon- was preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Irbil% last Sunday morning—recognised in the Wesleyan Connexion as Temperance Sunday—by the Rev. R. Dillon to a good congregation, from Proverbs 23rd chapter and the 21st verse. The discourse was powerful and impressive—sustained by facts—and heard with deep attention by the people throughout. WINSFORD. TEMPERANCE ENTERTAINMENT, WINSPORD.---A temper- ance entertainment was given in the Free Methodist school- room, High-street, Winsford, consisting of songs, choruses, recitations, &c. Mr. Mawdsley was in the chair, and after the opening hymn and prayer he gave an address, after which the following programme was gone through : Pianoforte solo, Miss Beckley; chorus, "Oh, the better time," choir ; recitation, The lips that touch liquor shall never touch mine," Miss M. Bennett; chorus, "Do what you can," choir; song, "1 wander why he comes not home," Miss Smith: recitation, Mr. W. Hough; chorus, Dash it down," choir; song, Mr. W. Hough. Mrs. Weedall opened the second part with a pianoforte solo, after which the choir sang "The doc•or ;"son, 'Touch not, taste not," miss, C. Smith ; dialogue in character, "The pillars of intemper- ance," Messrs. E. Bennett. C. Kay, W. Year sky, and J. Davies; duet (pianoforte and piccolo), Mrs. Weedall and My. Hamlet ; recitation, " Beauti'iul snow," Miss Smith ; chorus, "Hark, the temperance trumpet," choir. There was a very good audienv, who showed by frequent aPPlau" their appreciation. Another temperance meeting was-held in the same place on Tuesday night, presided over by Mr. Joseph Slater, and again on Wednesday night. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.. a. series LIBERALISM IN Wisr Cmcsorno.—The first of of Liberal demonstrations in furtherance of the candidature of Mr. James Tonekinson and Mr. Duncan for the represen- tation of West Cheshire was held on Monday night at Crewe, under the presidenzy of the Rev. W. Mellor. Mr. Tomkinson said the Liberal creed was to trust the people, to educate, elevate, and improve their position, and this they should do in spite of all opposition from the Tories. The Liberals had been in office during three-fourths of the, period that had elapsed since the passing of the great Re-. form Bill, and had been engaged in enacting wise and hence ficial laws in pite or the opposition and tnisrepresentation:, of the Tories, who were at present enjoying the labours of Liberal Governments. The same spirit existed now among the Tories that had plunged the country into innumerable disasters, that alienated the coloniee of America, and in- creased the national debt by £200,000,000. he was sure their confidence in the Government was unabated. Mr. Duncan, referring to educevion, said until they had school boards established all over the country they would heve a faulty system of education and that meant the greatest danger of this country drifting back and getting behind other countries.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1883.

ETERY earmest Liberal has this week cause for rejoicing that a Liberal has been re- turned for Ipswich, and a complete and deci- sive answer thus returned to York. Since the latter election our Tory friends have lost no opportunity of dinning it into our ears that the Government had suffered discredit throughout the country, that its so called in- competence had been found out, and that, in fact, like the election at Stroud in 187+, the return of Sir F. MILNER was a warning that the Cabinet could not much longer hold together. The tune of these Tory orators will now, we are sure, be pitched in a much lower koy. It is admitted on all.hands that the defeat of Mr. LOCKWOOD was a substan- tial Tory victory, but it is not difficult to ' account for it. There were local circum- stances surrounding the York contest which it is impossible to ignore in arriving at a sound judgment as to immense cause of the Liberal de- feat there. The influence and popula- rity of the M/LNER family, combined with the comparative obscurity of Mr. LOCKWOOD and the fact that in a corrupt constituency such as York he was the supporter of the principle of the Corrupt Practices Act by which so many electors were deprived of the payment they had received at previous contests for their votes, are elements sufficient in themselves to explain Sir F. MILNER's success. A Govern- ment which redresses grievances and inaugu- rates salutary reforms always throws itself open to obloquy and abuse for a time, and at York this was experienced in no small degree. At Ipswich the contest, we should say, has been fought on very equal terms. Mr. WEST, the Liberal candidate, was well known, having represented the constituency from 1868 to 1g74; but he was defeated in the latter year, and again in 1880, so that his prospects of success in this contest could not be the brightest. His opponent, Mr. CHARLEY, it is true, was not known locally, but he had made himself somewhat famous as the mem- ber for Salford in the last Parliament, and as the Common Sergeant of the City of London he was not without a high testimonial in his favour. Ipswicki recently has been some- what fickle in its choice of representatives,

but as . a rule it 'has always proved itself more Li }:Jeral than Conserva- tive. The Liberals won both seats at the ele :ction after the passing of the firstP...eform Bill in 1832, it returned two I''.:oeral representatives in 1835 also, and sub- sequently, at the general election in 1841 the year in which PEEL was returned to power by a Conservative majority—the constituency remained true to Liberal principles and re- turned two Liberal members again. From 18+7 to r 868,however, therepresentation was divided between the Liberals and Conservatives. At the general election in iS6B the constituency again returned two Liberals to St. Stephen's, , but in 1874 these were supplanted by two Conservatives. The senior member died in 1875, and Mr. T. C. COBBOLD, the late Con- servative member, Who had immense local in- fluence, was then returned by 2,213 votes, against 1,607 recorded for the Liberal can- didate, Mr. W. NEWTON. The representa- tion,.therefore, still remained with the Con- servatives solely. At the general election in 1880 the representation was again divided between the two parties, a Liberal and a Conservative being returned. Mr. T. C. COBBOLD (Conservative) headed the poll with 3,142 votes, Mr. JESSE COLLINGS (Radical) came next with 3,074, after him came Mr. WEST (Liberal) with 3,025, and Mr. BULWER (Conservative) was last on the poll with 2,979. The poll on Wednesday, it appears, was an exceptionally large one The register contains the names of 7,826 voters, but it is estimated that deaths and removals will reduce the number to 7,000. Of these over 6,000 voters exercised their privilege, with the result that Mr. WEST headed the poll with 3,266 votes, Sir WILLIAM CHARLEY receiving only 2,816. Mr. WEST was conse- quently elected by a majority of 450, a majority which much more than counter- balances the adverse vote at York. It will be noticed from the figures that the Liberal candidate has on this occasion polled 192 votes mire than did Mr. JESSE COLLINGS in 1880, whilst on'the other hand Sir WILLIAM CHARLEY'S poll is 326 votes below that recorded for Mr. COBBOLD at the general , election. We accept the result of the contest as a convincing proof that Liberal principles are becoming more widely diffused and more generally adopted in the constituency, and NIT doubt not that before another election takes place the grewth of Liberalism will be still more marked. It is evident that the fight has been one for principles pure and simple, and in the result those which make for progress have been successful, as they are always sure to be. The electors prefer to a policy of brag, bluster, and unnecessary expenditure, a policy of peace, retrenchment, and reform. Their decision is another indication that the country is determined to have the borough and county franchise assimilated, and a more equal distribution of the electoral power; and we take it, moreover, that the decision of the electors of Ipswich shows ' they are opposed to the maintenance of an unreformed Corporation such as that which Sir WILLIAM CHARLEY represents. The vic- tory has been won notwithstanding the grossest misrepresentations, and in face of a violation of the spirit, if not the letter, of the Corrupt Practices Act. It is consequently the more significant. The appeal of the Tory agent to the cabmen at Ipswich to re- member, when deciding for whom they should vote, that the Liberal Government had made it illegal to let, or even lend, licensed cabs for the conveyance of voters to the poll, and the appeal of the Chairman of the Con- servative Committee to his Tory friends, and especially those in the country, to lend vehicles for the day of the clection,prove in the one case a reliance upon prejudice rather than prin- ciples for success ; in the other the existence of a fear of fightinz with clean hands, and a desire to, if possible, run a coach-and-four through one of the best Acts of Parliament which has yet been passed for the conduct of elections. A cause bolstered up by such con- temptible tricks can never be a winning cause, and the sooner such tricks are aban- doned the better. Lord SALIS3URY, by the I way, made merry over the York election; his lordship's explanation of the Ipswich defeat will be awaited with much interest. At Ips- wich there has been no Irish vote to quibble about; what, then, will the quibble be? Without attaching too much importance to the contest, we think w e may fairly claim that Mr. WEST'S return is at least a severe re- buke to Tory jubilation jubilation of a character not justified by the facts and cir- cumstances surrounding the York contest.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The well•kn OW n coloured jubilee singers gave entertainments of sacred songs in this place of worship on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday even- ings. FORTHCOMING MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.—A. musical festival, in connection with St. Paal's Wesleyhn Chapel, will take place in the Public Hall, on Monday even- ing. Several local vocalists are announced to sing, and there will be a powerful chorus of 200 voices. TIER CONSECRATION OF ST. AMBROSS CHURCEL—The services in connection with this ceremony were continued on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. H. A. McNaughten, vicar of Prescot, preached ; and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. J. H. Chambers, vicar of Hale- wood. Collections were made on behalf of the Boundary Wall Fund.

Tnß SMALLPDX EPIDIIIIIO IN WIDNES.—We regret to state that Mr. Higginson, surveyor to the Local Board, has been attacked with a mild form of smallpox, and for several weeks he will be unable to perform:his duties. There is no doubt be received contagion while assisting at the hospital, where he has been zealously working for some time. On Monday, the walls of the town were -placarded with large posters urgently recommending all parents whose children had not been successfully vaccinated to have the operation performed at once. During the night several of the posters were defaced with tar. There was a good deal of comment in the town on the matter. Another smallprix patient was admitted into the hospital on Sunday, and thus the discharge of the whole of the patients who were nearly convalescent will be delayed about a fortnight.

ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Sohn Rush, a middle-aged man of dissolute ap- pearance, was charged with stealing a jacket, value 23., the property of the executors of Charles Neil, pawnbrokers, Widnes. About three o'cldck, on the Bth instant, the jacket (produced) was hanging over the shop window of the pro- secutor. On the evening of the same day the prisoner gave it to Thomas Smith, labourer, Lugsdale-road, who gave in- formation to P.C. Moore. The prisoner was also charged with stealing five shirts, worth 68., the property of Sarah Colquitt, of 33, Anne-street West, Widnes. These articles had been missed from the shop. The prisoner had sold four of them at Is. each to the witness Smitla.—The prisoner, who protested that he had purchased the articlas in a pub- lic-house, was sent to gaol for a month-14 days' on each charge.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AIITHORITY.—Tbe usual fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there were present John Ashton (in the chair), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, and Messrs. J. Challoner, E. Wallington, J. Weir, J. Mclntyre, C. Rigby, J. Darbyshire, W. Pickering, IL Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (delatty-clerk), and J. Far% rington (inspector.)—The inspector reported that a nuisance was existing in Halton-road, arising from defective drainage. A notice had been served but had expired. After some con- sideration, it was decided that proceedings should be taken. It was also reported that various cottages situate at Wilders- pool and Helsby were without a wholesome water supply, and directions were given for notices to be served for a proper supply to be provided.—Certificates of analysis of waters from pumps and wells in the townships of Appleton, Moore, and Kockwick were read and considered satisfactor'y. It was reported that a new house at Helshy had been oc- cupied in contravention of the Public Health (Water) Ace, 1878. It was decict d that proceedings should b. taken The inspector was directed to submit a sample of this water for analysis. Permission was also given for sample!: to be procured from pump Wells at Wilderspool.

div.head: TITE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15. IRR3.
div.p: TITE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15. IRR3.

PROMOTION OF A RUNCORN CUSTOM ROUSE OFFICIAL. The changes at the Customs House, Runcorn, have resulted in the promotion of Mr. J. Harty, to the position of beard lofficer. THE CHILD DESERTION AT WlDNES.—Catherine Dog- hasty, domestic servant, Bolton, who deserted her child under circumstances reported in our last issue, was again brought before the Widnes magistrates on Wednesday, and after promising to pay the amount owing to the Guardia's, via., £2 5e., she was discharged.—Mr. Scannell represented the Guardians. LECTURE AT RUNCORN.— The Rev. J. Williams, of Chester, on Monday evening delivered a lecture on " Watts and his hymns," in St. John's Presbyterian Chapel. Mr. W. B. Gibson- occupied the chair. At intervals the choir sang hymns composed by Dr. Watts; Mr. Richardson aceom- panyiag on the organ. The proceeds were devoted to the Sunday School Library. Tan VALUATION OF Wanxes.—The appeal of the Widnes Overseers against the basis or standard of county rate was heard at Preston on Wednesday. It was supported by Mr. Wareing (overseer), Mr. Goff (assistant overseer), and Mr. Allen (clerk to the Local Beard). Mr. S. H. Hartley was also present to represent the Guardians. The justices ac- cepted the overseers' valuation. TEMPERANCE MEETING AT RUNCORN.—The first of a series of temperance meetings in connection with Bethesda Congregational Church was held in the lecture-room on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Rev. J. D. Thomas. Addresses were delivered by Mrs. Vanse and Mr. J. D. Jones. Mrs. Vause advocated the establishment of a Women's Temperance Soeiety at Runcorn. WEsToie CHURCH BAND CONCERT.—A concert in aid of this band was held in the National Schools on Tuesday. The Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., presided. Songs, recitations, and readings were given by Miss Clarke, Miss Hibbert, Messrs. W. Armsrong, J. Yates, J. J. Speakman, and John Hough. The band, under the conductorship of Mr. T. Wood, rendered several pieces in good style. THE REV. EDWARD SMITH AT WIDNES.—On Sunday night this popular Wesleyan preacher, who some years ago was a scholar in one of the local Sunday schools, occupied the pulpit at Victoria-road Chapel. The interest in his ap- pearance was manifested by the large congregation which assembled. During his discourse the preacher paid an elo- quent tribute of praise to the late Mr. Gill for his labours in the Methodist cause. RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB V. LIVERPOOL GYMNASIUM.— From our announcement columns it will be seen that these clubs will play at Runcorn on Thursday afternoon next, on behalf of the Y.M.C.A., which incurred a some- what heavy debt in their charitable undertaking last Christmas. On the evening of the same day the members of the gymnasium will give an assault-at-arms in the Public Hall, when some clever and interesting performances may be anticipated. CONCERT AT THI3 NATIONAL SCHOOLS, WIDNES.—In the National Schools, Widnes, on Tuesday evening, an enter- tainment of a very interesting and enjoyable character was given by the pupils of Mrs. Pemberton's seminary, Simm's Cross, who were allied with Mrs. Barfoot, Misses Barfoot, Mr. Barfoot, and their pupils of St. Helens. The programme was varied and tastefully arranged, and the performance gave unbounded delight to the large audience which had assembled. The proceeds were devoted to St. Paul's Build- ing Fund. VOLUNTEER PARADE AT RUNCORN.—TIIO .twentY-fourth anniversary of the 2nd Chester Rifle Volunteers oj..7"rred on Sunday, when the Runcorn companies attended divias service in the morning under the command of Captain C. , W. Hazlehurst. The other officers present were Adjutant Kerr, and Lieutenants Timmins and Joule. The muster was not so large as on former occasions, about 100 of the rank and file putting in an appearance. An appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev. R. Edwards, curate in charge of Newtown Mission Church. THE SALVATION ARMY AT RUNCORN.—The members of the Runcorn Salvation Army haeing secured ground for the proposed new barracks, are now seeking funds wherewith to commence operations. On Saturday and Sunday Com- missioner Railton, of London, took command. There were also present contingents from the various points of battle- field. The captain and lieutenant of the Runcorn corps are about to leave the town to conduct engagements with the army in another quarter, and both gave farewell addresses to large audiences. The utmost enthusiasm characterised the whole proceedings. SALE OF WORK AT RUNCORN.—In Holy Trinity Church schoolroom' on Wednesday afternoon, a sale of work was held on behalf of the Church Missionary Society and Past- oral Aid Society. The varied selection of goods which occupied the delis were the work of a number of young ladies who meet fortnightly at the Trinity Parsonage. The stalls were in charge of Mrs. Preston, Mrs. Martin, Mrs. Lea, Mrs. Buckley, Mrs. Whitaker, Mrs. Fisher, Mrs. Rob- inson, Mrs. Garrett, Mrs. Tomlinson, the Misses Smith, Miss Martin, Miss Fisher, Miss Timmins, Miss Preston, Miss Lea, Miss Liaison, Miss Middlebrook, and Miss Warner. I refreshment stall was under the management of Miss Stubbs, Miss Tyrii' and Miss Leathwood. The receipts of the sale of the work amounted to £22.

IMPORTANT SHIPPING CASE. At Whitehavera County Court, on Thursday, a case from Runcorn, connected with the Bridgewater Navigation Co., was decided. In August last a W hitehaven shipping firm conveyed per steamer 230 tons of pig iron from Glasgow to Runcorn, consigned to Messrs. Baird and Co., iron merchants. On arrival at Run- corn the iron was weighed at the quay, and found nearly three tons short, but there was nearly three tons of sand and scrap cleared out of the vessel's hold. The agent of this Bridgewater Canal, considering that that they were respon- sible to the consignees, the action was brooght against the shippers for three tons short of iron. The shippers pre- tended that they delivered all iron as shipped with them, and that it was well known that quantities of sand adhered to pig iron which must be knocked out when shipped. Mr. Linaker, of Runcorn, who appeared for Messrs. Baird, con- tended that the shippers were responsible for 250 tons of iron specified in the bill of lading, and the Liverpool judge had so decided in similar oases. Judge Ingham now decided in favour of the shipping firm, and against Messrs. Baird. Notice of appeal was given.

RUNCORN BOARD OF G lIARDIAIT S.—The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. There were present :—Mr. John Ashton (ii the chair), Revs. J. Lockwood, and J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. J. Weir, J. Challoner, W. Pickering, E. Wallington, T. Nor- man, J. Handley, Whittaker, J. Mclntyre, J. Derbyshire, C. Rigby, J. T. Hamilton, Joseph Smith, Francis Fairhurst, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board ask- ing for a list of the children in the schools entitled to certifi- cates. Mr. Linaker said that there were 31 boys and 16 girls entitled to them. This was considered very satisfac- tory.-4 precept from the county authorities was presented for payment amounting to £1,139 14s. 3d., which consisted of county rate, £713 17s. id.; constabulary general ex- penses, £B9 3s. id.; constabulary local expenses, £336 14s. ld.—The Rev. J. Lockwood gave notice that that day ntonth he would move that Mr. Alfred Woodyear be ap- pointed school attendance officer for the ,iistricts of Weston, Halton, Clifton, Stockham, and Norton, at a salary of £l5 a year, in the place of Mr. Wright, who resigned at the last meeting.—the ntixt meeting of the Board will be held on Monday, December 24th.

- WIDNES POLICE COAT.—Yesterday, before Messrs. Pil- kington and Brock, John O'Brien, a young man, was charged with stealing a coat, the property of Mrs. Jameson, pawnbroker, Ann-street West. About six o'clock on Tues- day night Mrs. M,.oney, who occupies a shop facing the prosecutor's, saw the prisoner take a coat off a nail inside the door and put it under his arm. She informed Mrs, Jamieson,who seized the prisoner, but he had in the meantime passed the coat on to a confederate, who had run away. He was pursued, but when captured the stolen article was not in his possession. It was subsequently found under the window of Neil's pawnshop. Subsequently P.C. Moores ap- prehended the prisoner, who in extenuation of his offence, pleaded that he was drunk. He was sent to gaol for a month.—Alfred Knock, 24 years of age, living in Warring- ton-road, Widnes, was brought up on remand, charged with urglariously entering the Castle Inn, and stealing 28s be- longing to Mrs. Rachael Brown, on the 28th November. The circumAances have been previously reported. Inspector Wood said he had no further evidence to (der, and he bad been instructed by Superintendent Barker to ar.k their wor- ships to discharge the prisoner. The pi isoner was dis- charged.

THE CANADIAN JUBILEE SINONLIS la RUNCORN...-. The Canadian Jubilee Singers, who are making a tour through- out England for the purpose of raising funds to establish a theological institute for the training of young men for the propogation of the Gospel in Africa, visited Runcorn on Thursday. Mr. T. Handley pre- sided, and delivered an appropriate address. During the eveninc, Bishop Disney, who is in charge. of the party, de- livered an address. He said the singers who had taken patt I in the concert were Africans, whose parents had fled into ' Canada so that they might enjoy liberty and their God.given rights. They bad been engaged in various branches of Church work in the provinces of Canada, and in the West Indies, ani the Southern States of America. Their object was to establish a mission in their beloved fatherland. Africa was near and dear to them, and while there were teeming millions of their countrymen bowing to gods of their own they felt it their duty to give a helping hand to christianize sad civilize their brethren. They were fitted for the work, and there were hundred° of young men willing to share in the work. For the purpose of establishing the institute they came to England and appealed for help. The music was of a quaint description, rendered with great taste and effect. The collections realised upwards of £3. LECTURE ON " LIFEBOATS "AT NEWTON. Under the auspices of the Newton-le-Willows Working Men's Club, a public lecture on "Lifeboats, and their adventures" was de- livered in the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, by Mr. Jos. Corbett, hon. sec. to the Manchester Branch of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. The Newton club some months ago was affiliated to the the Manchester and District Working Men's Clubs Association, one of the benefits of which is the providing of lectures at stated intervals, or when required. The lecture on Tuesday last was the first given under the new arrangement, and there was a mode- rately large audience. The chair was occupied by the Rev. IL Mink, and there were also present Dr. Watkins (vice- president), Messrs. E. Fairclough, Parks, W. D. Burdis' (tn. The lecture consisted of an interesting history of the life- boat from the earliest period up to the present, with a pleasing narration of several remarkable incidents connected with the liCeboat. Illustrated with miniature models and diagrams, the subject was made much more attrh,ctivs, and at the close a bearty vote Of than!-3 was accorded to the -lecturer.

Eastlake is nothing at all. A play of this kind shims the difference between inaaufactured and spontaneous acting. One wants Ellen Terry or Madgeeka. But the play acts itself. The interest is incessant, and is a crescendo, till the great scene comes, of which no small part ef the praise due to it is that, spectacular and sensational as it is, it is an integral part of the play, and not a bit- of vulgar car- pentering excrescence. Miss Auderson's " Galatea" is but a qualified success. The great art is the art that conceals art ; the little art—and that is hers—is the art which con- ceals nature. She is very statuesque, aud there are those who think she is very beaatiful. It is a face that you like best, first. There is little variety, and the poses are all graceful ; the transitions from one to another show how arti- ficial they all are. Two provincial successes have ceme to London this week. The Compton Company are at the Strand. That rattling, kind-hearted, rather laoister-. one play of "Wild Oats" takes and deserves to take. One likes to be reminded of a style of play and acting that delighted our fathers, and our fathers like to go and see it. But the truth is we have got so luxurious in our ideas of stage management, that anything ekort of perfection breaks illusion. Twelfth night has been given, and the audience felt themselves in the Strand Theatre, not at the Court of the Duke of Ulzria. We have been made spoilt children. Mr. Terry is delighting his audience over the way with the Rocket, and that stupid " Ariel," with its crowd of well-made sparsely-covered fairies, kas been with- drawn after a not very successful run.

Every one will be sorry to hear of the death of Dicky Doyle. He had to some extent survived his immortality— as an artist, and this generation needs to be reminded that the present title page of ?tench was the work of his pencil. To that periodical he contributed larger cartoons in the days when Mark Lemon was editor, Thackeray, one of the writers, Lord John Russell, the favorite butt, and before illanniel had. come upon the scene as an illustrator. Then he dropped out of public notice. He was not heard of and he was forgotten. But when the Grosvenor Gallery opened its wall space to the kind of talent that the forty Academicians were resolved to reject, a little bit of room was kept for the forgotten Dicky Doyle. He came back upon the new race of picture seers like an old man of the mountains, and like him brought in his company a whole troupe of sprites, and goblins, and warlock. For three or four seasons we ha tl their diorama of goblins, curious little ariel subjects that no other painter would have had the peculiar fancy to evoke except Doyle's own countryman, Maclise, whose illustra- tions to the chimes might well have come from Dicky's pencil. He and Hablpt Brown and Leech were a school of their own old-fashioned crew, aid thrust into ob- livion by younger and stronger men. They had still a grave and a humour that more clever pencils hays some- ko,i missed, and it is to be renteiribtred of them that they were the 11:et reaction from the yalgar strength and brutal , power of such sten as Gilroy antl Aoniandva, On Monday poor Dicky diPerl with home Meade at the old fogej flub the A.thensium, where in his salad days he and Thackeray used so often to meet. On Tuesday his fellow guests learned with a shock tkat he was dead. They could have better spared a better-known Plan. I saw Mario this winter in Rome, a white haired oli man with the bright little black eyes and the same look of distinction and dignity that was one of his chief charms on the stage. He was living in a state of what, to such a men, must have been great poverty, occupying—if Ido not mistake—the basement of his own house, the rest of which had been let out. What money he made in hie time, aud bow royally he spent it. Mario was a virtuoso strange that he should have ended his days as the curator of a museum. Once he had a musenm of his own, as the crowd, who thronged Christie's Rooms when his col- lection was sold some years ago, could well judge. He sang frequently in almost every great city in Europe, but London and Petersburg were his favourite cities. He made his debit in Paris, but he did not care much for the Parisians, and in the end they hissed hint. Everyone has heard the story of him and Grisi and the childsen walking in St. Petersburg and the Czar coming up. "Are these your little Grisettes," said Etnperor Nicholas.- Grist was not quick at repartee. Her husband was. " No, sire. They are her Marionettes."
RUNCORN AND WIDNES CANARY
SOCIETY'S SHOW.

The third annual show of this society was held yester- day afternoon in Lacey-street schoolroom. There was a splendid show of birds, and they were viewed by a large number of spectators. The entries numbered 21, being a great increase on last year. The show was under the patron- age of the Right Hon. Sir R. A. Cross, M.P., Colonel J. Ireland-Blackburne, M.P., and other local gentlemen. Mr. J. Sherratt is secretary of the society, Mr. W. B. Pickthal! treasurer, and the following form the committee of manage- ment :—S. Davies (chairman), J. Smith (vice-chairman), J. Barnett, J. Stevenson, J. Coiner, J. Lewes, D. Dale, J. G-le- nean, S. Walker, E. Knowles, R. Crompton, and J. Whalen. The prise list is unavoidably held over. _
