div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, Mr. F. H. Gossage, and Mr. John Brock, Thos. Woods, Church-street, John Bennett, Waterloo-road, and Mary Clark, Ann-street, were each summonei to answer a charge of keeping a refreshment house without a licence.— Mr. Heal, supervisor of Inland, Revenue. Runcorn, prose- cuted.—The charges were all proved by Mr. Coghlan, Inland Revenue officer, Chester.—The defendants, who pleaded guilty, are retailers of a liquor termed herb beer. Mr. Coghlan hal paid a visit to each establishment after ten pm. on the 13th October, and bad been supplied with a glass of the liquor, although the defendants were not licensed to keep refreshment heusee.—Mr. Gentles, solicitor, ef Warrington, wk 4 appeared for Bennett. explained that it was his client's boy who, served the liquor.—The Bench fined each defeadant 20s. and costs, 12e.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the cemetery on Wed- nesday afternoon, Mr. Moss in the chair. There were present Messrs. J. Handley, Coleburn, Littler, Briscoe, Nor- man, and Salkel (secretary). Mr. Handley moved the con- firmation of the Finance Committee's report, which siat,d that the fees received during the month amounted to £27 78. The secretary had received ZSO from the overseers on account of current expenses, and that sum had been paid into bank. Accounts amounting to £22 14s Pd were passed for payment. The secretary reported that consols had been purchased with the £l2O received from the overseers for sinking fund and that the whole of the sinking fund was now invested in consols. The committee recommended that interest amounting to £32 6e 3d be paid. The minutes were passed. The secretary stated that during Tuesday night the cemetery palisadings had bead seriously damaged, some portions of it being thrown down through the contrac- tors' hut on the opposite side of the road having been carried across the road very violently. The secretary was instructed to write to Mr. Berkett, the contractor, with reference thereto.
A DANGEROUS LEVEL CROSSING AT WIDNES. FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENr.

On Tuesday- morning, Mr. T. W. Barker, the ceunty coroner, held an inquiry at the Albert Hotel, Appleton, touching the death of Malachi Cassidy, 58 years of age, who lived at 17, Joseph-street, Appleton, who was killed on the London and North-western Railway on Friday evening. Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street station, Liverpool, represented the railway company. Mr. W G. Hargreaves was foreman of the jury.—Evidence was adduced by Mrs. Catherine Cassidy, wife of the deceased, Mr. J. A Bullough, 19, Deacm-road, Appleton, Mr. Charles Davies, Page Villa, Appleton, and Mr. William Coulter, stationmaster, Appleton. It seemed that about a quarter past five on Friday evening, the deceased left home with the intention of visiting a man who lived in Lugsdale, and in order to get to his destination, he would be _compelled to pass the Bradley railway crossing. About twenty-five min- utes past five, Cassidy was found lying in the four-foot a few yards from the crossing by Mr. Bullough, who im- mediately went to the railway station to stop all trains; and then returned to the scene of the accident, accompanied by the etationmaster. Cassidy, who was conscious, was re- moved to the station, where he was attended by Dr. McLen- nan, who pronounced the case hopeless, the deceased having a fractured skull and other injuries. The stationmaster was of opinion that the deceased had been knocked down by a passenger train which left Appleton at 5-23, and then run I over again by a coal train which went in the same direction I a minute or two afterwards.—The foreman of the jury re- marked that the crossing was quite nnprotected.—Mr. Fer- rand: The company are building a footbridge there. Mr. Farrant (a juryman) said the crossing was much used by workingalen and school children, and there ought to be some protection.—The Coroner: Are there no gates ?—Mr. Far- rant: Nothing at all. The Coroner: Is there no notice board warning the publie of approaching trainc—Mr. Far- rant: There is not.—The Foreman said the road was an old highway and the company could not close it.—Mr. Coulter said the footbridge would be completed in a week.—Mr. Farrant thought the week would not be one of seven days, and in the meantime he thought a person should be placed at the gates to warn foot passengers.—Mr. Ferrand said al- though the company were placing a footbridge at the cros- sing there were very few people he felt sure who would take the trouble to use it even for their own safety.—The Coro- ner: Responeibility will be removed from the railway com- pany Mr. Ferrand said he would convey to the proper quarter the wish of the jury with regard to placing a man at the crossing until the bridge was completed. A verdict of accidental death was recorded.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE NEW SPEAKER AND THR NEW PEER-A RETIRING JUDGE-SIR CHARLES DILLE ON CIRCUIT-ENGLISH ART AND FRENCH MANU- FACTURES-LORD COLERIDGE AND THE BENCH- MR. ISWINBURNE -THE THEATRES, CLAUDIAN, PYGMALION AND GALATEA, THE COMPTONS, EDWARD TERRY.--DICKY DOYLE- MARIO.
LONDON, TMSDAY.

The appointment to nee Speaker's chair may be regarded As filled. Of course the Speaker is the officer not of the Government, but of the House. Still the present selection is not likely to be opposed. Three weeks ago Mr. Peel would have been thought scarcely a likely candidate, and three months ago he would almost not have been mentioned. The retirement of Sir Healy Brand adds no new peerage tie the rolls of the Upper House. Sir Henry will succeed by inheritance to the barony of Were. The new peer, who is to take his seat when Parliament meets, has met with but a sorry reception from the country. It is not a political ap- pointment, and Tories, Whigs, and Radicals are combined in thinking that Mr. Tennyson is making a blunder. I fancy the explanation is family iniuence. The whole tendency St the laureate's writings, as well as of his life, is against the enjoyment or even the appreciation of such a dignity, but Mrs. Tennyson will like to be called "My Lady," and the civil service clerk will be glad to pat " The Honourable Lionel" on his card. The new peerage is not likely to die out. There are sons and granicens.

What has often been prophesied sometimes comes true. Vice-Chancellor Bacon, tke last of the Vice-Chancellors and the oldest Judge in the world, is going to retire. For many years he has had two peculiarities. He understood Eng- lish bankruptcy laws, and he was (and is) exceedingly deaf. There have been other Judges nearly as deaf, and some one or two who understood bankruptcy, but the combination only existed in this ermined Nestor, now in his eighty- seventh year. The Judge on the bench who most nearly approaches hind in deafness l 3 Mr, Justice Field, and Mr. Justice Field is to be his successor.

All through the week Sir Charles Dilke has,been engaged in hie eireuit tbrongh horrible London. He has visited chiefly tha East End, but squalor and poverty are to be found under all the postal letters. The great tracts and continents of misery are chiefly in the east, but the present movement has shown that in some of the richest quarters there is sharp wretchedness and destitution. Every parish has its rookery, as the parish olergy well know. But what is strangest is that these are often quite cuss to highly- rented squares and terraces. There was a very notable rookery inKensingtoi, a sort of Tom-All-Alone's; there it had been for years a fever trap, a. haunt of crime, of drunken- ness, and of disease, till Baron Grant conceived the idea of building his palace. The tenants were compensated and ejected from their squalid tenements, and the new little reel brick seethetic colony which is to be planted on the site of his pleasure erounds will be the only thing left to show where Kensington Rookeries were the plague spot of a rich neighbourhood. This is not, however, the way a statesman must treat each a difficulty.

Sir Charles had a pleasant duty when he gave away the prizes to the art claws at Hammersmith. One statement that he made to the students was in its way very memor- able. lie spoke more as a minister than as a mere member of Parliament when he alluded to the conduct of the French Government in sending over Commissioners to inquire into our system of technical art training. Sir Charles said the Government took this course under alarm at finding its ex- port trade falling off, because our own manufactures were coming to the front. We no longer needed to import French 1 taste. Our own had made latterly a great start, and had kept it up. There is, of coarse, great comfort in this. But the significance of the fact should not be overlooked. The intimate connection of art with manufactures is well estab- lished in France, and the Government saes to it. It thinks it worth while to take hints from England even in matters of taste the moment England shows that she can give hints to France. In the Kensington Museum there is a gift from the President of the Republic of a ease of Sevres china, a pleasant sort of international amenity. We English are proud of our ceramic maneacturers, and the French think that we might as well see what they can do. It is a peculiarity of oar nation that we don't like to take hints. We are very happy to give them, but we have a kind of insular arrogance about adopting from our neighbours. Other countries are less proud and are more successful. The Swiss Government sent A commission to see how our leading railway was managed, the train service, and the luggage arrangements. That was some years ago. They took plenty of hints from us, and indeed I think we might have taken some from them. And now Sir Charles tells us th at the French are adopting the same course with regard to certain of our mauufactoties.

I hear that Lord Coleridge is greatly disappointed that the judges rejectel his proposal. The Lord Chief Justice suggested that the legal day should be extended by at least half an hour's addition, either at 'its commencement or its @lose. The papers say the proposal was negatived by an overwhalmiug majority. If I afll rightly informed the ad- jective was not top strong. It was said in the court, to-day, that the only advocates of its adoption were its proposer and its seconder. I know that amongst the bar there is a vel y general feeling that it ought to have been more largely sup- ported. Four or five years ago the Equity Courts always sat at ten o'clock. The Vice Chancellor had a' practice of amiling in Rotten Row in the early morning. Sir Richard Matins was better at conveyancing than trotting. He was thrown and broke his leg. When he was able to resume his seat (on the bench) he used to come down later to Lincoln's Inn. He would not hold his court until half-past ten, and gradually the other judges followed his example. Sir George Jessell oiten sat at ten, and not unfrequently till hall-past fear or Ave, though he was a great stickler for the Saturday half holiday. There was, therefore, plenty of precedent for Lord Coleridge's suggestion—and plenty of sense in it too. I tkink if it had been made in spring, instead of so very near the shortest day, the suggestion would have been adopted.

It is curious how all our great literary men are impelled to go to America and to deliver lectures, and to be inter- viewed; and, when they return to b 3 welcomed with a public club dinner, and soon afterwards to lecture the Londoners on Yankee institutions. Oscar Wilde, indeed, adds to this menu the item of being married. We could spare Oscar Wilde, and even if he were absorbed into 'Yankee land, literary London would not be ineoneolable. Moat of his pathetic girl worshippers have grown fat in his absence, have put on sensible frocks, and in consequence been married. But it is sad to think of Swinburne leaving us. There was a foolish suggestion made the other day that Enilancl should have its academy of eminent men, _like France; and there was a poll to determine who should be the lb immortals. I never knew how badly off we were for great men. There was Tennyson, Ruskin, Fronde Swinburne. and Arnold—and the rest were nobodies. We can't spare Swinburne; all the same, I hear he leaves in February.

The two great theatrical events of the week have been the production of Claudian at the.Princ3ssea, and et Galatea at the Lyceum. One has been an undoubted success. Every- one knew Mr. Wills' gift of poetry. Bat he was not master of a plot. He has produced more failures that deserved to be successes than any living dramatist. New Mr. Hermann is an admirable constructor of a plot. That was (pate evident from the production of the Silver King. He was Wilson Barrett's stage manager at the Court, and he thoroughly understands that part of his business. Wilson' Barrett is the husband of Mies Heath, and his faith in Wills dates back as far as the prodpotioa of Jane Shore, with which eke made money, both here and ia the provinces. In patting the poet and the contriver into karaass together the manager felt* that he had got a power that would draw any public, and so he spared no money in the wonderfal pie's' which he has put on the stone. Ent it has faults. One is that the lion's share is so ellOr moo that he is quite hoard front roaring. Poor Miss

div.head: SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC.

The minutes of the Health Committee contained the fol- lowing report of the medical officer :—" Births 79, equal to 37.93 per 1,000; deaths (total) 53, equsl to 25.44 per 1,000 ; including children under 1 year 17, equal to 816 per 1,C30; children between 1 and 5 years 10, equal to 4 8 per 1,000; zymotic diseases 7, equal to 3.3 per 1,000; in- quests 3. I have been requested by several residents in the neighbourhood to draw the attention of the Sanitary Com- mittee to a nuisance said to arise from the Glycerine Works."—On the let December Dr. Booth wrote complain- ing of a disagreeable smell said to emanate from the Glycerine Works, and the Chairman of the committee was requested to investigate. On December 4th the Sanitary Inspector reported that "several cases of scarlet fever have been reported, and three of them at No. 98, Kent-street, proved fatal. There have been three deaths from small-pox, viz., two in the hospital Sand one in Midwood-street. Since 14th May, there have been 32 cases of small-pox, and of these five proved fatal. Thirteen patients have ben recoived into the hos- pital; of these two died, five were discharged convalescent, and the remainder ate almost con- valescent. The three outside patients are quite recovered." The minutes of the committee contained the following with regard to ihs Infectious Diseases Hospital:— Recommended that Joseph Cook, who !eft the hospital before being discharged, be summoned; that Mr. Dickson be authorised to procure the necessary food, rtc., for use in the hospital, and submit the accounts monthly. Letters, dated 22nd November, from the authorities of Warrington, St. Helene, and Runcorn, respecting medical atteatnce, also 3rd December, from Local Government Board, stating that section 131 of the P. H. Act, 1875, empowered the provid- ing of medical attendance and medicine. The committee acknowledge, with thanks, the donations of linen and maga- zines, as reported by the inspector, and they trust the good example will be followed by others. It was recommended that Mr. A. Edwards be paid £lO 105 per annum, and Mr. J. Palmer £1 per a-mum for mortality and vaccination returns, and 2s 6d each special report, as heretofore. Th.e receipts from the market for the past month were £l5 15s 3d, being a decrease of is 4d. Dr. O'KEEFFE moved, and Mr. MARTLEY seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes.—Mr. WEBSTER said there were three cases of fever in Kent-street, and he wished to be informed whether the disease was caused through neglect in regard to night soil work or through pig keeping.—Dr. O'KEEFFE re- plied that the sanitary arrangements in that locality were in good order, and that there were no pigs kept there. The doctor remarked that Dr. Thorne Thorne, of the Local Go- vernment Board, had paid a visit to the temporary infectious diseases hospital. He was very much pleased with its con- struction, which he said met with all the recommendations of the Local Government Board. He (Dr. O'Keeffe) thought this ought to be satisfactory to the people of Wid- nes, and pointed out that the tent was constructed without any advice from the Local Government Board. He then criticised at some length a sensational article which appeared in a Liverpool contemporary on the 19th November with regard to small-pox at Widnes. It bad tended to cause an immense amount of injury to the tradesmen of Whines by preventing people from the outeide districts from visiting the town. Such articles ought to possess a modicum of truth in thou), but he contradicted every statement made in that article, which were with-out foundation. He was serry a respectable Liverpool paper would take reports from people who knew nothing about what they were writing of. The•article,amongst other things, stated that there was no bye-law in existence by which the Boaid could deal with the festering nuisances in the town, and that families uf pigs " were kept in back- yards within a few feet of the doorways, and not unfre- qaently the pigs "ate, drank, and slept" with the family. A more outrageous and disgraceful libel on the members of the Board and the people of Widnes he (the doctor) had never read. After pointing out other mis-statements, the doctor referred to the placards, with reference to smallpox, issued by the Preseot Guardians. He was very sorry the Guardians were interfering with the Local Sanitary Authority. When the Board wanted a favour from them they refused it, and now, when they found the Board succeeding in stamping out the disease, they interfered like a lot of impertinent individuals—(laughte7)—in order to make Widnes look the plague spot of the Mersey.—The minutes were passed. with the exception of the accounts of Messrs. Carlile and Dale.

THE -GALE AT WIDNES. A COPPER WORKS DEMOLISEIED. A gale of unexampled fury swept over Widnes on Monday night and the greater part of Tuesday, and property wait destroyed to an enormous extent. About 11 o'clock on Monday night the partially erected copper works of Messrs. J. H. Dennis and Co., situate in Lugsdale, were laid in ruins, and the anticipations of the firm that smelting opera- tions would commence with the New Year are doomed to disappointment. 'The works, which were of an extensive character, occupied two acres of land. The main building was a long brick structure with a wooden roof, in five sec- tions, in the form known as "basket." Iron pillars and girders supported the roof, which rested on one side upon a brick wall eighteen inches thick and 103 yards long, with windows with oval tops. The ether side of the building was open to the full blast of the wind, which rushed in with tremendous force, and the roof was lifted bodily off and crashed to the ground. Seven iron pillars were broken, and the girders were twisted into numerous fantastic shapes, while the wall was razed to the ground. At the time five men in the employ of Mr. Wilson, of Runcorn, the contractor for the brickwork, were working near the spot, and hearing the terrible uproar ficei in fear. They did not return until the expiration of two hours, when they found the greater part of the works de- molished. A high chimney, which was com- pleted about three weeks ago by Mr. Wilson's men, escaped all injury, and the furnaces also were not damaged. A single brick wall, being one side of another shed, Was left standing, and also the pillars and principals of another building. The force of the wind must have been tremendous, as the following incident will show. Abeut ten feet from a furnace was an iron pillar, weighing 1 ton 1 cwt., and fastened to a stone, weighing about 7 cwt., which was embedded in the ground. During Monday this bare pillar and stone were lifted bodily on to the furnace, a height of neaily eight feet. A similar pillar, a few yards distant, was also hurled on a furnace. The damage is estimated at up- wards of £3,000, principally for woodwork and ironwerk for which 111 r. Latham, of St. Helens, is the . contractor. The damage to brickwork is about £3OO. The site of the works on Wednesday afternoon presented a most desolate appearance, but under the direction of Mr. Wilson;. jun., the workmen were rapidly removing the debris. It was only a weak ago since the same buildings were damaged to the extent of £lOO. Sheds at the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., Golding, Davis, and Taylor, and Galloways have been damaged to some extent, but not very seriously. A chimney stack on the office at Messrs. Gos- sage's works was overthrown, and descended through the roof into the private office of Mr. Timtniss. Alighting on the table, the falling brickwork drove the legs of that piece of furniture through the ceiling on the roof below. Hap- pily no one was injured. Slates, shop signs, and shutters strewed the streets early on Tuesday morning, and during the day pedestrians traversed the thoroughfares at some risk to life and limb. No fatalities are reported. Between Widnes and Fidlera Ferry, on the London and North- Western Railway, considerable number of telegraph poles were blown down, and communication was stopped for several hours.

SHOCKING FALL OF A LABOURER AT EARLESTOWN.— Laia evening (Thursday) a hod-carrier employed at the ex- tension of the Barn's Head Hotel, Market-street, Earleitown, was seriously injured. While standing en a ladder near the roof one of the spokes gave way and the poor fellow was precipitated to the ground floor, after falling through the " Hats " above. - It was found that his left leg had been badly injured if not broken, and he was conveyed to his home at St. Helens in a cab.
THE '1`01(1\.1 AT 'RUNCORN.
EXCIIINa SCENES ON THE MERSEY: NARROW
ESCAPES.

At Runcorn the storm caused considerable havoc amongst • property on land, and on the Mersey the wind blew with fearful intensity, and the shipping suffered very heaviby. , At high tide on Tuesday night two steamers left the port, . having a 'umber of flats in tow. Experiencing the full ejects of tho gale, they were unable to reach Liver Pool, and oa Wednesday morning no intelligence of their where. abonte coald h'? ‘t,rathered. As there were about forty men on the boats the greatest anxiety for their safety prevailed, and it was feared that tue crews had perished. About mid- day on Wednesday, however, a telegram was received from Liverpool stating that one steamer, with its full comple. ments of flats had reached the port in safety, but that the Captain of the flat Booth, named George Penchebury, had been nashed overboard, and that the flat was adrift witb another man on board. It also transpired that the aet Seine had sunk at the eatrance to the Brunswick Dock, the crew narrowly escaping with their lives. Pendlehury leaves a wife and eight children. Later in the day the second steamer arrived back at Runcorn with the flats in tow. Alt appeared that finding it imposb.ble to reach Liverpool, the steamer anchored off Eastham Ferry, where the water was comparatively calm, the captain in- tending to proceed on the short voyage next day, but the gale showing no signs of abating the steamer and fiats re turned to &racer% where tney found a haven in the docks. While the gale was raging at its highest. pitch early ou Wednesday morning a fiat, belonging to Messrs. Hicksaa, was sunk at Weston Point. On board were the eaptain's wife and two children, whose screams attracted the atten- tion of the piermen. The wives rolled over the deck ot the sinking vessel with great violence, and the three persons by the aid of a lamp athicle was on the craft, theunfortunate woman was:discerned knee deep in water, and holding the two children in her arms. Their pLeition was one of great peril, but the piermen, who were several times nearly blown off their feet, succeeded in rescuing the woman and children, although nearly sacrificing their own live& Soon after they were landed in safety the fat sank close to the dock entrance. About nine o'clock the same morning a flat laden with sand for St. Helena attempts' to make the voyage up the river. She was observed to roll heavily, and the five men on board were seen to jump into the small boat, which was astern. The flat immediately sank in deep water. The men were not yet however out of danger, and it was impossible to render them any assistance from the shore. By skilfully managing their bat the men reached the pier, where they were congratulated on their narrow escape by a large throng of people, who, amid great excitement, had watched their efforts. A fiat belonging to Mr. Richard Abel, and one owned by the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company also sank, and several fishing boats were capsized. The schooner Lady Stuart, a vessel owned solely in Runcorn, was totally wrecked at Connah's Quay. The crew eves saved. At Weston and Halton a number of houses were partially un- roofeel, and suns trees IVCC3 uprooted. The contractor's hut on the site of the new church in Greenway- road was blown down. Some of the timber was carried across the road, and smashed a portion of the ornamental palisading of the cemetery. A lamp post also was broken. A portion of the Theatre Royal was demolished, while on every hand chimney stacks, tiles, 4:,e, , were dislodged and hurled into the Sis.reete A brick wall at the South Bank Hotel was demolished. P. 3. While; had a very narrow escape. Whilst passing Mr. Farrell's worke?eop, off Lord; street, in company with P.C. Kelly, a portion of :Ile roof? which is formed of zinc, was removed by a gust of wind. A piece of the metal fell upon the sergeant's helmet, which it cut comeletely through, and had it not been for the strength of the head gear there is no doubt his head would have been seriously injared.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A SHIP'S CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A SHIP'S CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Benkes and Mr. C. Reynolds, Jehn Corcoran summoned Charles Thomas on a claim for £4 5s di. for wages due.— Mr. Burton appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Lake for the defendant.—Mr. Burton stated that the summons was taken out under the Merchant Shipping Act. Corcoran was an ordinary seaman and cook on board the Soot of London, of which the defendant Thomas was mister. One the 30th September last, at Llanelly, South Wales, the defendant en- gaged Corcoran as ordinary seaman awl cook at £2 104 per month. Corcoran remained on the ship tint lit arrived at Runcorn on the sth December, being two months and one week. During that time he received by instalmente £1 7s 61. This action was for the difference. Section 155 of the Merchant Shipping Act stated that articles should be signed before the ship went to sea, cr as soon after as prac- tic tble, and they were to be read over to the seaman by the captain under pain of a penalty of £5. In this instance no articles were read or signed, but as soon as the plaintiff wanted to leave at the port of Run- corn, the defendant sent for Corcoran into the Icabin on the night of the 4th December, and the articles (produced) were brought forward. The wages were put in 15s per mouth. Thera were eight men on board, the captain £4 a month, and the lowest wages paid was £2 ss, to a youth younger than the plaintiff. The plaintiff stated that the alticies %vele not read over to him but he signed them as a matter of form, because he wished to get his discharge next day.—Corcoran was then called and corroborated his advocate's statement.—Mr. Luke cross-examined him to show that he was not competent to perform the labours of A cook or an ordinary seaman. The witness admitted that he had stolen a cake of tob loco and put a muffler in his bag " by mis- stake."--Re-exatnined by Mr. Burton, witness made a state- ment showing that the captain had on one occasion behaved in a disgusting manner towards him.—Mr. Lake submitted that the plaintiff had made out no case against the articles which purported to be signed on the 2nd October. After the plain. tiff had admitted, as he had done, in a most unblushing manner, that he had taken a cake of tobacco, and attempted , to steal a muffler, that he was unable to reef a sail or cook, anti offered another man 5s per month to do the cooking for him, he (Mr. Lake) thought there was little doubt that hie wagc& had been quite in proportion to his ability. It was an improbable tale that the plaintiff told with regard to the signing of the articles.—The defendant was called, and in answer to the magistrates, said that he had never paid less than 25s per month for a cook and seaman. lie said the plaintiff was not worth anything as a seamen or cook. THE PPOSED -INFECTIOUS DIS- EAS2S HOSPITAL FOR PRESCOT UNION.

A_ meeting of the committee appointed at the recent con- ference, with regard to the proposed establishment of an in- fectious diseases hospital for the Prescot Union, met on Thursday in the Workhouse, Whiston. Them were present the following representatives from various sanitary authori- ties in the union, viz. :—Mr. R. Pilkington and Dr. McNicoll (St. Helens Corporation), Mr. J. T. Allen (Widnes Local Board), Mr. Meadows (Prescot Rural Sani- tary Authority), Mr. Dobell (Huyton and Little Woolton Local Boards), Mr. Stockley (Rainford Local Board), and Mr. E. Et Hartley (clerk-to the Guardians.)—On the motion of Mr. SrocELEY, seconded by Mr. ALLEN, Mr. R. Pilkin,g- ton was appointed chairtnan.—Mr. HARTLEY said he ha 4 re- ceived a letter from ths clerk to the Much Woolton Local Board stating that that Board had resolved not to join in the hospital scheme. The Yrescot Local Board, he said, had appointed their chairman Mr. Spencely, to attend that meeting, or failing his, Mr. Fogg, but neither of the were there.—The CIIAIEMAN, after explain. jog the _object of the meeting. said he thought it Wail very likely that St. Helene, which had a hospital of is own already, would entertain any scheme by which it should receive patients iota this hospital from districts situated outside, but conveniently near its beundaries.—Mr. ALLEN also stated that the Widnes Board was at present thinking about building a hospital for their own district. If they did this he thought they would also be willing to take in patients from tbe neighbouring townships, such as Cronton. Ditton, STOCILBY said that the Rainford Local Board did not intend to join in a general hospital scheme. They had, however, written lo the St. Helens Corporation to ascertain on what terms they would take patients from Rainford into their hospital.—The CHAIRMAN thought that what seemed to be wasted was a hospital for the western portion of the Union.—Mr. MEADOWS thought if the Prescott Huyton, and Little Woolton Local Boards combined to build a hospital the Rural Sanitary Authority could send its patients from its district nearest to the hoopital into it and pay for them. In the portions of its districts near to Widnes and St. Helens, the patients could be sent into the hospitals of either of these places in the same viray.—Mr. Donau. thought this scheme would not be enter- tained by the authorities ite represented, who had very few fever cases.—After considerable discussion il was resolved, on the motion of Mr. MEADOWS, seconded by Mr. ALLEN, "That, as the St. Helens Corporation and the Widnes Local Beard are so well advanced in providing accommo- dation for infectious cases for their districts, the question of further provision in the shape of another hospital in a morn westerly situation be brought under the notice of the Huy- ton-with-Roby, Little Woolton, and Prescot Local Boardg, and the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, with the view of sufficient accommodation being provided for the whole Union, with the exception of Much Woolton, who have de- clined to join in any scheme. Copy of tkis resolution to be sent to each local authority concerned."

SAD ACCIDENT AT THE VIADUCT WORKS, EAIi.LESTOWN. A young man named William Rigby, residing in Earle-street, Earlestown, and employed at the Viaduct Works, met with a serious accident on Wednesday morning. He was 9n- gaged in testieg a waggon spring, when the bolt holding the plates became displaced, and the plates flow out. Rigby was caught on the right leg, which was brokea in two places, and a deep gash owed. He lost a great qnantity of blood, and was conveyed to his home as speedily an. possible, where he has since been attended by Dr. Handy- side.

THE TRADE INTERESTS OF ENGLAND Sir,—The correspondence in your paper of Saturday last, under the bead "Trade interests of Engtand," requires a reply from a public point of view. One correspondent writes, "Mr. Lawtenson displays to our view a quantity Gf truisms ;" then, if truth, in the name of common sense ac- Uept them: what is wanted more? Again, it is stated "Our gdld goes to maintain foreign countries ;" I thought Free Traders believed we never paid gold away; however, thanks for the admission at last. !t is suggested that an attack should be made upon the land question; who would he at- tack? Would he go first to the members of the present Government—to the heart of the Cabinet itself—pluck Lord Hartington and. divide the walls of Chatsworth, lay the axe to the Gladstone estate demolish the Duke of West- minster, and pillage the Earl of Derby? Afterward he would, no doubt, pay the manufacturer a visit, and make a Bright, a Rylands, or a Chamberlain disgorge their past pro- fits. If all the money in the world was ecoelly divided there is only £lOO for everybody, so surely your correspon- dent has at least got his share. Is there not at present a Liberal Government in office? yet they do not move in either the land or railway matters complained of. Again, there appears to be a suggestion that churches and chapels would be better destroyed, and ministers, who are called drones' dismissed. May my country never see that unhappy day. I hope every man and every parent in Warrington may remember this Free Trade plan. Let me ask, are there no churches, chapels, and ministers in America, or has America grown poor under her protective policy? She has developed into the most pr( sperous nation upon earth. But surely everybody ought to be happy and prosperous in Eng- land if Free Trade is worth supporting, especially as no other nation upon earth appears likely to rob us of it, or have anything to do with the same policy. Any nation which has a home trade to depend upon is in a better position to do a foreign business than a nation which has little or none, Germany finds a good market in England, take this from Germany and you marten the profits of her manufacturers; place a duty upon manufactured articles coming into Eng- land and you at once compel the foreigner to place a lower price upon the article he seeks to sell, to give him a chance to secure our orders; whereas at present he can secure the duty value as an extra profit to grow rich upon, increase his business, and fight us for ever. In addition to this, Ger- many has the profit made upon home orders, so they are able to sell cheaper abroad than they otherwise would be; if your correspondent cannot understand this he deserves our pity. Fair Trade is far from being a neglected idea, I seed only point to Preston or York to establish this, and England will answer for the rest at the next time of asking. Your other correspondent may perhaps be writing under dic- tation frem big guns who fire their shot under cover. I fancy there was too much truth in my last letter to be agreeable. The opening statements made by this correspondent are simply incorrect, and help to throw discredit upon the sincerity and accuracy of his following statements. I shrewdly guess that your corres- pondents are themselves protectionists notwithstanding all they write or are made to write. Free Trade is a delusion, for how can trade be free so long as it is fettered by such protection as trade unions, which seek to prevent any man from working who does not sell labour at the society prices, and blames a man because he dares to be free. So long as it pays to manufacture, so long will manu- facturers invest capital, if only in limited companies ; if one manufacturer buys German goods instead of employing British labour, others can easily copy the trick. The ques- tion is, can we cease to produce and become purchasers? Yet this appears to be what Free Trade is driving us to, whilst deliberately robbing us of the labour upon our home trade. The exports from the Board of Trade returns are significant :-1831, November, £20,713 Id 4; 1882, Novem- ber, £2O 292,948; 1883, November, £20,054.698. I think the direct ratepayers care little for borrowed statements which seek to prove the reduction of pauperism, but not of poor, so long as the poundage or rate of the poor tax is not reduced, notwithstanding the fact of a greatly increased number of ratepayers, which must render the amount col- lected greater now than ever. The statement respecting dear bread before the repeal of the Corn Law requires ex-

planation; the fault really lay with the corn dealers, wheat being sometimes as cheap before the repeal as after. For instance, from 1834 to 1838 the average price was 42s 2d per quarter ; from 1843 to 1845 it was 50s 81 per qr.; whereas from 1871 to 1873 (these being most prosperous years for all, a return of which we would gladly welcome,) the price was 57s 5d per quarter, so that the price of wheat could not be the cause of dear bread; I discredit the ex-

travagant statements made by your correspondent, indeed they simply read absurd. If we take an average price of wheat for 30 years before the repeal of the corn laws, and the average price during 30 years after, the difference is only 5s 10,1 per quarter, which is equivalent to td per loaf (reckoning 133 loaves 4lbs. each to the quarter) advantage since the repeal; for the rest we must look to the dealers for explanation. We might with equal justice blame the free trade policy for the 50 per cent. advance in the price of beef during the last 20 years; price of beef before free trade policy 6-id per lb , present price 1044 per lb; bacon, originally 40 per lb., now 81 per lb. ; fish also is sold re- tail to the public at extravagant prices compared with the value at the fishing stations. I have never yet advocated a return to the tax upon wheat, my subject is to deal with employment and manufactured articles. The supply of wheat is far greater now than at any time in the history of nations. America has annually a surplus growth, which it is as much to her interest to sell as it is ours to buy, there- fore there could no morebe now a scarcity of bread than there is a a scarcity of tea, which is to-day taxed 6d per lb., and is an article we do not produce. if a workman's wife asks for lib. of tea at is 6d she really gets is worth of

tea, and 6d worth of taxation. In the prospectus of some extensive new flour mills erected in America it is stated "We are rapidly increasing the manufacture of flour, and hope the day is approaching when not one single bushel of wheat will leave the shores of the United States. but that all will be sent away in manufactured flour." This of course means increased trade for America and less

for Great Britain, by this course England is also deprived of the external or cattle feeding portion of the wheat, thereby causing the winter keep of cattle to be more ex- pensive, and consequently raising the value of cattle and beef ; the fact is our countrymen in America are one too many for as. No wonder that emigration still continues lowing like a mighty stream, 11,719 English left our shores daring the past month of November, and where have they gene to? they have fled to the arms of protection, let free traders racks a note of this. Driven from borne, however,

is not one of the most pleasant contemplations. Allusion is made to the decrease of criminality; it would indeed, be a strange thing if this were not so, considering the amount of money spent, and the great army of police engaged throughout the country to preserve order, compared with 11 efacility for keeping order in the days of special con- The antount of money in the savings banks proves 11 i ctycr dthe fact that people are grown more thought- ful, anxious, and provident; the fact of a workman earning •35s per week and saving 5s does not prove that the manu- facturer upon whom he is absolutely dependent for his wages, is making a profit upon his business. Free traders 'would do well to take the Gazette and look over the long list of weekly bankruptcies. We have lately had an amend- ment of the Bankruptcy Act, very consistent eondnct, to kat invent the free trade policy, and then be compelled to manufacture a bankruptcy act to take care of it. In a pre- letter I wrote" whilst poverty lasts, crime will never eimac"

Or Satan Ands some mischief still, For Idle hands to do.. Your correspondent writes "a statement having more truth in it than is good for his poretienp Does he dare to force his hollow arguments by a threat? My object is to confer a benefit and not an injury, to secure wages and employ- ment for the people. Many valuable industries have all but ceased in Ireland since the introduction of the Free Trade policy, consequently a great deal of the suffering in that unhappy land is due to the action of Free Trade. In 18fs7 there were 253,257 acres of land in Ireland laid out in the cultivation of flax. In 1879 there were only 123 004 acres with the quantity annually decreasing. In 1867 there was an export of linen to the value of £9,578,245, this was re- duced to £5,473,127 in 1879. In 1880 we imported £4,000,000 worth of flax whilst Irish labourers were trying to exist upon potatoes, and it only becomes a question of time, when the workmen of England will stage by stage drift into the same unhappy position if the foreigner is al- lowed to continue to rod them of employment. The an- imal amount of meaufactured imports for home use alone after deducting the value of articles imported for what may be termed re-exportation amounts to £31,718,54 with the quantity and value increasing. Your correspondent is made to suppose, and it is well he does only suppose, a mercantile transaction of sub surnaming richness as to make one wonder why there should be a poor man left in the coun- try. Allow me to inform your readers, notwithstanding anything he has been told, that no such transaction ever took place. The ancient custom or Barter is almost entirely abolished, indeed it is now a rare thing to find a businem house which does both an export and an import business, see my last letter upon this subject. There ars business establishments abroad similar to our own, it would ,

be latighable tersee -one of our own ironmongery crstablish- ments receiving iron goods, and offering to pay for them with loads of flour or sides of bacon. The tendency of the times is in fact to bring our own manufacturers in direct communication with the foreign buyer. Exporters also often sell at a 1099, yes, and become bankrupt also, as the Gazette will prove. I think my several letters have pretty well disposed of the purely. manufacturing, trade of the country, and this is really what we as a manufacturing people are most de, ply interested in. As a last resource your correspondent introduces the bullion question. Your correspondent will next be compelled to bring the members of the Cobden Club to the rescue; indeed, I am not at all satisfied that they have not already done so. Let me ask, Who does the money coming into a bank belong to? Not to the bank, but to the depositors, who can withdraw it at will. England as a constitutional country stands pre- eminent atnongst nations, the stability of her Government under either political party, the obedience and order of her people, together with the defence of this sea-girt island, affords a security second to none upon earth. Is it a wonder then that London, the metropolis, should be selected as a bank for all nations, and the centre of finance? The silver from the mines of Peru, and gold from the fields of Cali- fornia and Australia, are transmitted through their respec- tive banks for safe keeping and financial employment in London, but the owners abroad stand credited through We banks for the amount of their deposits; a large proportion of this deposit being loaned at interest, often upon mortgage security to British manufacturers, yes, artd ex- porters also, to enable them to continue their business; the bank loans or advances of this country being really enor- mous. Let your readers particularly remember that the advantage received by this country during the past 40 years is due principally to the discovery of steam power, in fact' to a Stephenson, and not to a Cobden; but Free Traders are wilfully blind to this great fact. If British workmen cannot see and understand that every order given to the foreigner robs them of a corresponding amount of wages and employment, then I shall think there is some truth in the well-known statement that England contains 30 million people for the most part fools. I would not have spent five minutes trouble upon this subject if I did not believe that its adoption would greatly benefit the manfacturers and workmen of this country. I have answered point by point all that has been written against the subject, whereas I notice that your correspondents are compelled to pass over ray arguments or admit them to be truisms and truths. I ads, air, yours respectfully, Warring ton, Dec. 12th. 1883. S. LAWRENSON.

DISPUTE AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. Sir,—l beg to call attention to the following statement which appeared in your paper last week :—" The Sunday school -recently lost, either by resignation or dismissal, several teachers and scholars." I, as one of the Sunday school teachers, beg to contradict that statement. Some ,considerable time past most certainly the late superinten- dent was dismissed, together with a female teacher. With these two exceptions no other teacher has been dismissed, and no one of them has, as yet, sent in either his or her resignation. I shall feel truly obliged if you will kindly insert this contradiction to the above extract.—l am. ONE OF THE SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS. December 12th, 1883.

div.head: HARE AT THE CHASE.
div.p: THE HARE AT THE CHASE.
Sir,—The following rhymed version of the fifteenth fable in the second book of the Russian edition of Krilof may interest your readers :

Assembled in one mighty band, The beasts resolve to clear the land Of bears, and slew them all in one long battle. After the rout and ratle, It came to choosing each his share, And each got something. In their mldst a hare Was striving by the ear to drag a bear. "Halt there, thcu squinting dance! Who sent thee here? Be off with thee at once? What did thy help through all the chase avail ?" "What, brothers!" went the hare's reply, "Whom did the bu-h, then hide? Who made the bear turn tail And run into your arms, if 'twas not I" It seemed rare fun such boasting lies to hear, And was rewarded with a bit of bruin's ear. We laugh at boasters, but to share in what • They've nothing done to gain is oft their lot.
It is taken from the volume by Mr. I. H. Harrison, recent published.—Yours, Sic., ANGLO-SCOTUS.

div.head: ILBERT BILL.
div.p: THE ILBERT BILL.

Sir,—After the singular emanation which appeared in your columns last week, signed "M. Mull," perhaps, as one who attended theeiate Conservative meeting, you will allow me to say a word or two. I heard the whole of the much- maligned speech of Mr. Atkins,and I have very carefully read the letter of M. Mull ; and, as an impartial witness I am decidedly of opinion that, even if the oratorical exuberance of Mr. Atkins led him into rather stronger language than was necessary, he certainly did not wander nearly so far from the path of moderation of tone and decency of expres- sion as his indigant and unreasonable critic. And I can promise M. Mull that if his audacious request were granted, and he were allowed to ratiocinate at the expense of others before a Warrington audience, he would, if he wished to succeed in demolishing Mr. Atkins, have to furnish some- thing much more substantial than the wild expletives and the rhetorical rhodomontade with which his epistle abounds. Without committing myself to an approval of Mr. Atkins's style, or to an unqualified acceptance of all the views he advocated;l am bound to say that he did at least bring some evidence to support his indictment. M. Mull does not even attempt to adduce any facts to controvert the statement that there is danger larking in the Ebert Bill, nor does he ven- ture to deny that from our English fellow-subjects in India, who surely ought to know something about the matter, a well-nigh unanimous protest has arisen against the dreaded innovation. Mere valleys of moral balderdash and salvoes of sentimental twaddle are not sufficient to disprove the allegations of Mr. Atkins, nor is your correspondent's extreme intemperance of phraseology the best means of rebuking the somewhat teo extravagant vituperation in which Mr. Atkins indulged. Perhaps the following extract from a letter I have received from a Wesleyan missionary who has laboured in our great eastern dependancy for many years, may prove not uninteresting at the present crisis. "There are, indeed," he writes, "great political changes going on in this country just now. The Viceroy, who is no doubt a sincere and honourable gentleman, is, I think, a little bit too fond of experimental measures.' His Criminal Procedure Bill has created intense and bitter feeling. Personally, I think such a measure unnecessary and premature. I have spoken with several educated gentlemen (native) upon the subject, and they think it a mistake. If such a power were given to natives they would not be able to use it rightly. Their ideas and standpoints are so totally different from ours, and, notwithstanding their education, their moral sense is low and weak. The system of caste renders the condition of Hindoos quite unique. As other nations, for instance, have felt their way up to a higher civilization, their social institutions have kept pace with their intellectual advancement. But this is not the case with Hindoo society, for while the intel- lect is cultured up to a very high state (and they are cap- able of great ,things),caste with an iron grip, holds down the whole community to Vie most absurd and degrading prac- tices. And a stern, relentless taskmaster is caste! The Hindoo M.A. or BA., who sits on the magisterial bench, or has a voice in the councils of the country, bows, like the most illiterate pariah, with servile obsequkoness to the dictates of a stupid and debasing caste. Intellectually free, they are morally slaves; intellectually livipg, they are morally dead, and the fetter which binds them to this body of death' is caste. Thus, while Hindoes may be intellec- tually fitted for the work of judging Europeans—and I think nobody will question this—yet in all other and higher respects they are quite unfit.' —I am, Warrington, December, 1833. div.head: INDIA: THE LATE CONSERVATIVE MEETING.
div.p: INDIA: THE LATE CONSERVATIVE MEETING.

To say nothing of his "choice and well selected" beha- viour on the platform at the above meeting, the amusingly solemn contribution of "M. Mull" in your impression of last Saturday will be read by most with eyes which will open wider and wider as they wade through the wailings, shudderings, ehiverings, and tremblings of your eccentric correspondent. If we were not assured by the position this gentleman holds in the literary world that his letter would not entirely escape observation, the palpable absurdity of the imponderable effusion would alone be a sufficient an- ewer, and upon that ground we might feel disposed to ex- cuse it. But when a gentleman who should know better, and who declares himself a stranger to Warrington, and to be "connected with no political society," seeks to display his impartiality (?) under the cover of "personified" utterances of horror, and professions of overwhelming grief, and so grossly misrepresents his fellowman with such flagrant and uncalled-for abuse, I will join Mr. Mull in ths sentiment ef Mr. Pierpoint, which he so cheerfully adopts in his letter, and say with him "There are moments when a deep sense of plainest though painful duty makes a man to speak out, and this is one such moment." If Mr. Mull has anything to object to in the address of Mr. Aitkin it is quite unnecessary that he should consume himself with disgust, and is it not ungentlemanly also to vilify his fellow-men without offering one single argument in support of such out- rageous criticism It Mr. Aitkin has advanced anything of a antravertible nature, the first step for Mr. Mull should be to prove him wrong and leave the public to judge whether he has wilfully cammitted himself • and as Mr. Mull seeina a stranger amongst us, it ma.y not he out of place to tell him that in Warrington such a course would have had far mere weight. Passing over the cataclysm of epithets and insults which Mr. Mull in his complimentary style pours upon the audience of the meeting we come to a point in bin letter wher he insists that a great " stain " ha 3 been broug'at upon our town, and that the Warrington Conservatives are morally liable for the disgrace, and, moreover, that Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett is im- plicated in it. To purge our iniquity Mr. Mull prescribes. and strange and incredulous thoeeh it may appear—and asking your pardon,Mr. Editor, far again filling your valu- able space with such a childlike and ludicrous requee—lea modestly submits as a"reasonable" proposition that the Con- servative:3. of Warrington than, "at their own expense," again hire the Public Hall, but this time for Mr. Mull, to deliver an opposition addre.s on the people whom he says "have been so slandered." If this pedantic assumption were ie might be annoying. not so laughable Does Mr. Mull suppose that the self-righteous "Tories, which he in his bountiful goodness has also been graciously pleased to desig- nate " morbid" and " vulgar," are likewise benighted idiots ? As one of the rank and file only I venture to predict that the Conservatives will dc• cline to accede to such a pauper-like request, and that they will teach Mr. Mull that their favours are not to be extorted by abnse and flimsy threats ; nor will his

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1883. ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1883. ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL.

exquisite subtlety lead them to-blindly bestow their charity upon any except our necessitous poor. Mr. Mull remarks that many years of his life have been spent in India, and that he is "virtually a stranger here." Amen ! Yea, and it may be said a " simple" stranger here. But he cannot seriously suppose that the Conservative Association of War- rington is constituted to encourage and pamper the per- sonal vanities of non-political hornilists. Yes, Mr. Mull, the Conservatives, as you say, do claim to be the " Consti- tutional " party, and as they have no desire to forfeit that title, they do not propose to certify themselves eligible for I the lunatic asylum by voluntarily subscribing their funds to further the views of inimical disputants. Awake, ye vile and slumbering men of dark and ignorant Warrington to the dazzling reflection of India's bright and burning sun now thrown upon your mindst in the person of "M. Mull." Warrington, December, 1383. ON GUARD.

FREE BREAKFAST FOR RUNCORN CHILDREN. Sir,—Will you kindly insert this in your next issue.: In connection with the free concerts for the people, which are held weekly in Ellesmere-street sahoolroom, it is proposed to give a free breakfast to a number of poor children. The committee have not sufficient funds in hand at present to carry out this intention. Will your readers kindly help us by sending anything they can spare, either in money, coffee, tea, sugar, bread, &c., so that we may be able to make some poor children happy for once in their lives. Christmas time will not ha a time oi lejoicing to them iii their homes. There they get half starved, badly clothed, and beaten by drunken parents Do assist us in this effort, for we cannot do it without help. Contributions will be thankfully re- ceived by Mrs. W. Vause, Ellesinere-street, or Mrs. Gandy, 7, Leinster-street.—l am yours, Runcorn, Dec., 1883. W. VAUSE.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of " HIRELL ; OR, LOTH BORN OF STRIFE," "ABM. DRAKE'S WIFE," "ISRAEL MORT, OTHRMAN," kc., kc.
CHAPTER LIE-CRITICAL GLANCBS.

The influx of news mentioned in the last chapter, same of which reached Stephen first, gave him an excuse for another visit to Major Etheredge in the ante-room. It must be acknowledged that the desire to catch a glimpse of Mies Vandeleur gave factitious importance to all he could have to say. The Major came out and treated with all due respect Stephen's new facts, but ensied with one that impressed Stephen more forcibly than any he had succeeded in irapres- sirg on the Major. He told him he was satisfied that in this part of the coun- try at all events the movement had collapsed, the Flying Column had done its work, and he had already given the order for the march home at ten next morning; the Earl undertaking to make the troops as comfortable as he could during the intervening hours. "regretting it was impossible to find them beds," said the Major, with a laugh. He ended what he had to say by again telling Stephen to wait where he was while he wished the host, hostess, and guests "good night," when he would go with Stephen to make the necessary arrangements for safety, as though daßger still threatened: "For mind," he said, "a soldier at such times leaves no- thing to trust!" Once more then Stephen could dream of the possibility during these few moments of seeing the face and form that hourly grew more absorbingly attractive in remembrance. And fortune WAS so kind to him as to give him even more than he sought. A livery servant opened wide the door which the Major had left ajar, and two persons came forth, arm in arm, the lady in white with a spray of blush roses in her hair, the gentleman tall, rather nompous in manner, ' by conversing, she looking tired and weary, he as if feel- ing he did her a kindness y trying to amuse her. "I think, Frances, I have a surprise for you, and that is why I brought you this way." "Indeed, and what is that?" "A. portrait of your father in his youth that you have never seen—perhaps never heard of." "That will be indeed a pleasure," and the sudden anima- tion in her face testified to the sincerity of her words. Stephen might have:heard and understood this conversa- tion, but that the very first glance revealed to him who they were—Miss Vandeleur, and his brother, the Earl; and left him too deeply affected to listen. It was too late to move, and he could not turn away. His eyes were drawn by an irresistible fascination to her face, watching for the moment when she would possibly recog- nise him, and beyond that all seemed chaos. He was, however, conscious that Lord Harlaxton saw him, but only as a common soldier, who needed no second glance; and that Miss Vandeleur was looking towards the Earl's face as if he had said something which she failed to hear, and so he thought he should escape recognition after all. But at the moment when she was nearest to him in pass- ing, she did turn to look at the young soldier; thinking probably it might be the one of whom the Major had spoken. She gazed with kindly interest, which sud- denly changed when she saw—yet for the moment tried to disbelieve it could be—Stephen, but the emotion of his face answered her. Hardly knowing what he did he confirmed his identity by a sort of instinctive appeal to her for silence, by touching his lips with his finger; which she answered by a bow so slight that only one who hung upon her slightest movement would have perceived it, and known its meaning. During the rest of the night, when he might have slept, he found sleep impossible. Every minute he expected some message, some visitor—perhaps his mother—possibly the Earl—and at times he fancied even Miss Vandeleur might some, if only to renounce her tacit promise of silence, and to beg him to go with her to his mother. But when he remembered where he was—among a num- ber of other 'soldiers—he saw the absurdity of supposing either of the three would come there to claim him by the right of family ties. But how would it be in the morning? Something then would surely happen. He speculated on the possibility of getting away before the other troops. But finally he satis- fied himself by reflecting that Miss Vandeleur would in all probability keep his secret for a time—perhaps purposely delay until he had gone—and then treat her silent promise as sufficiently fulfilled, and then—and then only—reveal that she had seen him and in what capacity. Nothing occurred in the morning to contradict this pros- pect. The troops were paraded on the lawn, the guests watching from the windows, and at one window and alone Stephen saw Miss Vandeleur. The march began. The troops passed the front of the mansion in honour of their.host.

He and Miss Vandeleur had by that time assembled in the entrance porch. Stephen saw them there, and felt sure he would be recognised by his brother. In vain he sought for the face of his mother. She was perhaps still in bed, worn by the late festivities of the night. The moment he dreaded, yet coveted, came. But the Earl's eyes were seeking those of the Major and other officers and bowing to them. Miss Vandeleur's, he felt, were seeking only him. When that second recognition happened she waved her handkerchief, and Stephen, while bending in acknowled- ment, knew that she would be supposed to be simply taking leave of the troops. And as to him—why nobody would trouble to ask why so an unimportant a man bowed—if any- body happened to notice the occurrence at all. Once more, when he had passed, he looked back, and again the handkerchief bade him farewell. "She has forgiven me," he thought with emotion, "but perhaps too late for me to draw any other conclusion."

whispering, the Sergeant angrily listening. Look, look! There they are again, in close talk together. If it is about you, they may as well not suspect I have warned you, or Grabbe may indirectly through my sergeant pay me the debt he thinks be owes you. Good bye." And therewith Gentleman Jack moved away, but with a sauntering air as if thinking of nothing in particular. Now t...tephen had noticed a fact he did not chose to tell his former friend, and that was that Sergeant Grabbe— a good sort of a man in his own way, but credulous and obstinate—who had been friendly to Stephen frons the time he first enlisted him up to his departure with the Flying Column, had since his return unmistakeably shown him the cold shoulder; and when he had occasion to speak to Stephen had done it with something uncommonly like an ebullition of disgust. This Stephen had passed over with the reflection it was only a fit of jealousy, which does sometimes break out among military men who have not had chances they think they Ought to have had, and which is apt to tura against those who have been more lucky. But this was quite a new aspect of the matter ; and led him to try to resin anything that might have happened likely to be turned to evil purpose, if Tommy Atkins was scoundrel enough to try it on. He tried in vain. He could think of nothing that promised enlightenment. Should he go at once to the pair before they separa- ted, and challenge a statement of anything he had done ' amiss P

But then that would implicate Jack, and perhaps get him once more into trouble and serious danger if be spoke truly about the state of his heart, which Stephen had heard of before, in connection with the severity of the pack drill. While thus deliberating he saw the two men divide, and the Sergeant cross the grass directly towards himself. Now then he would know all. Calmly and respectfully he looked towards the approaching sergeant, whose face he saw darkening as he drew near. "Shand, I want to ask you a question or two. I have reason to believe somebody has been poisoning the Sergeant- Major's mind about me, and that you are the man." "Will you tell me why you think so ? " "Will you answer mmuestions P " 'Certainly, if I can.'
"1 understand you have been speaking to him sgveral times within the last two days, when there were no matters of military duty to require it."

, !or a moment Stephen was tempted to reply, "Why that is what I am told you and Tommy Atkins hare been doing about me," but his good sense arrested the impales. So what he did was to acknowledge the truth of the statement, and to accompany it with the explana- tion, _

"The Sergeant-Major is personally friendly to me, and we often have a chat together." The Sergeant was silent fora few seconds, looking baffled, but incredulous. And from his silence, his manner, and his hesitation Stephen saw there was evidently something in his mind which it was not agreeable to bring out, and which he had perhaps hopei he might avoid by making Stephen take the initiative. Bat as Stephen showed no inclination to do this, he said, "Did you toll the Sergeant-Major you had seen me speak- ing to a woman outside the camp, and when I ought to have been in the barracks ?" "Never l" said Stephen indignantly. But the word was Accompanied by a slight tinge of colour in his face as he spoke, for he now remembered he had seen Sergeant Grabbe, where and when described, though thinking nothing of the matter, fcir he might have had a pass; and the woman might be a relative or other person come to see him on perfectly legitimate business, though so late. "Did you see me, as I have said ?" yes.” "And than told the Sergeant Major !" "No—l—" but the Sergeant waited for no further expla- nation—

"You lie! You are a-- liar! he roared out, and the seat instant was sprawling on the ground; for Stephen, be- fore the words were well out of the Sergeant's mouth, for- gutting everything in the world but the insult, knocked him down.

As the Sergeant regained his feet and looked at Stephen, there was in his face an expression that intensified all the latter felt at his own want of self-control, and at the danger now confronting him. "Sergeant," he began—and for once his voice showed the agitation in which he spoke—" I trust you will in a calmer mood see that it was the man who, under what he felt to be a great provocation, and having no time to think, retaliated. As a soldier I have done very wrong, and I humbly beg your pardon." "You can explain that distinction to the Court Martial. *insider yourself under arrest. Stay where you are, or it will be worse for you." And away went the Sergeant. "Will he go at once for a guard, or will he take time to reflect," ruminated Stephen. "Madman that I was so to forget myself Well, the job is done. And lam likely to have plenty of leisure to think of the consequences." In this state of mind Stephen lay down on the grass, and was presently joined by Gentleman Jack, who 'thew nothing of what had happened.

They talked for a minute or two on any topic that came appermost, Stephen's whole thoughts being absorbed on that one other topic he ca!sfully shunned speaking of; when be was interrupted by a very peculiar sound from some drummers at a little distance. "Jack, what are the drummers doing ?" "I've been asking thit myself. When a man is dogged,
he'd apt, you see, to disturb the sensitive ears of his officers by unreasonable noise; but the drummers are ready, and they effectually stop all cause for scandal. These are learners."

"Is there any case of that kind likely to come on ?" "1 judge so, within a few days, by this preparation. The new Colonel, who joined while you were away, flying with the column is, they say, a man with but one notion in his head, that if things go generally wrong be Must flog till they get particularly right. This is his first chance to tell the regiment his mind so plainly that there can be no future mistakes, and he's not likely to let it slip." "What's his name ?" "Hobson."
"He was in the same packet that brought me from Holy- head. He locks the character you describe. What has the
man done ?"
- " " While half drunk was abusir t) his sergeant, and ended by striking him. If he's in ole mettle of the last man who was flogged some morn; the drummers needn't be troubled."
"Tell me—it isn't a chearful subject," renurked Stephen

parenthetically; "but if you or I should ever—" - "There !" exclaimed Gentleman Jack, "That'!! do! My &ash creeps already! I shall feel the lash if you say any more "But about this man of mettle ?" "Did you hear me cry Domino, when I won the game? No, I remember, that was before you returned, and when I was getting inquisitive as to the identity of the 'Swell,' so talked of and so praised, and whether he was my valued friend. Well, when I cried Domino! I was then thinking of that man's story: He went quite coolly to the triangle, gave no one the least trouble, and even, they do say, smiled in acknowledgment of the attentions paid him in the presence e the entire regiment drawn up in square.-The first lash fell— he winced, drew a long, deep, shuddering breath, but gave forth no cry of any kind. Then lash after lash, but still no response—not one single groan was wrung from him. But as the last lash was given, and he was released, he threw up his arms and shouted so that the whole regiment would hear, 'Domino! I have won the game!' And he had. He pitted his courage and endurance against the worst they could do, and he won. " Ah," added+Gentleman Jack, thonghtf ully, after a pause, "if only one could be sure of going through the job in that style, one might run the risk under sufficient temptation. What do you think ?" "The question is weighty," rejoined Stephan, "and re- quires deliberation. Ask me to-morrow !"

THE VIOLENT GALE.
GREAT DAMAGE AT EARLESTOWN: THREE MEN HURT.

Earlestown and the neighbourhood did not escape the serious effects of the gale which passed over the country on Tuesday night and early on Wednesday morning. Large numbers of persons were disturbed in their rest by the blustering and whistling winds outside, while the occasional rattle of slates acd chimney pots along the roofs created the greatest alarm and fear. Fortunately, however, cases of personal injury were but few in number. A sad occurrence took place at the residence of Mr. Rylands, manager et the glass works of Messrs. Borron and Co. Mr. Rylands' house is situated near the works, and was exposed to the full force of the gale. About half-past one, on Wed- nesday morning, a loud crash alarmed the inmates. A por- tion of the large brick chimney-stack had been demolished, and crashed through the roof, and a heap of bricks, slates, tiles, and debris fell through the ceiling into the bedroom, occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Rylands. It was providential that the inmates escaped unhurt. About an hour aid a half after another load crash of slates was heard, and almsot immediately a great heap of bricks and slates came crashing through the ceiling of the room in which two young men were sleeping. A coosiderable por- tion of them alighted upon the bed, and one Daniel Rylands escaped unhurt, but Joseph was seriously cut and bruised about the head with the falling states and bricks. Blood flowed profusely from his wounds, and it seas at first thought he had been mortally injured. The works of Messrs. Borron and Company also suffered severely, many slates and tiles being displaced from their positions on the ro)fs of the various buildings. It is stated that two of the hands emolo!,•ed thereat had their heads cut and bruised with falling slates. In other parts of the town numberless slates and chimney pots were torn away, whiie one or two wooden huts and railings were partially demolished. The plate glass front of the shop (at present unoccupied) on the Market-place, and owned by Mr. Lambert, was blown in; • and a wall connected with the aeff property recently erected in Legh-street, near the Mission Tent, was blown down. Considerable damage was also caused to Mr. Forster's new cottage premises in Houghton-street • nearly all the large windows both upstairs and down being blown into the street. The slates and tiles on the Congregational school, Crow-lane, were disarranged, and a number fell into the yard below, whilt_Wmanve %arch suffered to a great extent. The portion of the roOlneirest to the tower was almost stripped of slates, and the latter as they fell alighted upon one of the side entrance porches, which was thereby much damaged. Some of the panes of glass were blowa out of the windows over the front entrance to the church. Other cottage property in the Wargrave and Vulcan districts lost slate,. tiles, and chimney pots. At the Vulcan iron foundry much damage was sustained, the roof of the old paint shop presenting a vesy dilapidated and broken down, appearance; the new, or erecting-shop skylights were smashed, and numerous slates on the roof were displaced; and lumps of lead stripped from:the roof in exposed places. At the bottom of Newton Common, near the canal, a large portion of a haystack on the farm of Mr. Hodges was blown into the field, and a similar fate met a stack on the farm of Mr Gleave, at Burtonwood.

At Newton the force of the gale was not experienced to the extent it was at Earlestown, or its effects were not as plainly visible. The thatched roof of the farm-cottage in Golporme-road was carried away to a great extent, and several large trees were blown into the roadway. Many buildings were rendered almost roofless at Gol- borne.

Ashton suffered very much throught the hurricane, which left a track of damage and destruction. The most damage appears to have been caused in, Long-lane. Here a Mr. Bur— ehall used as a store-room for household furniture what was formerly a barn. The roof of this was entirely destroyed, and it is stated that neasly £lOO damage was done to the building and the furniture. An extraordinary affair °marred in Harrington-road at one of the entranca to Hair. dock Lodge, directly opposite to the, lodge gates of Lord Gerrard's park. Here was standing a massive tree, about I 12 or 15 yards high, and a trunk eight or nine feet in air- I cumference. This was completely uprooted, thus showing' the extraordinary strong gale that was blowing. In falling I the tree alighted on tie lodge at the ehtrance to Haardock Lodge, and the reef end a portion of the wall was very much damaged. The inmates inside were four in number, and as the tree fell against it they were coasiderably alarmed, but they escaped qnhurt. It is surprin:pg bow the Ige escaped entire destruction.
