div.head: CHAPTER LIV.-TILE CALM BEFORE A STORM.
div.p: CHAPTER LIV.-TILE CALM BEFORE A STORM.
Passing over as uneventful the return to the camp, and the settling down of the Major and his troops into the ordinary gate of things, we resume our narrative a few weeks later.

The adventures of the Flying Column, enhanced and adorned:by the more imaginative of the sharers in it, formed for a long time a subject of animated talk and com- ment among those left behind. As to Stephen:laimself when day after day passed without that summons he was hourly expecting to receive, perhaps from the-Colonel of the regiment, to meet before him his relatives, his anxiety began to cease, his belief to strengthen that Miss Tandeleur was still keeping secret the fact she had seen him; and so he might rest and turn once more to his duties, and the consideration how te so fulfil them as to ensure what he now greatly coveted—rapid advancement. But strange to say, he no longer found satisfaction in them, because he no longer seemed to have the same ambi- tions motive; each day seemed snore wearisome than the one before; he became depressed in spirit, though he knew not why, unless it was that he looked forward to a long period of blank dulness of life that seemed intolerable. But it often happens in life as in the natural phenomena of the seasons, that such periods are only precursors of sig- nal importance, that rouse up to new struggles and new emotions, which whether tending to our welfare or the re- verse, certainly leave us in no mood for listless melancholy self solace. -

Stephen was destined to receive in his own person an il- lustration of this truth, when Gentleman Jack came with effusive congratulations on his courage generally, and of his wonderful presence of mind in partieular, in that magnificent exploit of shooting the Scout, and saving the M ajor's life.

Ti stop all thii, Stephen, who had already hoard some- thing about Jack's behaviour during his absence, drily said, Yirliat about yourself? If I remember rightly net you in prison ?" •• Yes—and to tell you the truth—l liked it so well on the whole that when I did get out I didn't mind getting into it once or twice more. That pack drill nearly broke my back, it has affected rsy heart, so I got into the Infirmary on the last occasion; and enjoyed myself, and read or slept all day.'
" Does the doctor credit you about the heart ? " "Well, he was rather sharp—unpleasantly personal,. and decidedly suspicious, but on the whole dubious, so gave me the benefit of the doubt.'
" 1 wouldn't try him, again, Jack." "Well, now you are come back I feel more comfort- able, and able to put up with the rascAlly amenities of my life--"

"-Hash, Jack! I aee Tommy Atkins near, and I suspect listening. Besides lam a non-commissioned officer myself, and sail feel it a duty to report any insubordinate language." "Tommy Atkins," said Jack, in a low voice, while care- fully avoiding to look in the direction indicated. "Lreryou sure he is there ? "

"Yes," responded• Stephen. "Then I must tell you some other time things I wanted b 4 say." "There he goes," interrupted Stephen. `gone." "Well, he did not lore yen before you went with the Flying Column, now he hates you with an almost develish hatred, because of the distinction you have achieved, and because all men speak sa well of you." "I hope not, for if that was the case I think should be really in a bad way." "Beware of him!"
"He is now

"Oh, really Jack, you talk sad nonsense. Isn't it your head rather than your heart that is getting weak. What can a poor czeature like that do to injure me r "Tell tales of men that can hurt you, and make them believe it is you who are engaged in that dilectable occupa- tion. If there is one crime more black than another in a soldier's eyes, it in telling tales about one another; and if a super'or is cone.2roed the matter becomes ten times worse and more dangerous." "And have you any reason whatever that will bear ex- amination for coming to the belief that Tommy Atkins is either fool enough or rogue enough to try to hurt me in , this way?" " Judge; For some time before your return I noticed , what a liokspittle Tommy was to Sergeant Grabbe of your :company, and how greedily the Sergeant enjoyed the pro- cess. Since your returu I have seen them again and again, carefully drawn apart out of hearin—Tomtuy eagerly

div.head: CHAPTER LV.-USEXPECTED YISITORS.
div.p: CHAPTER LV.-USEXPECTED YISITORS.

"Jack," said Stephen, hurriedly, after a long period of sileace on the part of both, "I see the Major coming this way, and I want particularly to speak to him alone." "All right," was- the reply, and Gentleman Jack set off to see if he could beg, borrow, or obtaia by any other con- nivance a copper or two, to refresh his depressed spirits in the canteen.

Stephen was greatly cheered by the chance of thus telling his own story of the Sergeant's downfall, perhaps even before the Sergeant himself had been to the Major; so prompt a meeting might be his salvation. The reader can, imagine his astonishment when as he rose to be ready, and looked the Major's way, he saw he had been joined by a figure he thought familiar to him, and in a few momenta more recognised as his brother, Lord Harlaxton. •

As the two came close Stephen saluted the Major, but made no sign as regarded the Earl, who for the moment was equally reserved. "Is that the gentleman you seek ?" asked Major Ether- edge of the new corner. "Thank you. Yes," said the Earl. "I do not presume to guess what your lordship's visit may portend," remarked the Major, who had noticed the mutual coldness, " whether we are to lose or retain the ser- vices of our young soldier; but it is only right to say that, apart from what I have told you of his behaviour in the ex- pedition, I have never met with one who has so much interested me by his performance of the most irksome duties in-a cheerful, unmoved spirit." "It is a. testimony that honours both,' said Lord lanai. ton. Bat there was no fervour, much less enthusiasm, in his tone or manner. And he proceeded to introduce his brother to the Major in the coldest most formal way as "the Honourable Stephen Chandos Fronde." The. Major's warmth on the other hand was equally remarkable. He shook Stephen by the hand as he said to him--

"I half anticipated some such result before. I. am truly pleased to welcome now the entire truth." "I shall immediately apply for his discharge," said the Earl, somewhat moved by the Major's behaviour to think of his own.

"Which I will facilitate in every way that I can," said the Major. Unluckily for their kind intentions, the person chiefly concerned was by no means prepared to accept the aid proffered. "Major," he said, "believe me I am truly grateful, but I am obliged to refuse. Ido not intend to leave the army, under present circumstances,-
The awkward and painful double-meaning or application of the last three words only occurred to Stephen after they had been spoken.

" Oh, come, come!" rejoined Major Etheridge, " talk that over with your brother." Then addressing himself to the Earl, he said, "Your lordship, I hope, will honour us with your company at the mess this evening?" "I should only be too glad," was the reply, "but I am in attendance on a young lady, a relative, who is waiting close by to see my brother on family business matters, and we leave immediately after our interview with him." "Then the sooner I take my leave the better," said the Major with a smile, and he and the Earl parted L'with cour- teous words and a feeling of mutual respect. And then Stephen and the Earl were alone, the former full of wonder at:what he had heard, and somewhat agitated at the prospect of again meeting Miss Vandeleur, while such a special danger overhung.
(To be continued.)

div.head: WARRINGTON LICENSED VICTUALLERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON LICENSED VICTUAL- LERS' ASSOCIATION.

ANNUAL DINNER. The members of the above Associati3n, held their annual dinner at the Norton Arms Hotel, Latchford, on Tuesday evening, when about sixty sat down to a capital pread provided by Councillor and Mrs. laylor, and which was served up in first class style. In theabeence of Councillor J. Pierpoint who was announced to have presided, the chair was taken by Councillor Taylor, supported by his Worship the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), Councillors Ashton and Bolton, Messrs. Evans, Candelet (Parliamentary Secre- tary to the Defence League), Hunt, J. L. Wilson, W. Brun- dreet, Geo. Wright, Thomas Brooks, Rudge, James Hlll, W. SliPlcock, Gilbert Riley, Pugh, Alfred Tanks, Gleave, Thos. Archer, R. Mellor, Thomas Maguire, J. Allen, J. Rowe, Roddy, Phillips, Hilton, Kilshall, Grundy, Thomas Clare, Stirrup, lLowson and Son (representing Messrs. Walker), A. Potter (secretary), tic. After dinner, the CHAIRMAN proposed "Tae Queen," "The Prince of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family," and " Her Majesty's Land and Sea Forces," Mr. Tanks responding to the latter toast. The CHAIRMAN, in giving "The Mayor, magistrates, and Corporation of Warrington," said it was a most important one in connection with their town. He believed no par- ticular fault had been found with the Mayors and Corpora- tion of Warrington up to the present, as they had carried oat their duties satisfactorily. (Hear, hear.) He coupled with the toast the name of their worthy and esteemed friend, Alderman J. Harrison. (Applanse.) Mr. CANDILBT said he should be exceedingly glad if they would allow him to make a few remarks in support of the toast. If there was one thing more than another whieh added to the honour of the civic chair it was when they found the gentleman who held that nigh position disposed to exercise his civic duties with impartiality towards all classes of society with which he leas so honourably con- nected. He thought that was a trait in their chief magis- trate's character which had gained for him the respect and esteem of his fellow townsmen, and which had made him so popular. (Hear, hear.) As to the impartiality of his Wor- ship, he did not forget that a short time ago they found him with the same disposition towards the associates of temper- ance on a temperance platform. Nevertheless the fact of the Mayor being on a temperance platform did not detract from the value of his services, his discernment, and lois goodwill towards all classes. (Hear, hear.) The present com- pany were quite as much in favour of temperance as the com- pany their Mayer was keeping the other night. (Applause.) Speaking of local affairs, Mr. Candelet referred especially to the gas question, and said he could not understand vir hi a eoriaoikiti; ti )e1.3- in any jowd liheuld not sell gag at a lees priee than they di t as a rule. He put the case before the Manchester publicin every ward, and the result was that there was a reduction from 5s to 3s per thousand. That was a great many years ago, but he did not think that was low enough. GAS—he knew it from enquiry and close ob- servation—could be made with a taro& at is 10d per thou- sand. They made something out of coke, out of ammonia, spent lime, and by selling tar, and that required to be taken into consideration in conjunction with the price which was charged for gas. There was, moreover, a lars,e outside public which consumed no gas at all, and the fact was that whenever improvements were promoted it was done out of the pockets of the gas consumers for the benefit of those who consumed no gas at all. He fonad fault with the quality of the Warrington gas, and hoped that it would be improved and reduced in price. Mr. Candelet next spoke of the tendency which existed to take the power of granting licenses from the hands of the magistrates and vest it in the hands of corporate bediee. He pointed out that a corpora- tion was a changeable body, and it would become a question as to whether a certain house or houses were necessary, and their houses were liable to be shut up without a farthing compensation. If ratepayers ever possessed that power the very people who voted for the closing of any certain house ought to be compelled by law to put their hands into their pockets and pay for the property they had destroyed. (Hear, hear.) The toast having been received with mnsical honours, The MAYOR was loudly cbeered on rising to reply. In the course of his remarks, he said their friend Mr. Candelet reminded them that he had been present on a temperance platform a short time ago. So he had, and he could assure them that he should have felt it as a reproach if he had re- fused. (Hear, bear.) The meeting be attended was a meeting called by the Church Gf England Temperance Asso- ciation. It was not necessarily a teetotal association, but purely a temperance association. And by that it was ex- plained by one or two speakers that they did not only mean temperance in drinking, but also in eating, and, in fact, temparanca in all the relations of life. Their aim was not so much to further the objects of the teetotallers as that of temperance, and to show them that it was so he need only tell them that a great many nesmbers of that association were net teetotallers at all, but were strictly temperance men —men who partook of those things, wines, spirits, or beer, in reasonable and proper quantities, and in such a way as not to forget themselves or to abuse what were; when they were not abused, good things. (Applause.) Their object was to promote temperance, and when people joined them and confessed they were unable to restrain themselves, they also opened their arms to the reception of teetotalers; and he did not think there was a licensed vic- tualler present but would agree with him that if a man could not restrain himself, if he was so unfortunately constituted that he could not subdue his passions in that respect it was the best thing for himself and family, and •for society at large, to abstain from it altogether. (Applause.) He did not believe for one moment, as Mr. Candelet said in his speech, that it was to the interest of the licensed victuallers to see a drunken man come to their houses, or conducive to their comfort to allow men to stay so long as to become in- toxic ited. He did not think an absolute drunkard was a profit to anybody, but beyond doubt a curse to society, and in that light the licensed victuallers looked upon him. He attended that temperance meeting with feelings of great pleasure, for he did not hear one single harsh word used from the commencement to the end that reflected in the slightest degree on licensed victuallers as a body, who were spoken of with respect. He came there that night by special invitation of the Licensed Victuallers' Association, and with much the same feelings as when he went to the meet- ing of the Church of England Temperance Association. He came there to witness for himself what he had witnessed, namely, a most orderly, respectable, and intelligent assembly of the inhabitants of Warrington engaged in a certain trade. He had seen nothing all night but what was highly com- mendable and if he staved until twelve o'clock he did not think he should see anything else. (Hear, hear.) He cunt) there perfectly unbiassed and unprejudiced, and he was sure he would go away very much prepossed in favour of what he had heard. For the kind observations which they had made with reference to him he assured them he felt very grateful to them indeed. He only regretted that in times past those who associated themselves with the movement of total abstinemee had done more to retard the progress of tem- perance by their intemperate language than the greatest enemies they could have to contend against. (Applause.) There was temperance to be observed in everything, and at the meeting of the temperances society referred to the other day, that was strongly impressed on the public assembling in that room. With reference to the Corporation of War- rington, he had no doubt that in course of time they would have both an improvement and a reduction in the price of gas (Hear, hear.) He believed nobody was more anxious than the Gas Committee to bring that about at the earliest pos- sible opportunity. Since the purchase of the-gasworks there had been groat difficulties to contend with, and when they had subsided he did not think they would have occasion to find fault with the Corporation of Warrington. He was sure Mr. Candelet must have been struck with the excellent character of our streets; they were well paved, well sewered, and the Corporation were now anxious to secure what they thought would be an advantage to them, namely, the control of the waterworks. He did not think that the watervrorks should be in the hands, if it could be avoided, of a private company. Water was one of the first essentials of life, and the very vital,ity of their manufacturing interests which they could not afford to ,neglect or be indifferent to. Therefore, if the Corporation succeeded in acquiring the Waterworks Company's property, and on reasonable terms, he believed it would tend greatly te the advantage of the community at large, and be a blessing to them in many res- pects. He could assure them the Corporation of Warrington were bent upon what would be to the interests of the whole community. (Applause.) Mr. HUNT, chairman of the Manchester and Salford Licensed Victuallers' Association, proposed "The Warrington Licensed Victuallers' Association," and observed that he had been informed that never in the annals of its history had the members been so numerous or working more in harmony with each other, and he had great reason to believe they would yet be far more prosperous in the future. He coupled with the toast the nese of the chairman. The CHAIRMAN having suitably responded, Mr. BRUNDRETT proposed "The Town and Traie of War. riugton," and spoke of the increased prosperity of Warring- ton of late years. They were always doing something, and within the last 20 or 30 years works had,sprung up rapidly amongst them. When they looked at one firm alone at Bewsey with a capital of a million of money, he thought something was doing in the trade of Warrington. There were other trades which had sprung up and flourished of late years, in which he might include the brewing trade. ( Hear, bear.) Mr. BUDGE, in responding, remarked that there was only one trade in Warrington which was bad and that was the -licensed victuallers', which was owing to bad legislation and the growth of out-door licenses. He hoped Mr. Can- delet would do what he could to obtain the repeal of those licenses. Councillor Bolton, in proposing "The Licensed Victual-

lers' Defence League, and other societies for the protection of trade interests," said it behcyed them to do what they could for themselves, because other societies were arrayed against them, formed for the purpose of harrassing the trade and securing class legislation. The people who were engaged in opposition to them haci got an idea that it would benefit them; that the money which now went into the hands of publioans and brewers would go into the hands of grocers for instance. Those people forgot that brewers and peblicans were as long-head.d as themselves, and that the money which they now iaVested in their own trade would be invested, in the event of giving up their own leasines, in oppesition to those very people who now clamoured so much against them. Mr. CANDELET, in responding, said the League had become necessary in connection with their trade, and he hoped it would be judiciously used in defence of that property which honestly belopged to them. Intemperately were they m- ailed from the public platform, and very often within the walls of St. Stephen's by members of Parliament, who ap- peared to have no sympathy with the trade whatever, simply•beeause they had never yet used in a combined form the power which they bad at their command. They were policed and inspected at every step they took; what was wanted was less law and [store freedom. (Hear, hear.) Mr. littoolcs proposed " The Presidaat for ti:e evening," and the CliAlitiLaN having replied, Mr. EVANS gave "Visitors and absent friends," responded to by Mr. J. P. WILSON, who wished long life and pros- perity to the association.

• The toast of the "Press " concluded the list. The pismire of the evening was greatly enhanced by the excellent sing- ing of Messrs. Hill, Potter, Howarth, Ashworth, and Wil- son. Mr. George Riley presided at the pianoforte with his customary ability.

div.head: ST. HELENS NEWS.
div.p: ST. HELENS NEWS.

Tim C Omni* a Gk.—A lig. FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.-0/1 Wed- nesday afternoon, an elderly man named Thomas Finnigan, who lived in Bold-street, St. Helens, died from injuries he received on the same day from a waggon while following his employ at the Deep Pit, belonging to the St. Helens Collieries Company. An inquest, it is understood, will be held. YORK-STREET SCHOOLS, Si. HELENS. On Wednesday evening a vocal and instrumental concert was given in these schools by Mrs. Barfoot and her "Little Folks," assisted by Mr. W. C. Eccles, the proceeds of the concert being given to the Rev. W. Chaplaink aid ot a new organ. The room was well filled, and the programme, which in many respects was similar to the one rendered by Mrs. Barfoot and- her pupils in the Town Hall a alert time ago, was, as on that occasion, very fully appreciated. ALLEGED ASSAULTS.—A young woman named Elizabeth Ponder was charged at the St. Helens Police Court with baying vsaulted another young woman named Catherine Connell, on the 2nd inst., and was fined 53 and costs.—Peter Pickavance was charged with having assaulted a girl named Margaret Pickavance, on Sunday night last, at Parr. The complainant said the defendant had set upon her in the street and beat her severely, but as there was some doubt as to the identity of the defendant the case was dis- missed.

ALLEGED THEFT BY A WOMAN.—Alice Lacey, a middle- aged woman, was on Friday charged at St. Helens Police Court with having stolen a sauce-pan, the property of John Murray, of 20, Warrington New-road. Both the complain- ant and the defendant in this ease live in the same house, and the prisoner, it seemed, alleged that the complainant's wife 9WO: her a debt, and it was in defrayment of this that she took the sauce-pan. The case was withdrawn.—On Saturday, however, the prisoner was committed for 14 days for having been drunk and disorderly. THEFT FROM THE MARKET.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a girl named Mary Cottrell, was charged with having stolen a watch guard, valued at dd., the property of James Pickup. The complainant is a draper, living at Blackburn. Every Monday he erects a stall in St. Helens market-place, and on Monday last, he had the usual goods displayed on this stall. P.C. Walsh, who was in plain clothes in the market-place, saw the prisoner pick the guard in question from the stall and put it into one of her stockings. He at once apprehended her.—She pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s.

- A NE.CiLEC-TED CHILD.—JOI;iI" Cottington, a half-clad sicklylooking boy, 10 years of age was, OR Monday, charged with having stolen of tobacco, the property of George G. Hughes, tobacconist, Liverpool-road—On Sunday afternoon Mr. Hughes was in her kitchen behind the shop, the door of which had been shut but not fastened. She noticed that the door was open, and on going into the shop she saw the prisoner behind the •counter with the tobacco in his band. She detained him, and called in a policeman. The tobacco was worth 53.—The prisoner was ordered to have four strokes with a birchrod. THE NEW PUBLIC-HOUSE IN WESTFIELD-STREET.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Mr. J. 0. Swift applied on behalf of Messrs. Greenal and Co. for a full and permanent license to the new public-house erected by them in Westfield-street, near to the brook.—Mr. Swift pointed out that it had been understood that on his clients giving up the licenses of four beerhouses, one being the Horse and Jockey opposite and the other three in Water-street, they should have a full license to this new house.—The applica- tion was granted, the chairman (Mr. H. S. Hall) saying that it was a great improvement to the town.—Mr. Swift: I aim glad to hear your worships say so. Sr. THOMAS'S TEA PARTY, Sr. HELENS.—The annual tea nteeting and entertainment, in connoction with this church, were held on Thursday evening last week, in the schoolroom, Lyon-street. There were about 500 persons sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by the fol- lowing ladies :—Misses Pigot, L. Pigot, Fishwieb, Small- show, Ormerod, and Bridge ; Mesdames Bothwell, Norman, Edmundsen, J. Webster, E. Burgess, Latham, Taylor, McNelly, Ward, Beckett, Porter, Wardlow' Lowe, Craven, Ashcroft, Baddeley, Bate, Adams, Slather, Hardy, and Hill. After tea the chair was taken by the Rev. J. C. Pigot, and d very enjoyable evening was spent. A MANCHESTER PUBLICAN FINED AT Sr. HELENS.— Jame' Dawson, the keeper of the Bee Hive public-house, in Manchester, was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having travelled between Manchester and St. Helens Junction without a ticket.—The defendant is in the habit of travelling between Manchester and St Helens, and on the 26th ultimo he was seen to alight from a Man- chester train at St. Helens Junction. He was asked for his ticket but would not give any. He afterwards booked at St. Helens Junction to St. Helens. Since the summons was issued the defendant had offered to nay the fare from Man- chester, but it had been refused by the railway authorities. —A fine of 40s. and costs was imposed. CHARGE AGAINST A PUBLICAN AT Sr. HELBNS.—At the _ _ _

St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, James Thorpe, i 1; landlord of the Black Bull public-house, Church-street, was charged with having permitted drunkenness on his licensed premises. Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—On the night of the let inst. P.C. Ewan, it seemed, was called into the Black Bull by the manager to eject a man named Gaffney, who was behaving in a very violent manner. Gaffney was ejected with considerable difficulty, and it afterwards took several policemen to convey him to the police-office. He was proceeded against and tined for having refused to quit, and the present charge was chiefly based on the statement of the manager on that occasion that Gaffney had been in the house an hour and a half, and that he had had three glasses of beer and was drunk.—The case was dismissed.

THE VICISSITUDES 07 A HORSE STEALER.—A young man named Fred Anson, who said he belonged to Macclesfield, was on Thursday charged, at the Sr. Helens Police Court, with having stolen a horse, horse cloth, and cart harness, value £25, the property of Elizabeth Wigglesworth, of flanging Bridge Farm, Sutton.—lt appeared that the horse and trapping had been stolen from the farm buildings on the sight of the 27th November. On the 28th the prisoner, who had then the horse with him, had breakfast at the Bridge- water beerhouse' Leigh, and then said that he wanted to sell the horse, as he had two or three others. On the same day he was taken into custody by Constable Sykes, at Booths- town, near Manchester, for being drunk in charge of the same horse, and was sent to_gaol for 14 days for that offence. He was afterwards handed over to the St. Helens Police.— He was committed to the Qulrter Sessions. POACHING Main ST. HaLENs.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, three men named James Greener, Peter Fildes, and Joseph Kaye, were charged with having had nets, used for taking game, in their possession on the 4th inst.—Mr. J. O. Swift said he prosecuted on be- half of Colonel Gamble, who leased the game en the farm of Mr. Boardman, near Windle Smithies.—lt appeared that on the day in question P.C. Watters bad been, in Owen's- lane, Windle Smithies, when he saw the defendants doing something, but he could not exectly tell what, lit a field close by. Ha watched them till they came on to the road, when he went up to them, and on searching Fildes he found a net in his possession, on Greener he found some twine which apparently was used in the working of the net, but on Kaye he did norfind anything. Greener, it was stated, had been committed 37, Kaye 29. and Fildes 1& times pre- vionsly.—Greener and Fildes were each fined £3 and ,14s. costs, or one month's imprisonment; Kaye was fined £1 and 14s. costs, or a fortnight's imprisonment. MILL Cilia Arrecimp BY TRAMPS IN WALD& On Saturday night the driver of the mail car between Bedge- lett and Carnarvon was attacked by tramps when ab )ut three miles from the latter town. One man jumped to the horse'. head, but fell nnder the wheels of the vehicle, whilst another, springing on the box !rem behind, attempt‘d to disable the driver and seise the mails. After a desperate struggle the driver knocked over his aseailant arid brought the mails wifely to Catnarvon. A woman returning Iron Carnarvon fair was also attacked by a !ramp, but mar..—:ed to escape. The police have been put on the track of the ruffians.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

- *** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the had office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

OUGHTRINGTON PARE V. /TORTHWICX VICTORIA. (2ND TEAM). —Played oa the ground of the former. The match resulted in favour of Oughtrington by 4 goals to 2. HAYDOCE Races/mole v. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT NORTHWJCH. On Wednesday night, a large demonstration was held at Northwich, in the centre of the Cheshire salt dtstrict, in favour of the extension of the franchise. Mr. Cf. W. Latham, Liberal candidate for Mid-Cheshire, presided, and there were upwards of two thousand persons present. The Chairman, in the course of his address, said there must be a uniform resident franchise. At present there were some- thing like two millions of men in the United Kingdom who had not the right to vote, although equally deserving with their fellew-men, and equal in intelligence and in intellect. He did not agree with Lord Hartington when he said, in reference to the Leeds conference, that he would prefer, instead of passing general resolutions, that the Liberals would turn their attention to some particular point. They had a right to ask the Government to look into the whole question, study what the feelings of people are, and carry out their wishes. It was the duty of the Govern.nent to gather from public opinion the general feelings of the people. (Applause.) They must have the franchise extended not only in this country but also in Ireland, aad they must have equal elec- toral rights. They did not, of course, agree with everything done by the Irish, hut they believed in representative go- vernment, and they must net interfere with the course of it. —Mr. Hobert Verdin moved a resolution urging the Go- vernment to give precedence to the measure dealing with the franchise. He also moved a resolution in favour of giving the franchise to women.—Mr. Brodie, workingman, Altrincham, seconded.—Mr. Tomkinson, Liberal candidate for West Cheshire,in supporting:the extension of the franchise said he agreed with Mr. Latham that it would be an injus- tice and ungracious to refuse to embrace Ireland in an ex- tended franchise.—Mr. Briggs, M.P., Miss Becker, and others supported the resolution, which was carried.

The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connec- tion with Holy Trinity Day Schools was held last evening, when a crowded audience assembled to witness the perform- ance of the scholars. • The Rey. W. Freaton, the vicar, oc- cupied the chair, and he was supported by Sir W. B. For- wood, of Liverpool, who was present to distribute the prizes, and the Rev. D. Llewellyn (curate). A tasteful and inter- esting programme had been arranged. The children sang several pieces of music during the evening in a manner which abundantly testified to the excellent training they had received, and reflected the greatest credit upon Mr. Arnett. Miss Lucy Robinson rendered "The dying child " very tastefully, and as "The crossing sweeper" Master Hulme was greeted with hearty applause. Miss Cattrall sarg "Christmas chimes" with good expression, and a , dialogue, entitled "The trials of a patient man," was given in capital style. Miss Robinson was again very successful in the sang "Cherry ripe." Before distributing the prizes, Sir W. B. FORWOOD delivered an address in which he complimented the scholars upon their excellent entertain- ment, and referred to the fact that the proceeds were to be devoted to the purpose of providing a day in the country during the summer for those who attended school 400 times out of a possible 440. He urged upon those present the importance of their children attending school regularly, which he said would centribute to their welfare in after life by inculcating methodical habits. It was a sincere pleasure to him to see the church school so efficiently managed br their very indefatigable head master, Mr. Arnett. (Applause.) It was a glorious thing to find that the Church of England Schools in the district were doing such a good work. The Church of England Schools throughout the country were doing a noble work. (Applause.) They were the instructors of the people. At the present time two-thirds of the children attending elementary schools in this country attended Church of Eng- land Schools, and the increase in the number of scholars in those schools since the Elementary Education Act Was passed in 1870 was greater than the total number of the children at present attending Board Schools. That was abundant proof that the people of England attached great importance to religious educa- tion going hand in hand as it were with secular education—(applause); that the people of all denomina- tions were anxious that white their children were being taught secular subjects they should also be taught these great religious lessens which they valued and esteemed so highly, and from which they one and all had received so much comfort and guidance, and to which they must all attribute so much of their happiness in this life, and on which they based their hopes for the future. (Applause.) After referring to the loyalty and Christian principles of the artizan classes, Sir" William deprecated the practice which too many of the working classes followed, of training their sons to be clerks. He pointed out the advantages which would result if they were taught trades, or brought up to be tradesmen. He did not think it possible to overeducate children, but it was pos- sible to teach them many things which would be of little use to them in after life. He hoped that at no distant day boys in elementary schools would receive a technical train- ing to some trade—(hear, hear)—and girls would be taught how to cook. (Applause.) He concluded by giving a few words of advice on thrift, and then proceeded to distribute the prizes, a list of which is annexed : St. VU—Henry Edward Annett. St. Vl.—Martha Cattrall. DAMAGING RUNCORN BRIDGE. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.

Ay Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Robert Bush. a young man, was sum- moned on a charge of wilfully breaking five lamps on Run- corn Bridge, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Co., doing damage to the extent ef £2—The de- fendant pleaded guilty.—Alfred Williams (for whom Mr. Knowles appeared), Frederick Cox, and Thomas Jones were charged with similar offences, and pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Preston, junr., prosecuted on behalf of the company, and stated that about 10-20 on Sunday night, the 2nd December, the defendants, who were in an excited mood, were crossing Runcorn Bridge. They were walking from Runcorn towards Widnes. A flatman, who was walking behind them, saw Bash strike at and break the first lamp put there to light the pathway, besides bending the frame. The flatman also saw Bush break two other lamps': He then hurried on to the end of the bridge and informed the ticket-collector, who ascertained the names and addresses of all the defendants.—James Smith, a flatman, living at Runcorn. and Samuel Machlin, ticket collector at the Lan- cashire side of Runcorn Bridge. coroborated this statement. Neither of the witnesses saw any of the defendants except Bush break the lamps, an 4 Mr. PresOn therefore asked leave to w thdraw summonses against Williams, Cox. and Jones, and the Bench granted the request.—Henry Price, of the gas department, Crawe, proved the amount of the dam- age- The lamps, he said, were broken three or four times a month, alai the lights were frequently exiinguished. The company had been put to great expense and trouble through such conduct. The bridge was a dangerous place.—Mr. Lewin: And there are not many lamps on the bridge as it is.—Witness: I Cannot say that.—Mr. Brock: Perhaps you are speaking fee:ll3oY, Mr. Lewin ?—Mr. Lewin : I can months and thear d speak to it., being a very dark place.—The Bench fined Bush damage £2, total £6 9s 61; or in labour. Mr and Mrs John White, Mr and Mrs Littlewood, Mr and Mrs Fisher, Mr and Mrs Wright, Mr and Mrs Kay, Mr and Mrs Hayes Mr and Mrs Wood, Dr and Mrs Gornall, Major and Mrs Hayes, Mr and Mrs Parker, Mr D W Finney, Rev B B Prescott, Rev M Schonberg, Mr and Mrs Royston, Mr and Mrs Wrightson, Dr and Mrs Mackie, Mr and Mrs Bay- ley, Mr and Mrs Picton, Mrs Jackson, Mr and Mrs Dutton. the Misses Garland, Mr and Mrs Scotson, Mr and Mrs Mil- ling, Dr and Mrs Fox, Mr and Mrs J Hesketh, Mr and Mrs Carter, Rev A Harrison, Councillor and Mrs Broadbent, Rev F W Cory, Mr and Mrs Williams, Mr and Mrs Litton' Rev H and Mrs Stevens, Mr and Mrs Rowson Mr and Mrs Dun, Mrs Radford, Mr Twiss, Miss Hesketh, Rev and Mrs J Eglinton, Mr and Mrs. J C Thompson, Mr, Mrs and the Misses Kidd, Mr and Mrs Cook, Mrs Moores, Mrs Hannah, Mr and Mrs Brundrett, Mr and Mrs H G Linaker, Mr and Mrs Jeans, Rev J and Mrs McTurk, Mrs Bradbury, Mrs Sherratt, Mr and Mrs Bramhall, Mr, Mrs, and Miss Down, Councillor R. W. Frincotnb and Mr Shurrock. Mr Hollowell, Herr Huttman, Mr C A Rowley (masters). Rev. E. J. WlLLcocics, the 11, al mister, who wasfcordially grested,opened the proceedings with the following speech : My Lard, Ladies, and Gentletnen,—We bid yeu all we- come here to-day, and our best thanks are due to our noble friend Lord Winmarleigh for his presence here amongst us. His lordship is always ready to help on any good cause, and lam sure we are all glad to see him. (Applause.) You will expect me on an occasion like the present to give some account of my stewardship, and I am prepared to stand or fall by the results of the school's success. In point of num- ber, I believe the school is as large as it has ever been. We number this term 111 on the school register, which is, I think you will admit, most satisfactory, considering the ad- vance in the school fees, which presses bard on many, and deters others from sending their sons to us. The free scholarships are a great boon. and I wish we could give more—perhaps we may be able to de so when the funds permit. At present we have established twelve scholarships, half of which are given to deserving boys in the school on the results of the Mid- summer examinations, and the other half to boys from elementary schools within the borough of Warrington. Turning to the successes gained by the school in competi- tion with others, I should first mention that as an experi- ment last Christmas we sent in nine boys for the Cam- bridge local examinations, all of whom passed—seven with honours' and four of these with distinction in various sub- jects. These examinations are very useful to us, as boys who obtain certificates—provided they pass in certain speci- fied subjects—are excused the preliminary examinations for law and medicine, Sze. We also took a higher flight last Midsummer, and two boys in the VI. Form succeeded in gaining the higher certificates, granted by the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, which excuse the holders from responsions and previous examina- tions at those universities respectively—besides answering all the purposes of the Local Examinations. (Applame.) I should add tl,at in this examination we competed with the best Public Schools in England, and that our candi- dates passed in Latin, Greek, French, Mathematics, and Divinity, with a knowledge of the Greek Testament. (Ap- plause.) The report on the School in Mathematics and Chemistry was most satisfactory, but in the latter subject we are greatly in want of a laboratory where boys can work out experiments for themselves. The Examiner in Modern Languages said that the French was improved, and that the German continued satisfacary. In Classics the Examiner summed up by saying :—" 'There is good promise for the future of the School, Farms V and VI containing each of them several boys who seem likely to do very well." (Hear, hear.) I should like to say a few words to parents with regard to the removal of their sons from school at too early an age. As a general rule boys can do little in business and nothing in a profession before they attain the age of 10; but the two years from 14 to 16 in a boy's school life are, I consider, the most im- portant. (Hear, hear). Up to the age of 14 the time is taken up with grounding him in his various subjects. but after this age we begin to see the fruits of our labour, and a boy will generally learn more in these last two years than in all the other /4 put together. (Hear, hear.) We should always remember that in education we give a boy that which .can never be taken from him. / have pleasure in announcing that three new spetial prizes have been added to those already existing. Dr. Gornall offers prizes amount- ing to the value of £3 3s. for the encouragement of modern languages; the Rev. E C. E. Carleton one for Old Testament history ; and Mr. J. C. Thompson one for drawing from nature, as an application of the model and shading taught in the school. / beg to thank these gen- tlemen for the interest they take in us. (Applause.) You will, perhaps, expect to see a Greek or French play this afternoon, but I have found from experience that this is impossible without upsetting the work of the school ;, so, in place of the more severe, several of the boys have prepared, chi-Ily out of school, a humorous piece of English comedy, which I hope will amuse you when we have got through the heavy part of our entertainment. The scenery has been painted in the tower by eurse.ves, with the invaluable help of Mr. J. Hesketh. I will now read the names of those wha have gained the school prizes, together with those who have won certificates and prizes at the last Cam- bridge Local Examination, and will then cal? on the Right Hon. Lord Winmarleigh to distribute them. (Applause.)

THE EXAMINER, NA TUTDAY, DECEMBER ]5, 1883:

THE FATILITY AT WIDNES WORKS. At the Mersey Hotel, on Monday afternoon, Mr. T. W I Barker held an inquiry respecting the death of John Walker, a labourer, 32 years of age, who resided in Cromwell-street. —Mr. A. G. Kyle represented Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.. and Mr. T. J. Peters the relatives of the deceased.—From the evidence of Martin Webster, 76, James-street, John Berney, Thomas Walker, and Miss Janet Downie (matron at the hospital), it appeared that the deceased, who was em- ployed at Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical Works, was en- gaged with four others in removing an acid cistern. 'The cistern consisted of four large slabs of Yorkshire stone, each weighing about 13cwt., and these were held together by "the rods." Deceased and Webster had loosened the tie rods, and iron clamps had been fastened at three corners to keep the stones in position until removed by the derrick which had been erected at one side. When removing the last rod one of the stones fell to the ground, and deceased was crushed beneath it. His skull and right arm was fractured, and he died in a few hours. The jury diverted their inquiry to discover whether there had been any neglect on the part of the worlimsn. A model of the cistern was produced, and the method of removing it was demonstrated. The witnesses stated that three clamps were quite sufficient to hold the stones, and that the usual method of removal had been fol- lowed. Only one of the clamps was wedged. The Coroner said he would leave it to the judgment of the jury as to whether there had been any negligence or want of care in removing the cistern. He was much obliged to the manager of the firm for producing the model, which had been of great assistance. His theory of the accident was that through some vibration the atone fell over.—After a short consultation in private, the jury returned a verdict of acci- dental death, but recommended that in future greater pre- cautions should be used in removing cisterns. In reply to the Coroner, the foreman (Mr. Wharton) said the jury did not attach blame to anyone, they thought it was an error on the part of the men not to wedge the clumps.

Lord WINICUILEIGH then rose to address the company, and he was received with loud cheers. He observed he was quite mare that it mast have given those present the same pleasure as it had himself to hear the speech of his friend the head master, and to witness the distribution of such well-merited prizes as he had the honour of giving to the several candi- dates. He knew there must be many present that day to whom a meeting like that must be very interesting as reminding them of similar proceediags in their youth. (Hear, hear.) He, amongst others, had always looked upon Speech Day at the school where he was at with great in- terest, and he could recollect now every school companion of his who gained prizes on those Speech Days. He men- tioned that because, looking at his young friends in the gal- lery, he knew they would regard with feelings of more than ordinary friendship their school-fellows who had dis- tinguished themselves on that occasion, and thus added credit to the Warrington Grammar School. (Hear, hear.) To them who were in several ways connected with the borough of Warrington, the state of their Grammar School had always been a subject of very great interest, and ever since be recollected there bad been a number of persons in the town who had devoted their minds ia supporting and maintaining the school in its former credit. At the present moment it was more than usually important that the War- rington Grammar School should retain its position as' an educational establishment in this country. They were go- ing through now, as they were doubtless aware, a sort of education flood, which covered tha whole country, and in that movement every educational establishment was included—it affected all their high-class public schools, their Grammar Schools, and even the Universities them- selves. They had all toeeri re-modelled in order that they should give increased facilities for education to every class of Her Majesty's subjects. He had no doubt that in the end beneficial results of all those changes would be manifest throughout the kingdom. (Hear, hear.) But the Grammar Schools of the country bad laid on them a great deal more responsibility than formerly attached to them, and if they were to Maintain their position they must take care they kept ahead of those schools below them. (Hear, hear.) He had much pleasure on the present occasion of giving an instance of his own knowledge that that school was trying to maintain its position in mentioning that under the alteration he had alluded to there were free scholarships given to their school, and one of those free scholars had gained no less than six prizes that day. (Applause.) That educational movement was now carrying everything before it in the conntry,and it was supposed that any person taking advantage of the opportunity given him at any one of the schools had a chance of advancing himself in life more than he had in former times. Probably they remembered what the Emperor Napoleon once said to his army, that every private soldier carried a field-marshal's baton in his knapsack. (Hear, hear.) He thought he might say the same in an educational sense in this country now. Every scholar in a school might carry the Bishop's mitre, the Judge's ermine, or the Lord Chancellor's seal. (Laughter.) However, the managers of that Gram- mar School did not aim at giving them the mitre, the ermine, or the seal of the Lord Chancellorship; their object was to give the pupils a good sound eipcation, and if they only took advantage of what was taught therein they would be able to pass through life with credit to themselves, no matter what position they might enter upon. k Ap- plause.) At the same time, those who distintnished them- selves would have an opportunity of going into the Univer- sitie3, or the Army, or other places where situations were attainable by merit, and be had no doubt whatever that from the statement of the Head Master Eeveral of those pre- sent before many years were over would show that they had taken advantage of the education they bad received at that school. (Hear, hear.) He was not going to give them a speech on education, because iu the first place he was not in a position to do so, and secondly because he knew they were all anticipating a much better entertainment from-the actors who would succeed him on that stage. He would only express to them once more the very great pleasure he bad in distributing the prizas, and at seeing the Warrington Grammar School flourishing. (Applause.)

He spoke as chairman of the governors of the-804;1.as well as chairman of that meeting, and in both capacities he would say that they had every prospect of the Warrington Gram- mar School rivalling any other grammar school in the country. (Loud applause.) Let him tell the young people before him that it did not solely depend either on •the geverno,s, or the head master, or the teachers of the school ; it depended in some measure upon the young people them- selves. He daresay they had heard a good deal of the several great schools in the country, such as Eton, Harrow, Winchester, and Rugby. Those schools owed a cetrsiderable amount of their celebrity to those who had had the management of them, but a great portion of the celebrity depended on the credit and character of those who had been educated at them. Eton could boast of such men as Fox, Canning, Lord Grey, Sir John Lubbock, Lord Derby, and the present Prime Minister, the Right Hon. W. E. Glad- stone—(applause)—whilst ;farrow had the late Sir Robert Peel, Lord Palm': ton, and a number of others. Rugby and Winchester could boast in the same way. the cele- brity of those men had added to the celel, ay of the schools to which they belonged, and he would ' 'I them that the celebrity of their own grammar school was a good deal depending on their future conduct, and in showing to the world that it had brought up young men who did credit to the society in which they lived. (Applause.), He hoped they would never be led away by the belief that education depended entirely upon learning those particular arts which were applicable to the professions which they were individually going to in the world. There was in Warrington same time since a strong feeling that they were going too far, in introducing other matters which did not belong to the several professions for which the pupils were intended. There never was a more foolish or false idea than that. He could give them proofs that some people believed that the learning which was given is that school interfered with the subjects reepisite for their different employments in life. But he could give them, if he had time, a long list of persons in this country who had risen to the top of the tree in commerce and manufacture, and who had also been celebrated for their literary and scientific abilities. He would not, however, take up their time by mentioning all those whom be had in his mind. He would mention one. He saw in the newspapers that the Lord Mayor of London, in proposing a toast at his meeting, illustrated his observations by two beautiful quotations, the one in Greek and the other in Latin. Now, the Lord Mayor 11 of London was one of the first merchants of that city, and ' he was distinguished by his literary character at school and at the university, and he was now raised by the merchants of London to be the first magistrate of the first city of the world. (Applause.) He gave that to prove that it was a great absurdity to suppose that they would interfere with their progress in life by devoting themselves zealously to the higher subjects of education taught at their school. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, his lordship wished the pupils every success in the various occupations in which they might hereafter be engaged. (Cheers.) The entertainment shortly afterwards commenced by one of the pupils (Down) playing a violin solo in creditable style. MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON OVERSEERS.

The usual monthly meeting of the Warrington Over- seers was held at the Town Hall on Thursday evening, when there were present: Alderman Kean (in the chair), Mr. John Harrison, Dr. Mackie, and Mr, John Tunstall (assistant overseer.)
THE NEW RATE: DR. MACKIE AND THE SNIP CANAL EXPENSES.

Alderman KEAN said their first business that evening was to make the new rate for the ensuing half-year, and he would ask Mr. Tunstallsto lay his estimate before them.— Mr. TUNSTALL said to meet the precept would demand a rate of Is. 6d. in the borough for the next half-year, and 93. out of the borou... It was made on the same principle as before, and the amount depended upon the purposes for which the rate was required. The last rate was 1:s. 4d. in the borough and 7d. outside.—Dr. MACKIE asked if there was any special reason for the increase ?—Mr. TUNSTALL: There was the opposition to the Manchester Ship Canal, which caused an increase.—Dr. MACKIE : Cart you tell us about how much ?—Mr. TUNSTALL replied that he could not, as is res Led with the borough authorities. The latter gave the overseers a precept which they bad to meet, and the expenses of the Mancheter Ship Canal opposition was included in that, although he could not tell the amount.—Dr. MACKIN : I would like to find out something about this opposition to the Ship Canal, and what you can tell, us about it, if anything.—Mr. TUN- STALL: I know a sum is included for that, but how much I cannot say.—Dr. MAcnrEt Do you know of your own know- ledge who has the making up of this call ?—Mr. TUNSTALL said it was prepared by Mr. Choriey, and the estimate had been brought before the Council. The particular item in question would be passed by the General Purposes Commit- tee in the first instance.—Aldermaa KEAN: We have paid over £2,000 for the opposition given to the Ship Canal scheme.—Dr. MACKIE thought there had been only two calls made, viz., £l,OOO and £2oo.—Alderman KEAN: The survey of the river is included in the amount.—Dr. MACKIE: That's another special item of £5OO by itself.—Alderman KEAN: Altogether the amount is over £2,ooo.—Dr. MACKIE believed the calls actually asked for had been &00 first, £l,OOO afterwards, and £5O on account of the last survey, but which really had nothing to do with the Ship Canal He wished it to go forth accurately what the opposition to the Ship Canal had cost.—Alderman KEAN: And that we cannot do without seeing Mr. Chorley and know exactly what he has paid.— Dr. Adams: Is that a business we have a right to ?—Alder- man KEAN though if any explanation was necessary that it could be obtained.—la reply to Alderman Kean, Mr. TUNSTALL stated that the last precept, made in October, amounted to £4308 lOs 83.—Dr. MACK-IN said that was be- fore the call for the river survey was known about.—A conversation ensued as to the classification of the rates, Alderman KELN remarking that they, as overseers, had nothing to do with anything but the peor's rate.--Mr. TUNSTALL said they made one rate only, but that included items for other rates, and the whole rate was called the poor's rate.—Mr. HARRISON supposed the peer rate proper only comprised about a third of the amount.—Mr. TUN- STALL stated they would require 7d in the Z. for the poor rate proper, 9ad for the borough rate (he could not say what that consisted of), id county rate. and Id..for the overseers' expenses. For the rural portion,of the township they would require a poor rate of 7d, the same as-in the borough; county rate id, sanitary rate id, school attend- ance expeases id, and overseers' expenses },d, making one cost Is:6d,..and the other 9d. In the cormsponding:half of last year the poor's rate proper was Bd, whilst now it was 7d.—Dr. Mims observed that,that was-an absolate reduc— tion so ftr,as they were concerned, but the total rate was 2d more than last half year,.. but the rise wan due to the borougle, requirements. If it had been shown that they were asked foz-£.2,000 for the Ship Canal scheme, he should have gone into the matter and emleavoured to have had it over- haulede—Mr. HARRISON then moved, and Dr. MACKIE seconded, that a rate of fid in the borough and, 9d out- side Is made.—Agreed to.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
_ REPORTED SAFETY OF HICKS PACHA.

A Cairo telegram of yesterday's date says :—The Khedive this morning received a telegram from the Mudlr of Don- gola re-asserting that Hicks Pacha was quite safe at Birket about November 15th, and that his communications had been cut off by the Gawama tribe. The intelligence was derived from the Kowaweer tribe. The Mudir adds that the news was generally credited by the Bedouins at Debbe.

DIABOLICAL ATTEMPT TO WRECK A MANCHESTER EXPRESS. Yesterday, at the Prescot Police Court, before Mr. W. L. Evans, Daniel Clifford. a middle-aged man, was charged'on remand with having placed two obstructions on the Che- shire Lines Railway, between Halewood and Hough Green, on the night of the 28th November. Mr. Harper, of Man- chester, prosecuted. The particulars of the offence have already been given.—Among the witnesses examined was May Helsby, wife of James Helsby, who ;formerly, lived next door to the prisoner, and who stated that on going into his house one afternoon about two years and a half ago (prisoner having then had a dispute with Mr. Thompson, a stationmaster), she found him sitting with a report on the table, and he said to her, "Do you see what I am doing ? " She replied 'No," upon which he said, "Well, it is a report against Mr. Thompson," and he added, "If ever I get sacked I will do the company one either one time or the other."—Frederick Simpson, an insi3ector of police in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, said the prisoner had been discharged on the 25th June this year from the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and he had also been since discharged from two other employments. Wit- ness also spoke as to the arrest of the prisoner at his resi- dence. Walton-on-the-Hill, *hen he denied having been on the railway on the 28th ult.—Prisoner was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes, without bail.
Messrs. Jones Brothers' cotton mill at Leigh was burnt down on Thursday night. The damages are estimated at £30,000.

The Gazette of last night publishes the Royal proclama- tion summoning Parliament to meet for the despatch of business on Tuesday, sth February. It is stated that an important step is about to be taken ' to bring about the complate reorganisation of the Royal Artillery by re-establishing the field artillery depots which I were abolished on the introduction of the present brigade ! system about two years ago. BIRTH AT A RAILWAY STATION.-A young woman gave birth to a child in the waiting-room at Over Darwen railway station on Thursday afternoon. The only person near at the time was Georg.° Sutton, an out porter, who for many years was foreman porter as the station. He fetched assist- tance, and had both mother and child removed to a neigh- bouring house. _

BIIRLARY AT A POLICE STATioN.—During Thursday night tliives broke into Upper Gornall Police Station, and took several joints of pork from a pig which had been killed by the officer in charm 9f the station. At the time the ttur- glary was committed the officers were out on duty. It is believed that the burglary was committed as a practical joke. _ _

At a meeting of the Central Committee of the North and North-East Lancashire Cotton Spinners and Manufacturers, held yesterday, at Manchester, it was resolved to hold meet- ings of employers at Preston, Burnley, and Accrington, to consider the advisability of working short time in order to effectual support to employers in places where men still refuse to come to terms.

SUPPOSED SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.—On the arrival of the 10-30 a.m. train at Hammersmith, yesterday, a middle-aged man was found in a third-class carriage with his throat cut, and he died shortly a..,er being removed to the hospital. He was well dressed, and had a gold watch and chain. and some money, including gold, in his posses- sion. It is presumed he committed suicide. DISTURBANCES AMONGST SCOTCH FISHERMEN.—Her Majesty's ship Jackal left her moorings in Rothesay Bay yesterday, at half-past twelve, in order to proceed to Loch Houra where some disturbances are going on among the fishermen. The Jackal's tender, Daisy, has been there over a week, but the pressure of the larger ship is likely to have some more effect. The cause of the disturbance is unknown.

SWINDLING THE DUKE OF EDINDURGII.—At the Old Bailey, yesterday, Mina Jury, one of the witnesses in the Tiehborne trial, was convicted of having unlawfully ob- tained £5 from the Earl of Kilmorey and £l5 from the Duke of Edinburgh. She made representations that she was in Alexandria at the time of the siege, and last her husband and all her property. She was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour.
